item.title: Remarks At Beer Institute Annual Membership Meeting, CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig, Washington, DC | November 13, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. Thank you to the Beer Institute for bringing us all together today. I’d also like to thank the President and CEO of the Beer Institute, Brian Crawford, and Chairman of the Board of Directors, Rahul Goyal, for all their work on behalf of brewers across our Nation.

Before I provide my remarks, I must note that the views I share today are my own as Chairman and don’t necessarily reflect those of the Commission.

I appreciate the opportunity to speak with you all about an issue that plays a crucial role in American manufacturing, supports over 870,000 jobs,[1] and defines the cost of doing businesses in this country.

In March, at the Futures Industry Association’s annual conference, I highlighted my commitment to bringing base metals and critical minerals markets back to the United States, decreasing reliance on foreign nations, and diversifying reference pricing[2]. When it comes to pricing and warehousing, the U.S. must define its own destiny. And I’m pleased to be here to update you on our progress thus far.

Aluminum is an American Industrial Priority

Aluminum is one of the most important industrial materials in the modern economy. It’s essential to transportation, construction, infrastructure, defense, aerospace, and of course, beer. That last one is critically important to everyone here today.

But when we talk about the price of aluminum, we need to distinguish between the global price of the metal and the price an American business pays to obtain it. The London Metal Exchange, or LME, provides a widely used global benchmark for aluminum. The benchmark remains important, but the contract’s “cheapest-to-deliver" structure means its price can reflect metal in the lowest cost eligible delivery location, rather than supply and demand conditions or the whole cost of securing physical metal in the U.S.

To domestic beer producers, the LME benchmark is only part of the cost of securing physical aluminum. An additional charge, known as the “Midwest premium,” is added to that benchmark to reflect delivery into the United States. That premium, which is an assessment made by the firm S&P Global, has become an increasingly significant component of producers’ aluminum cost.

According to S&P Global Commodity Insights, the Midwest premium is assessed at about $1.10 per pound. With the LME benchmark at $1.40 per pound, adding the Midwest premium brings the all in U.S. price to approximately $2.50 – an additional 75% cost on top of the benchmark.

That illustrates the concern for American aluminum consumers. The LME benchmark is anchored to a cheapest-to-deliver structure, while U.S. buyers pay an additional Midwest premium to secure physical metal. Yet the combined price does not necessarily reflect where their aluminum originates, or the costs actually incurred in delivering it. Metal sourced in Canada or the UAE need not pass through an Asian warehouse, and a standardized premium does not distinguish each shipment’s transportation costs or tariff treatment. The concern is that American manufacturers, including our beer producers, can face prices incorporating costs that do not reflect their actual supply chains – through a benchmark structure poorly aligned with the U.S physical market.

I know the Beer Institute and U.S. manufacturers have been raising these concerns for years without meaningful action by the Commission. Under my leadership at the CFTC, we intend to change that. I have directed my global markets team to examine these pricing mechanisms and develop concrete reform options that protect U.S. markets and American manufacturers. This is one of my top priorities as Chairman, and I invite everyone in this audience to participate in those discussions with my staff. With your support and cooperation, if we are successful, you’ll never have to hear the words “Midwest premium” ever again.

The CFTC’s Role

Now, the CFTC doesn’t set the price of aluminum. We don’t determine how much metal is produced, what it costs to transport, or how global supply and demand evolve.

Our responsibility is to oversee a nearly $600 trillion notional derivatives market and foster this market to be competitive, transparent, and financially sound. We also work to protect market participants from fraud, manipulation, and abusive practices.

In that capacity, we can examine whether the derivatives market infrastructure available to American businesses is meeting their needs. One area worth our time, in my opinion, is whether additional U.S.-based aluminum contracts could improve local price discovery and give commercial end users more effective hedging options. But launching a contract alone is not sufficient. That contract can only be useful if businesses actually participate. It needs liquidity from producers, consumers, and other market participants. That’s why industry engagement is so important – so we can hear concerns, and opportunities, for all stakeholders.

Our engagement with agricultural markets offers a useful parallel.

Over the course of the past year, I reconvened the Commission’s Agricultural Advisory Committee and Agricultural Commodity Futures Conference to hear directly from market participants about risk management, access to capital, and developments in agricultural derivatives.

The broader lesson applies to aluminum as well: market infrastructure works best when it’s informed by the needs of the people who depend on it. I plan to take the same approach to industrial metals.

Recycled Aluminum

We should also consider the role of recycled aluminum.

Recycling is a major part of the domestic aluminum supply chain. It recovers valuable material and generally requires substantially less energy than producing primary aluminum from ore. For the beverage industry, used cans can become the raw material for new cans, which supports a domestic recycling loop.

But recycled aluminum is not a complete substitute for every form of primary metal. Scrap must still be collected, sorted, processed, and transported. Different grades of scrap have different uses, and some applications require additional processing or primary aluminum.

Recyclers and manufacturers therefore face many of the same fundamental challenges: input costs, price volatility, and uncertainty about the value of the material they buy or sell. One of my goals is to strengthen this derivatives market by working closely with various stakeholders to develop a derivatives market structure specifically for recycled aluminum. While better risk-management tools cannot solve every supply chain problem, particularly in a market for recycled product, they can help businesses manage price exposure and make investment decisions with greater confidence.

Consider a manufacturer that uses aluminum every day. It may be able to hedge movements in the global benchmark, but if the regional premium rises sharply, the manufacturer can still face a significant increase in its actual cost of delivered physical metal. That leaves businesses exposed to a risk that can be difficult to manage.

A useful market needs credible price information, and it needs enough participation to support reliable price discovery. It also needs contracts that allow commercial users to transfer the risks they face. If businesses cannot effectively hedge the difference between the global price and the price of physical metal delivered to their market, we should ask if additional tools could help.

That brings me to my broader question: should American businesses have more options for discovering and managing the price of aluminum delivered in the United States?

London has played an important role in global metals markets for decades. Recognizing that role does not mean we should assume that the existing market structure is the only structure worth considering.

The U.S. has deep financial markets, sophisticated exchanges, and extensive experience developing derivatives that serve commercial end users. Our Treasury and agricultural futures markets demonstrate what effective market infrastructure can accomplish. These markets help participants discover prices, transfer risk, and make decisions about production, investment, and financing.

Businesses should have access to markets that reflect their commercial needs, not simply be expected to adapt to whatever tools happen to be available. For aluminum, that means examining whether a U.S.-based contract tied to physical delivery in the American market could provide a useful additional benchmark or a more effective way to hedge regional price exposure.

Tokenization

Now, tokenization is another area that the CFTC spends a lot of time thinking about. When most folks in this room hear the word “tokenization” or “blockchain” they likely think of crypto assets like bitcoin or ether. But tokenization is much broader than native crypto assets. Real-world assets, such as U.S. Treasurys, are also quickly moving from standard electronic warrant systems to being issued on blockchain networks. There’s even been experimentation tokenizing agricultural commodities, like cattle, and energy products. Going forward, I see ample opportunities for tokenization to provide innovative ways to address warehousing and collateral frictions – maybe even for some of the folks in this room.

For example, frictions in warehousing could fall as settlement becomes near instantaneous and lot sizes can be customized. No longer will a small warehouser be forced to purchase lot sizes that exceed their capacity. Nor will they have to wait several days for settlement, which would otherwise increase holding costs. Furthermore, auditable warranting made available through tokenization and blockchain networks could improve efficiency and transparency in warehousing, reducing the overall cost of doing business.

We at CFTC recognize that this technological transition is happening quickly. Moving from an ingrained market structure to another entirely new way of doing business can be jarring. And this is why we want to hear from you on how to get this technological transition done right. We cannot stop technological change by looking away from it. Instead, I hope that many of you in this room will help ensure that it develops in a way that best serves American markets and market participants.

Competition is Necessary

Across the Trump administration, we’re focused on strengthening American industry and reducing unnecessary barriers to economic growth.

We have also prioritized fighting unfair trade practices which benefit foreign producers, while revitalizing domestic production of aluminum and other metals. These efforts are critical to ensuring a strong, durable domestic aluminum sector.

The success of domestic manufacturing depends on whether businesses can obtain inputs at competitive prices, plan around their costs, and make investments without taking on risks they cannot reasonably manage.

For example, a beverage can manufacturer that can better hedge its aluminum costs will be in a stronger position to plan production. A recycler with better tools to manage price exposure will be better able to evaluate an investment. And a brewer with more predictable packaging costs will have greater flexibility to invest in its workforce, facilities, and products.

Those outcomes are not necessarily guaranteed by a new derivatives contract, but well-functioning markets can help businesses make better decisions and compete more effectively.

That’s why we should be willing to challenge the status quo when the evidence suggests that existing arrangements may not be serving commercial users as well as they could. If an existing benchmark serves the market well, it should be able to demonstrate that value. If another venue can offer a better product, commercial users should have the opportunity to choose it.

Ultimately, the CFTC’s role is not to pick winners or losers. It’s to maintain market integrity and ensure that the rules don’t unnecessarily stand in the way of fair competition and responsible innovation within derivatives markets.

*         *         *

The U.S. has built world-leading financial markets by allowing competition, encouraging innovation, and insisting that markets serve real economic needs.

We can, and should, bring that same discipline to the markets that support American manufacturing.

Thank you.

[1] New jobs report shows strength, resiliency of U.S. aluminum industry | the Aluminum Association. (2026, June 10). Aluminum.Org. https://www.aluminum.org/news/new-jobs-report-shows-strength-resiliency-us-aluminum-industry

[2] Chairman Michael Selig. Remarks at FIA Global Cleared Market Conference Remarks at FIA Global Cleared Markets Conference | CFTC (Mar. 2026).

item.title: CFTC Files Lawsuit Against Arkansas As The Agency Defends Its Federal Jurisdiction Over Prediction Markets
item.content:encoded:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today announced that it has filed a lawsuit against Arkansas to block the state’s attempts to halt event-contract trading and impose up to hundreds of millions of dollars in civil penalties on CFTC-registered exchanges. 

Arkansas is bringing a civil enforcement against Kalshi in state court, a CFTC-designated contract market. Arkansas’s efforts to obstruct the functions of CFTC-registered exchanges operating lawfully under the Commodity Exchange Act are preempted by federal law. 

“As prediction markets continue to prove their value in being useful for risk management and providing the public with valuable information about the future, Arkansas seeks to shut down event contracts ranging from sports and politics to other important world events,” said Chairman Michael S. Selig. “The CFTC will continue to defend its sole jurisdiction over these federally regulated markets as granted by Congress under the Commodity Exchange Act, and the Commission will not let state interference thwart its regulatory efforts and destroy federally regulated markets.” 

Arkansas is the 11th state the CFTC has sued to vindicate federal sovereign interests. The CFTC has also submitted amicus briefs in four federal Courts of Appeal and one state Supreme Court.

RELATED LINKS

item.title: Statement On Proposing Release For Executive Compensation Disclosure Reform, SEC Commissioner Mark T. Uyeda, Nov. 13, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Twenty years have passed since the Commission’s last comprehensive evaluation of executive compensation in 2006.[1] Since then, the Commission has added to that framework on a piecemeal basis. For example, Title IX of the Dodd-Frank Act directed the Commission to adopt a series of new disclosure and governance requirements—say-on-pay, pay ratio, pay-versus-performance, and clawback rules among them.[2] In implementing the Dodd-Frank mandates, the Commission took these requirements up one at a time, through separate rulemakings, without stepping back to consider how they would function together within the broader Item 402 of Regulation S-K framework.

Last year’s Executive Compensation Roundtable made clear that this accumulation has come at a cost: disclosure that is increasingly duplicative, costly to produce, and in some instances only loosely tied to what a reasonable investor actually needs to make an informed investment or voting decision. That is, the executive compensation framework is at times both costly and ineffective—the worst regulatory outcome.[3] Today’s proposal reflects the discussion at the Roundtable and other feedback received by the Commission and its staff.[4]

The objective of our proposal has not changed from the Commission’s longstanding goal: find the “best methods for communicating clear, concise and meaningful information about executive and director compensation and relationships with the company.”[5] With this proposal, the Commission takes a step toward untangling and streamlining an executive compensation disclosure framework that has, for decades, grown by accretion rather than design. Too often the focus has been on adding granular line items rather than evaluating whether the overall structure is cohesive and rational. In other words, we have missed the forest for the trees.

The proposed amendments would refocus disclosures on the principal executive officer (PEO) and principal financial officer (PFO), aiming to reduce unnecessary complexity and volume,[6] while aligning reporting with the individuals most critical to the success or failure of the enterprise. It also proposes to streamline and rationalize the tabular disclosure requirements, replacing the current array of tables with three clearer, comprehensible tables: the Earned Compensation Table, the Granted Compensation Table, and the Status of Equity Awards Table. Another goal of today’s proposal is to simplify the Compensation Discussion and Analysis (CD&A) to emphasize material, principles-based information, and eliminate boilerplate and immaterial repetition.

These proposed modernizations aim to provide registrants with greater flexibility to tailor disclosures to their compensation programs, while ensuring that investors receive the information most relevant to their investment and voting decisions. Finally, the proposal seeks to re-evaluate whether the rules implemented pursuant to the Dodd-Frank Act mandates can be improved. It satisfies the statutory intent without taking overexpansive interpretations resulting in confusing or irrelevant disclosure while imposing additional compliance costs that are borne by the shareholders.

At its core, this proposal is intended to re-anchor executive compensation disclosure to financial and business materiality rather than to special interest group opinions about whether pay levels are appropriate. The Commission’s role is to ensure investors have the material information they need to evaluate compensation decisions, not to shape or influence those compensation decisions themselves.

History counsels caution about using securities law disclosure as a means of regulating executive compensation. In the 1990s, Congress attempted to curb executive pay indirectly, by limiting the tax deductibility of CEO salaries above $1 million. The effort backfired: rather than constraining pay, it accelerated the shift toward equity-based compensation that has defined executive pay structures ever since. Former Chairman Christopher Cox later observed that this episode deserves “pride of place in the Museum of Unintended Consequences.”[7]

The lesson extends beyond tax policy. Disclosure requirements crafted to influence compensation levels, rather than to inform investment and voting decisions, risk producing the same kind of result—a rule aimed at one outcome that instead entrenches another.

I thank the staff of the Divisions of Corporation Finance, Investment Management, and Economic and Risk Analysis as well as the Offices of the General Counsel and the Chief Accountant for their work on this proposal.

[1] Executive Compensation and Related Person Disclosure, Release No. 33-8732A (Aug. 29, 2006) [71 FR 53158 (Sept. 8, 2006)] (“2006 Executive Compensation Release”).

[2] Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, Pub. L. No. 111-203, 124 Stat. 1376 (2010).

[3] Mark T. Uyeda, Remarks at the SEC Speaks Conference 2022 (Sept. 9, 2022), available at https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/uyeda-speech-sec-speaks-090922.

[4] Executive Compensation Disclosure Reform, Release Nos. 33-11455; 34-106873, available at https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/proposed/2026/33-11455.pdf.

[5] 2006 Executive Compensation Release, 71 Fed. Reg. at 53160.

[6] For instance, to determine the three individuals who are the most highly-compensated non-PEO/PFO named executive officers, it is often necessary to calculate summary compensation calculations for a much larger group of individuals in order to identify the top three.

[7] Christopher Cox, Chairman, U.S. Sec. & Exch. Comm’n, Testimony Concerning Options Backdating, Before the U.S. Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs (Sept. 6, 2006), available at https://www.sec.gov/news/testimony/2006/ts090606cc.htm.

item.title: Statement On Proposing Release For Executive Compensation Disclosure Reform, Paul S. Atkins, SEC Chairman, Nov. 13, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Today, the Commission proposed amendments to its executive compensation disclosure requirements contained in Item 402 of Regulation S-K. These amendments reflect a comprehensive reform of Item 402 that, together with other previously proposed actions, are central tenets of my agenda and focus on transforming the SEC’s public company disclosure regime to one rooted in materiality.

During each of my prior two tours of duty at the agency, the Commission amended Item 402. First, in 19921 when I served as Chief of Staff to Chairman Richard C. Breeden, and then again in 20062 when I served as a Commissioner. These prior amendments reflected a recognition that the Commission’s rules for executive compensation disclosure require periodic updating to reflect developments in how companies compensate executives and how investors use compensation information to make investment and voting decisions.

Unfortunately, the last time the Commission comprehensively reviewed Item 402 was twenty years ago with the 2006 amendments. Since then, the rule has become bloated—reaching nearly the end of the alphabet in its internal organizational system—through the addition of both congressionally-mandated requirements and discretionary rulemaking for nuanced issues. Not surprisingly, this accumulation over the past twenty years without a comprehensive retrospective review has resulted in a disclosure regime that no longer clearly informs investors of material aspects of companies’ executive compensation decisions.

With the benefit of input from more than 80 comment letters received from investors, companies, and advisors in connection with the SEC’s roundtable on executive compensation in July 2025,3 today’s proposal aims to elicit more informative disclosure rooted in materiality. As the Supreme Court has stated, materiality is an objective standard based on the reasonable investor.4 The standard does not look to capture information that a particular investor is curious to know or would like to have as a datapoint, especially if there is not a substantial likelihood that the datapoint significantly alters the total mix of information for an investment or voting decision.5

As applied to executive compensation disclosure, a panelist at last year’s roundtable aptly analogized current Item 402 to an ice cream parlor that carries rum raisin and maple walnut; flavors desired by only a single customer.6 The proposed amendments would, if adopted, revise Item 402 to focus on an objective standard regarding needs of the reasonable investor, rather than on the specialized tastes of a specific investor.

Furthermore, the proposal would amend Item 402 to elicit information that clearly informs investors of when compensation is first granted and then ultimately earned, through tabular disclosure focused on the most common elements of compensation—salary, bonus, and equity. At the same time, amended Item 402’s principles-based and materiality-centric approach would reduce costs to companies and provide them with more agency when crafting compensation disclosure.

Of course, Item 402 includes disclosure mandated by Congress, such as the Dodd-Frank Act’s requirements for golden parachutes, pay versus performance, pay ratio, and clawbacks.7 With respect to these rules, today’s amendments aim to reduce compliance burdens for companies while remaining faithful to the congressional mandate. This approach reflects my regulatory philosophy of prescribing the minimum effective dose of regulation.

In the context of my overall policy agenda, today’s proposal represents the second of three pillars aimed at transforming the Commission’s public company disclosure regime. This past May, the Commission proposed amendments that would, if adopted, create two categories of public companies, with appropriately calibrated disclosure for each category.8 Today’s proposal signifies the beginning of the next phase of transformation—revising the specific disclosure requirements themselves, starting with the executive compensation portion of Regulation S-K. Looking ahead, Commission staff is making great strides toward recommendations for the final stage of the transformation, which is to reform the business, risk, and governance requirements of Regulation S-K.

***

I look forward to receiving and reviewing the public’s feedback on today’s proposal. Thank you to the following members of the Commission staff for their innovative ideas for, and dedication to, this consequential proposal.

Division of Corporation Finance: Jim Moloney, Sebastian Gomez Abero, Christina Thomas, Luna Bloom, Valian Afshar, Steven Hearne, Amanda Ravitz, Dennis Hermreck, Joshua Gorsky, Jessica Ansart, Dillon Hagius, Doris Stacey Gama, Michael Seaman, Lisa McCann, Jenny Choi, Melissa Raminpour, Diane Marciano, Ethan Horowitz, Jessica Barberich, Tiffany Posil, Michael Coco, Robert Errett, and Todd Canali.

Division of Investment Management: Brian Johnson, Pamela Ellis, and Angela Mokodean.

Division of Economic and Risk Analysis: Joshua White, Oliver Richard, Amy Edwards, Tara Bhandari, Mahdi Mohseni, Lyndon Orton, Lauren Moore, Charles Woodworth, Samantha Croffie, Matthew Pacino, Julie Marlowe, Paul Yin, and Michael Pessin.

Office of the General Counsel: J. Russell McGranahan, Bryant Morris, Dorothy McCuaig, David Russo, Cynthia Bien, Brooks Shirey, and Rebecca Orban.

Office of the Chief Accountant: Kurt Hohl, Shehzad Niazi, Patrick Foley, Sheri York, Gaurav Hiranandani, Greg Hillson, Ginni Fritz, and Sarah Esquivel.

  • 1Executive Compensation Disclosure, Release No. 33-6962 (Oct. 16, 1992) [57 FR 48126 (Oct. 21, 1992)], available at https://archives.federalregister.gov/issue_slice/1992/10/21/48122-48159.pdf#page=4.
  • 2Executive Compensation and Related Person Disclosure, Release No. 33-8732A (Aug. 29, 2006) [71 FR 53158 (Sept. 8, 2006)], available at https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2006/09/08/06-6968/executive-compensation-and-related-person-disclosure.
  • 3SEC Roundtable on Executive Compensation Disclosure Requirements, available at https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/meetings-events/sec-roundtable-executive-compensation-disclosure-requirements.
  • 4TSC Industries, Inc. v. Northway, Inc., 426 U.S. 438, 445 (1976) (“The question of materiality, it is universally agreed, is an objective one, involving the significance of an omitted or misrepresented fact to a reasonable investor.”).
  • 5Id. at 449 (“What the [materiality] standard does contemplate is a showing of a substantial likelihood that, under all the circumstances, the omitted fact would have assumed actual significance in the deliberations of the reasonable shareholder. Put another way, there must be a substantial likelihood that the disclosure of the omitted fact would have been viewed by the reasonable investor as having significantly altered the ‘total mix’ of information made available.”).
  • 6Unofficial Transcript: SEC Roundtable on Executive Compensation Disclosure Requirements Panel (July 26, 2025) at page 76, available at https://www.sec.gov/files/sec-roundtable-executive-compensation-disclosure-requirements-2025-06-26-transcript.pdf.
  • 7See Pub. L. No. 111-203, 124 Stat. 1376 (2010), sections 951, 953(a), 953(b), and 954.
  • 8Enhancement of Emerging Growth Company Accommodations and Simplification of Filer Status for Reporting Companies, Release No. 34-105515 (May 19, 2026) [91 FR 30086 (May 21, 2026)], available at https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/21/2026-10222/enhancement-of-emerging-growth-company-accommodations-and-simplification-of-filer-status-for.

item.title: SEC Proposes Executive And Director Compensation Disclosure Reforms
item.content:encoded:
The Securities and Exchange Commission today proposed rule amendments to make its executive and director compensation disclosure requirements more principles-based and materiality-driven, providing investors with clearer, more concise, and less complex disclosures. The proposal follows the Commission’s review of its executive and director compensation disclosure requirements, including a request for public comment and a roundtable discussion with representatives from public companies, investors, and other experts in this field. This proposal builds on Chairman Atkins’ efforts to reduce friction for companies looking to join and remain in our public markets.

The proposal would refocus these disclosures—last comprehensively reformed in 2006—on material information and improve investors’ ability to track equity awards through their lifecycle. The proposed amendments aim to reduce compliance burdens for registrants where there is not commensurate benefit for investors and would provide registrants with more flexibility to present their disclosures in a way that is consistent with how compensation programs are constructed today and better represents the intention of their boards of directors and compensation committees.

“Today, the Commission proposed amendments to its executive compensation disclosure requirements contained in Item 402 of Regulation S-K. These amendments reflect a comprehensive reform of Item 402 that, together with other previously proposed actions, are central tenets of my agenda and focus on transforming the SEC’s public company disclosure regime to one rooted in materiality,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins in a statement. “With the benefit of input from more than 80 comment letters received from investors, companies, and advisors in connection with the SEC’s roundtable on executive compensation in July 2025, today’s proposal aims to elicit more informative disclosure rooted in materiality.”

The proposed amendments to Item 402 of Regulation S-K would permit registrants to tailor disclosure in a way that provides greater transparency regarding the registrant’s compensation practices and is more efficient for investors to read and understand. In support of these goals, the proposed changes would, among other things:

  • Revise the named executive officers to encompass the principal executive officer and principal financial officer—the positions whose compensation are generally most material for investors due to their roles in managing a registrant’s most consequential matters—thereby reducing the number of named executive officers from typically five or more individuals under the current rule to two in most circumstances.
  • Modify the primary executive compensation tabular disclosure requirements into three new tables (Earned Compensation Table, Granted Compensation Table, and Status of Equity Awards Table) with accompanying narratives that would replace the primary four tables required under the current rule. The proposed changes would retain material information required under the current tabular disclosure framework but would seek to streamline and clarify the presentation.
  • Raise the minimum aggregate reporting threshold for perquisites from $10,000 to $150,000 and introduce a new de minimis tracking exclusion. The proposed amendments would retain disclosure of material perquisites for investors while reducing compliance burdens for registrants.
  • Revise the Commission’s interpretive guidance regarding perquisites to give registrants more flexibility to make the determination of whether a benefit is a perquisite, so long as the determination is reasonable and made in good faith.
  • Make the Compensation Discussion and Analysis (CD&A) requirement more principles-based, require registrants to address only three topics in the CD&A, and eliminate the list of 15 example topics contained in the current rule. The proposed changes would streamline the presentation of information, reduce complexity and repetition, and focus more clearly on material information. 
  • Simplify the pay-versus-performance disclosure requirement by reducing required performance measures and replacing the complex “Compensation Actually Paid” calculation with the total compensation earned amount from the proposed Earned Compensation Table. The proposed changes would continue to satisfy the statutory mandate of the Dodd-Frank Act while simplifying disclosure requirements.
  • Limit the population used in the determination of “median employee” under the pay ratio rule to U.S. full-time employees and reduce the required frequency of the determination to every five years.
  • Eliminate required check boxes from the cover pages of annual reports and certain potentially redundant disclosure requirements regarding the application of a registrant’s clawback policy that overly burden registrants without eliciting material information for investors. The underlying mechanics of a registrant’s clawback process would remain unchanged.

The public comment period will remain open for 60 days following publication of the proposing release in the Federal Register.

Resources

  • Proposed Rule
  • Fact Sheet

item.title: LuxSE Welcomes Angola's First Sustainability Bond - Banco Angolano De Investimentos And The Luxembourg Stock Exchange Mark A Milestone With The Display Of Angola’s Inaugural Sustainability Bond On The Luxembourg Green Exchange
item.content:encoded:
During an official Ring the Bell ceremony held at the Luxembourg Stock Exchange (LuxSE), representatives from Banco Angolano de Investimentos (BAI), Bolsa de Dívida e Valores de Angola (BODIVA), Comissão do Mercado de Capitais (CMC) and LuxSE came together to celebrate the admission of BAI's AOA 57.5 billion (approximately EUR 56 million) inaugural sustainability bond on LuxSE and its display on the Luxembourg Green Exchange (LGX).

As the first sustainability bond issued by an Angolan entity, the transaction marks a significant milestone for both BAI and Angola's capital markets. It represents an important step in the development of the country's sustainable finance market and highlights the growing role of capital markets in mobilising funding for projects that support economic diversification and sustainable development objectives.

"We are delighted to welcome BAI to the Luxembourg Stock Exchange with the admission of this pioneering sustainability bond and to enhance its visibility to the global investor community via our LGX platform. As the first transaction of its kind, it marks an important milestone for Angola's capital markets and demonstrates how sustainable finance can mobilise investment towards projects that deliver both economic value and tangible social and environmental impact," said Arnaud Delestienne, Chief Commercial Officer and Member of the Executive Committee at LuxSE.

Financing sustainable growth in Angola

Initially listed and admitted to trading on the Bolsa de Dívida e Valores de Angola (BODIVA) on 22 September 2026, the bond is now also registered on LuxSE’s Securities Official List (LuxSE SOL). An amount equivalent to its net proceeds is earmarked for financing and refinancing eligible loans supporting key sectors of the Angolan economy, including agriculture, manufacturing, logistics, healthcare and pharmaceuticals, in accordance with BAI’s Sustainability Bond Framework. Aligned with six United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), namely Zero Hunger (SDG 2), Good Health and Well-being (SDG 3), Decent Work and Economic Growth (SDG 8), Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure (SDG 9), Responsible

Consumption and Production (SDG 12) and Climate Action (SDG 13), the bond reflects BAI's commitment to mobilising capital towards initiatives that generate long-term value for communities, businesses and the broader Angolan economy.

" The dual listing of the BAI Sustainability Bond on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange marks an important milestone for BAI and Angola’s capital markets. What began as a bond issued in Angola, denominated in local currency and locally listed, was structured in alignment with internationally recognised ICMA principles and attracted international investor participation. Its listing in Luxembourg now brings this Angolan financial instrument to an international stage, demonstrating that our domestic capital market can deliver sustainable financing solutions that meet global standards and attract international capital. This achievement reinforces our determination to mobilise capital towards initiatives that generate tangible economic, social and environmental impact, while contributing to a more diversified, inclusive and resilient Angolan economy. This is our commitment, our responsibility, and the future we want to help finance,” said Luís Lélis, CEO of BAI.

Strengthening Angola's sustainable finance ecosystem

The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) provided technical assistance to BAI and relevant national institutions in the development of the Sustainability Bond Framework, as part of broader efforts to strengthen Angola’s sustainable finance ecosystem and mobilise private capital for sustainable development.

“Sustainable finance can accelerate investment when domestic capital markets offer accessible opportunities to invest. Angola’s first sustainability bond combined institutional demand with a low minimum subscription, giving individual investors a route to participate while allocating finance towards several multilateral environmental agreements and eligible social priorities. With the dual listing on LuxSE and its display on LGX, it further integrates capital markets across Africa, Europe and beyond,” said Thomas Beloe, Director, UNDP Sustainable Finance Hub.

Connecting African issuers with global capital

The transaction highlights LuxSE's ongoing commitment to connecting African issuers with international investors and facilitating access to capital for projects with positive environmental and social impact.

Through the display of BAI's sustainability bond on LGX, LuxSE continues to support the growth of sustainable finance across the continent and the mobilisation of funding for resilient, inclusive and sustainable economic development.

"Today, with the admission of BAI’s sustainability bonds to the Luxembourg Stock Exchange, we celebrate a new milestone: for the first time, a bond admitted to trading on BODIVA is also admitted to trading on an international exchange. As a member of the World Federation of Exchanges, this achievement brings Angola’s capital market internationalisation agenda to life and enhances the visibility of Angolan companies and their financial instruments within the international financial community. We extend our recognition to Banco BAI for its pioneering initiative and the confidence placed in the capital market as a means of mobilising resources to finance initiatives that contribute to Angola’s economic and sustainable development. We are confident that this transaction will pave the way for other Angolan issuers to explore new financing opportunities and access international markets," commented Cristina Lourenço, CEO of BODIVA. 

" The Capital Markets Commission (CMC), the regulatory and supervisory for the capital market in Angola, participated on November 13th in the listing ceremony of BAI's Sustainable Bonds on the Luxembourg Green Exchange (LGX), a specialized segment of the Luxembourg Stock Exchange.This moment marks a significant milestone for Angola's financial sector, demonstrating the capacity of our institutions to meet international standards of transparency, governance and accountability.The presence of an Angolan issuer on the Luxembourg Green Exchange reinforces international confidence in our institutions, our regulatory framework and our economy. As an ordinary member of the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO), the CMC maintains its commitment to the principles of transparency, market integrity, investor protection and international cooperation. We will continue to strengthen our regulatory framework and align it with international standards and best practices.We are confident that BAI's achievement will encourage other Angolan issuers to follow a similar path, expanding the contribution of sustainable finance to Angola's long-term economic and social development," said Vasco Januário, Executive Board Member of CMC.

item.title: The EBA Supports The NGFS Declaration On The Macro-Financial Dimension Of The Energy Transition On The Occasion Of COP31
item.content:encoded:
​As an active member of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the European Banking Authority (EBA) welcomes the publication of the NGFS Declaration on the macro-financial dimension of the energy transition on the occasion of the 2026 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye. The Declaration highlights how energy price shocks and increasingly frequent climate-related shocks are becoming a macro-financial reality, and calls for an orderly, whole-economy transition. 

​The EBA is committed to contributing to the greening of the financial system. The EBA integrates sustainability factors into EU banking regulation, consistently with its broader objective of contributing to the stability and orderly functioning of the financial system. 

​In practice, the EBA: 

  • ​sets out how banks should identify, measure, manage and monitor ESG risks, including through scenario analysis and transition planning, in its Guidelines on the management of ESG risks and Guidelines on environmental scenario analysis;
  • ​supports effective supervision by providing guidelines for institutions and their supervisors;
  • ​improves transparency and data availability through climate-related disclosure requirements and the publication of its ESG risk dashboard. 

​The EBA also incorporates climate considerations in its assessment of risks in the EU banking sector. As announced on 9 November 2026, the 2027 EU-wide stress test will, for the first time, assess physical and transition climate risks through a dedicated module, without affecting the core stress test results. 

​François-Louis Michaud, the Chair of the EBA, said: “Climate and energy shocks are no longer a distant prospect: they are already shaping the risks banks face today. Managing them well is not a trade-off between resilience and competitiveness. Sound risk management is what allows banks to keep financing the European economy and its transition. With the first dedicated climate module in the 2027 EU-wide stress test, we are moving from principles to practice, in a way that is simple, proportionate and focused on what matters most.” 

​Note to editors 

​The Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) was launched at the Paris One Planet Summit on 12 December 2017. It brings together central banks and supervisors willing to share best practices, contribute to the development of environment and climate risk management in the financial sector, and mobilise mainstream finance to support the transition towards a sustainable economy. By the end of 2025, the NGFS counted 170 members and observers across five continents. 

​For more details, visit the NGFS website, its LinkedIn page and the NGFS 2025 Annual Report, as well as the EBA's sustainable finance section.

item.title: Mo’ Data, Mo’ Problems, Jamie Selway, Director, SEC Division Of Trading And Markets, Baruch College Conference On Trading, Liquidity, & Market Structure, New York, NY, Nov. 13, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. Bob [Schwartz], thank you for that generous introduction. It is a great pleasure to be back at Baruch College for another conference with a rich agenda that blends industry and academic perspective in expert fashion. My first panel at Baruch was in May 2004, and the conference was titled “Electronic vs. Floor Based Trading.” Venues and trading tools have clearly come a long way since then, but spirited debate on core issues – such as achieving best execution, enhancing liquidity, and promoting efficient price discovery – continues and remains vibrant today. It is a privilege to be part of today’s program.

Please understand that I speak today in my official capacity as the Commission’s Director of the Division of Trading and Markets. These remarks do not necessarily reflect the views of the Commission, the Commissioners, or my Division colleagues.

I first met Bob roughly thirty years ago, before he came to Baruch from NYU. I worked for Dean Furbush, Nasdaq’s Chief Economist, who set up a meeting to discuss one of Bob’s favorite topics: call markets. At the time, Nasdaq did not have a formal process to open or close its market, and Dean wanted to explore the idea of an electronic auction. (Nasdaq would go on to launch opening and closing crosses in January and April 2004, respectively.)

The meeting took place in Lower Manhattan on a Fall night. In addition to Dean, Bob, and me, three or four heads of major Nasdaq trading desks joined, as well as Steve Wunsch, founder of the Arizona Stock Exchange, an early call market. The discussion was ultimately inconclusive and exposed the wide gap between theory and practice. But everyone came away a bit smarter. I’ll never forget Bob explaining to the group that it was “well-known” that market orders are simply limit orders to buy at infinity or sell at zero. I’m not sure what the Wall Street folks thought, but the elegance and importance of theory in market design made a deep impression on me.

In addition to Bob and Baruch’s Center for Trading and Financial Markets Research, another academic setting with profound influence on industry was built by Hans Stoll. Hans taught at Vanderbilt University and was the first to formulate options put-call parity.1In 1987, he started the Financial Market Research Center, which held an annual conference for many years. Bill Christie and Paul Schultz sparked controversy, and then fundamental reform, in the Nasdaq marketplace by presenting research on quoting behavior at Hans’ conference in 1995. As with Baruch, Vanderbilt’s conference was a valued forum for industry and academia to discuss and debate important and timely market issues. Unfortunately, Dean, Steve, and Hans are no longer with us. But programs like today’s conference keep their influence and spirit alive and meaningful.

Policy makers also benefit from the results of rigorous engagement between academics and practitioners. Commissioner Michael Piwowar served our agency from August 2013 to July 2018, including a stint as Acting Chairman. He is one of three Commissioners in our history to be a Ph.D. economist. On the role of economists and lawyers at the SEC, he noted:

“Good law and good economics are twin pillars of a healthy society. Both tend to promote efficient outcomes. Both modes of analysis are at their best when they hew closely to evidence and faithfully employ deductive logic. And straying from these principles leads to bad economics and bad law, with negative consequences for society. Economists and lawyers are fellow travelers on the road to a freer, more prosperous world.”2

A friend tells me that Brian Armstrong, Founder and CEO of Coinbase, is fond of saying that “action produces information.” By that axiom, the dynamic pace of change of today’s markets makes the environment for novel research incredibly fertile. Trading is going 24x7. New vehicles to gain exposures, such as tokenized securities and perpetual futures, are coming to market. The upcoming implementation of central clearing in the treasury market will introduce competition. Proposals to reform core aspects of the National Market System are under consideration. Retail investors and passive managers play outsized roles relative to historical norms.

Paired with this abundance of challenging problems is a ubiquity of data. Historically, access to differentiated data was the primary constraint to original research. Now, the substantial resources needed to handle ever-growing datasets may be the bigger lift. Researchers increasingly turn to tools driven by super intelligence to answer questions.

And while our Division adds to the growing pile of interesting questions, my friend and colleague Josh White, SEC Chief Economist and Director of the Division of Economic and Risk Analysis, or “DERA,” is in the business of finding answers. In addition to spearheading the Commission’s efforts to make good use of super intelligence, Josh is reinvigorating our engagement with the academic community. In particular, he has recently restarted DERA’s Distinguished Visiting Scholars Program. I know he would welcome outreach from this community.

Thank you for your time and attention. I hope you enjoy today’s program – and find as much value from engagement with Bob and his colleagues as I have over these many years. I look forward to your questions.

  • 1Stoll, Hans R., “The Relationship Between Put and Call Option Prices,” The Journal of Finance, vol. 24(5), pages 801-824, December 1969.
  • 2SEC.gov | Reflections of an Economist Commissioner.

item.title: IOSCO SupTech Sprint Regarding The Supervision Of Digital Assets Markets
item.content:encoded:
IOSCO’s SupTech Forum initiative marked a significant milestone with the presentation of the results of its first SupTech Sprint on the Supervision of Digital Assets.

Launched in 2026, the IOSCO SupTech Forum is a collaborative initiative that promotes innovation and knowledge-sharing among securities regulators worldwide. Its inaugural year included four SupTech Spotlight Sessions and one SupTech Sprint.

To address emerging supervisory challenges in digital asset markets, the Sprint brought together policy specialists, supervisors, and technical experts from 56 IOSCO member jurisdictions. The first phase of the initiative, the Sprint Lab, was held in Zurich, Switzerland, while the second phase, the Sprint Build, was launched in Mumbai, India.

The focus of the Sprint was the Supervision of Digital Assets. Key challenges included market surveillance and AML/CFT risk supervision. Digital asset market surveillance is complicated by fragmented data across exchanges, blockchains, and jurisdictions, limiting visibility into trading activity. AML/CFT risk assessment is similarly challenging due to complex transaction structures, multiple intermediaries, and the pseudonymous nature of many digital asset activities.

From September through November 2026, two multidisciplinary sprint teams comprising members from 28 different jurisdictions worked intensively to develop practical supervisory solutions to these challenges. The teams presented the outcomes of their work to the IOSCO Board in Madrid, showcasing two innovative solutions designed to improve visibility across fragmented digital asset markets and strengthen the identification and prioritization of AML/CFT risks within complex digital asset ecosystems.

The Sprint demonstrates the value of international collaboration in addressing emerging supervisory challenges and highlights the potential of supervisory technology to strengthen oversight capabilities in rapidly evolving markets. The solutions developed during the SupTech Sprint are expected to support supervisory activities across jurisdictions around the world.

“Supervisory technology plays an increasingly vital role in helping authorities be more effective and keep pace with rapid market innovation. The SupTech Sprint showcases how international collaboration can contribute to tangible solutions to enhance oversight capabilities across jurisdictions worldwide. I would like to sincerely thank Marlene Amstad, Chair of the SupTech Forum and Chair of FINMA’s Board of Directors, and her team, as well as the IOSCO General Secretariat, and all participants for their dedication and leadership in driving this important work forward.”

Jean-Paul Servais, IOSCO Board Chair

item.title: Financial Stability In A Rapidly Changing World - Keynote Speech By FSB Chair, Andrew Bailey, At The IOSCO Conference: 25 Years Of Standard Setting From Madrid And Of Stakeholder Engagement
item.content:encoded:
Thank you for the invitation to speak to you today.

I want to discuss two of the most difficult challenges in managing systemic risk. The first is transparency: whether market participants can see and understand the risks building in the system. The second is how we identify what is, and what is not, a systemic risk.

These issues are closely connected. A risk that is visible, understood and capable of being priced may be manageable. A risk that is opaque, interconnected and poorly understood can become destabilising very quickly.

As we approach Black Friday, an exciting day for shopping markets, I want to illustrate those challenges by looking back at a less enjoyable day for financial markets: Black Monday.

Back in 1987, just four years after International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) was founded, we learnt that a lack of transparency can greatly amplify stress in a crisis. By transparency, I do not mean perfect information. Markets will always operate under uncertainty. The issue is whether material information gaps prevent participants and authorities from understanding and managing risks, particularly how stress might spread through the system.

Capital markets were becoming increasingly international and the need for cooperation among securities regulators was clear. The founding of IOSCO reflected an important insight: markets do not stop at national borders, and effective regulation cannot do so either.

IOSCO’s initial focus was on sound securities markets and protecting investors. In 2013 its mandate expanded to include systemic risk, giving transparency a new importance. IOSCO’s former Secretary General David Wright identified four enduring themes: tackling risks before they build; creating risk-identification infrastructure; addressing the data deficit; and improving cross-border enforcement and compliance. He also warned that fragmentation would be a major challenge.

IOSCO has since made solid progress, working with the Financial Stability Board, the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures and through its own Financial Stability Engagement Group. As an IOSCO Board member when FSEG was established, I have seen its importance in developing IOSCO’s perspective on systemic risk. Yet material information gaps remain.

Let me turn back to Black Monday in October 1987. The Dow fell 22.6% in a single trading session and the S&P 500 fell 20.47%. The sell-off spread across the world.

The Brady Commission, established in the United States to investigate the crash, identified inadequate cross-market information as a central problem. Activity in futures markets had driven down equity prices, yet no real-time, cross-market information or coordinated tracking mechanisms helped participants understand what was happening. Fear of the unknown intensified asset sales.

Important reforms followed, including multi-tier circuit breakers, aligned margining rules and better coordination among regulators. But cross-market dynamics remain a challenge. When participants cannot see what is happening, they fill the gap with assumptions. In stress, those assumptions are often negative. Risk becomes uncertainty, uncertainty becomes fear, and defensive behaviour produces contagion.

The same issue was evident in the failure of Lehman Brothers in 2008. Creditors ultimately recovered significantly more than market pricing at the height of the crisis suggested, and some recovered 100%. Was the market wrong to be so concerned? No. The market was right to be concerned because it could not see how serious the problem was.

The deeper lesson is the need for visibility across an interconnected financial system. Participants need to understand exposures, legal entities, collateral, contractual relationships and possible channels of contagion. Otherwise stress can spread, not necessarily because every institution is insolvent, but because no one can be confident about who is exposed to whom.

Nearly forty years after Black Monday, the sources of opacity have changed but their capacity to amplify shocks has not. Let me give two examples.

The first concerns sharp market movements following US tariff announcements in April last year. Bond markets moved significantly, but it was not immediately clear why. The spike in long-maturity US Treasury yields was unprecedented and difficult to interpret. Explanations ranged from changing inflation and growth expectations to fiscal concerns, foreign demand and the unwinding of leveraged positions.

This points to a broader vulnerability. The composition of investors in government bond markets has changed. Traditional investors such as pension funds have become less active, while hedge funds and other leveraged non-banks play a larger role. Pension funds tend to pursue longer-term strategies. Leveraged hedge funds can build and unwind exposures much faster as conditions change.

We saw the implications in the UK earlier this year. During the most significant volatility following the onset of the Middle East conflict, moves in gilt yields were amplified by hedge fund deleveraging. Net hedge fund borrowing in gilt repo markets fell by around 40% between December 2025 and mid-April 2026.

Hedge fund participation is not itself a problem and can provide liquidity in normal times. The vulnerability arises when highly leveraged positions unwind rapidly. Neither market participants nor authorities always have a sufficient picture of those positions, especially where they span borders and jurisdictions.

This is precisely what the FSB’s Nonbank Data Task Force was created to address. Its first test case focuses on leveraged trading strategies in sovereign bond markets. More broadly, it is examining how authorities can identify vulnerabilities in the non-bank sector and how better information sharing, including data, can mitigate threats to financial stability.

Cooperation between the FSB and IOSCO is essential, and I am grateful for IOSCO’s engagement. We cannot conclude that information sharing is simply too difficult. But visibility is only part of the solution. Authorities must also implement the policy measures in the FSB’s 2025 leverage recommendations.

The second example is private credit. The FSB has highlighted uncertainty about valuations, leverage, liquidity, underperforming loans, lending terms, borrower concentration and links among private credit funds, banks, insurers and other investors.

This does not mean private credit will necessarily harm the system. It means its resilience is difficult to assess when information is incomplete and assets are not continually priced or traded. The absence of visible stress should not be mistaken for the absence of risk.

Some ask why we keep looking at private credit when it is not large enough to move the global financial system. The answer is interconnectedness. It may not move the system alone, but it could be one domino in a chain reaction. Shared exposures among banks, insurers and funds could amplify a shock. If markets can imagine that possibility and lack facts to counter it, they will act on the concern.

This echoes Brady’s fear of the unknown. Contagion remains central to financial stability because a problem in one market can spread through common exposures, collateral calls, margin requirements, forced sales, liquidity withdrawals or a simple loss of confidence. That makes it dangerous to believe we can judge precisely what is, and what is not, a financial stability risk.

Global systemically important banks are not identified by size alone. Interconnectedness, complexity, cross-border activity and the difficulty of substituting for their functions also matter. Since the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank, the FSB has increasingly used the language of institutions that can be ‘systemic in failure’. This directs attention to an institution’s connections at the point of failure and how distress may transmit through the system.

An institution or market can therefore become a key risk without appearing exceptionally large. It may become a domino in a chain reaction driven by fear, and that fear may arise from a lack of transparency. We do not need certainty that something will cause a systemic problem before examining it. We need to understand its connections well enough to know what might happen if confidence disappears.

This leads to an obvious question: how large, or how connected, must private credit become before it poses a financial stability risk? Stablecoin arrangements raise similar, if distinct, questions. Timely information about reserve composition, redemption mechanisms, custody, governance and operational dependencies can be missing. The issue is not simply market capitalisation, but whether lost confidence could generate rapid redemptions or disrupt a function important to wider markets.

In each case, we must examine exposures, liquidity arrangements, counterparty concentration, substitutability and the speed at which confidence can deteriorate. Information gaps and growing interconnections mean private credit and stablecoins could become financial stability risks sooner than conventional size measures suggest. That is why forward-looking surveillance matters. We should not wait for a risk to become large before examining its potential to generate contagion.

Greater transparency is not an end in itself. It must enable authorities and market participants to form a more accurate view of where risk sits, how it is financed and how it might move. That requires information which is timely, comparable and usable across legal entities and borders. A large stock of fragmented data is not the same as a clear view of the system. The tariff episode also illustrates why explanations formed in real time can be unreliable. Some participants focused on inflation expectations; others on fiscal concerns, growth, foreign demand for US assets or leveraged unwinds. Several of those forces may operate together. Without a better view of positions and flows, authorities can see the market move without being able to distinguish a change in fundamentals from an amplification mechanism.

That distinction matters for policy. We should not seek to prevent markets from adjusting to new information. Price discovery is essential. But we should seek to prevent hidden leverage, concentrated positioning or abrupt liquidity demands from turning an orderly repricing into a destabilising spiral.

The aim is resilient market-based finance, not the elimination of market movement. Private credit presents a different version of the same challenge. The assets are less frequently traded, valuations are less observable and contractual terms vary. Risk can therefore appear subdued for longer. But delayed recognition is not the same as resilience. When credit quality deteriorates, uncertainty over valuations, financing arrangements and links to banks and insurers may cause participants to reassess several exposures at once. Stablecoins add questions about the composition and custody of reserves, the credibility of redemption mechanisms, operational dependencies and governance. A loss of confidence can move quickly because redemption incentives are immediate.

The relevant question is whether the arrangement can meet those demands without forced asset sales, disruption to payment or trading activity, or transmission to institutions performing related functions.

Across these examples, size remains relevant but is not decisive. A smaller institution or market can become systemic in failure if it performs a hard-to-replace function, is connected to many counterparties or triggers common defensive behaviour. Conversely, a large activity may be manageable where exposures are transparent, liquidity is robust and credible arrangements exist for stress. This is why surveillance must combine quantitative indicators with judgement.

Authorities need to examine leverage, liquidity, concentration, substitutability and operational dependencies; run stress analysis; compare information across sectors; and consider how confidence might change behaviour. They must also be willing to investigate plausible transmission channels before conventional indicators flash red. International cooperation is indispensable. Activities and exposures cross borders, while data and legal powers remain organised largely by jurisdiction.

Effective cooperation requires common definitions, proportionate reporting, secure mechanisms for sharing information and a willingness to resolve obstacles rather than accept them. The FSB can bring the system-wide view; IOSCO can bring deep knowledge of securities markets and their regulation. Together, they can turn fragmented information into a clearer assessment

Conclusion

Let me finish where I started, with Black Monday. The financial system today looks very different from the one that experienced the crash of 1987. But the central lesson is the same: what we cannot see can matter just as much as what we can.

In 1987, opacity about activity and exposures across markets amplified uncertainty and contagion. Today, opacity takes different forms: private markets, leverage, complex interconnections and new forms of finance. The risks did not then, and do not now, lie neatly within one market or one regulator’s remit. Understanding them requires authorities to look across markets and borders.

That is why the relationship between IOSCO and the FSB matters. IOSCO’s principles have established common expectations around regulation, supervision, cooperation and market integrity. IOSCO and the FSB have also worked together on vulnerabilities in the non-bank sector, including liquidity mismatch in open-ended funds, margining practices and leverage. The aim is to prevent stress in particular markets or institutions from being amplified across the wider financial system.

IOSCO’s work with CPMI is equally important, covering margining, clearing, recovery and the resilience of financial market infrastructures. Central clearing does not remove risk. But it can make exposures more visible, standardise risk management, improve default management and reduce uncertainty about who owes what to whom.

The relationship between IOSCO and the FSB should be complementary. IOSCO brings deep expertise in securities markets and activities; the FSB brings a system-wide perspective across sectors and jurisdictions. Together, those perspectives can help identify where risks are building and, crucially, how they might spread.

Our objective should be stronger cooperation, better information exchange and earlier consideration of emerging vulnerabilities. Financial stability is not achieved by predicting every crisis with precision. It is achieved by building markets and institutions that are sufficiently transparent, resilient and connected to competent oversight that shocks do not become unnecessary crises.

IOSCO has a central role in that effort. I look forward to continuing our work together.

item.title: HKEX To Launch Digital Payment Solution For Derivatives After-Hours Trading From December 2026
item.content:encoded:
• New digital payment solution for advance margin deposits during derivatives AHT session launches 14 December 2026
  • The extended payment time window gives eligible CPs greater payment flexibility outside regular banking hours

Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) is pleased to announce today (Friday) that its new digital payment solution for advance margin deposits during the After-Hours Trading (AHT) session in the derivatives market will launch on 14 December 2026.

The initiative builds on the announcement by HKEX and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) in June 2026 to explore the use of e-HKD – a wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC) operating on a 24/7 basis – for advance margin deposit payments in the AHT session.

At launch, eligible HKFE Clearing Corporation Limited (HKCC) Clearing Participants (CPs) will be able to use this new digital payment option to submit advance margin deposit requests from 5:00 pm to 1:30 am for funds related to the corresponding AHT session. The extended payment time window supplements existing payment arrangements and provides greater flexibility in managing their Capital Based Position Limit utilisation outside regular banking hours.

HKEX has conducted Real-Value Trial Transactions with HKMA, settlement banks and CPs to validate the technical and operational readiness ahead of the launch.

This flexible payment option will be complementary to HKEX’s planned extension of AHT trading hours from March 2027, reflecting HKEX’s continued commitment to enhance market accessibility, connectivity and operational resilience.

Registration details and further information about this initiative are available on the designated webpage and in a circular published today.

item.title: ASIC Proposes Extending Relief For Time-Sharing And ASX-Listed Schemes
item.content:encoded:
ASIC is seeking feedback on a proposal to extend relief for time-sharing schemes and on-market buy-backs by ASX-listed registered schemes for five years. 

ASIC Corporations (Time-sharing Schemes) Instrument 2017/272 (ASIC Instrument 2017/272) and ASIC Corporations (ASX-listed Schemes On-market Buy-backs) Instrument 2016/1159 (ASIC Instrument 2016/1159) will expire on 1 April 2027. 

We are proposing to remake them in substantially the same form, with any necessary technical updates.  

Providing feedback  

ASIC invites feedback on this proposal. Submissions should be sent to IM.sunsettingconsultation@asic.gov.au by 5 pm AEDT 11 December 2026.   

Background  

ASIC Instrument 2017/272 provides technical relief relating to time-sharing schemes. The relief covers matters including finance, hardship, consumer protection, disclosure of fees and property valuations.  
 
ASIC Instrument 2016/1159 allows ASX-listed registered schemes to buy back their own interests on-market, subject to safeguards for members and creditors. These include trading and disclosure requirements, cancellation of bought-back interests and member approval when specified limits are exceeded.  

Separate ASIC work is being undertaken to extend buy-back relief to schemes listed on other declared financial markets.  

Related links

CS 71 Proposed remake of relief for time-sharing schemes and on-market buy-backs by ASX-listed schemes

item.title: Leading Finance Professor Michael Weber Appointed Monetary Authority Of Singapore Term Professor At National University Of Singapore
item.content:encoded:
The National University of Singapore (NUS) and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) have jointly appointed Professor Michael Weber as the MAS Term Professor in Economics and Finance from 15 to 28 November 2026. Professor Weber will be hosted by the NUS Business School’s Department of Finance and the Economic Policy Group at MAS during the term of the Professorship.

2 Professor Weber is Professor of Finance at the Mitch Daniels School of Business, Purdue University, and at ESMT Berlin, where he serves as Academic Director of the European Expectations Center. He is an academic consultant to several central banks and policy institutions, including the Deutsche Bundesbank, the Bank for International Settlements, and the Federal Reserve Banks of Cleveland and Dallas. He is also a Research Associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) and a Research Affiliate at the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR).

3 His research spans macroeconomics, household finance, asset pricing and international finance, with a particular focus on how economic expectations shape the decisions of households and firms. His work has appeared in leading economics and finance journals, including the American Economic Review, Econometrica and the Journal of Political Economy. In 2026, he received the Alexander von Humboldt Professorship, Germany’s most highly endowed research prize.

4 Professor Teo Chung Piaw, Dean of NUS Business School, said, “Professor Weber’s research deepens our understanding of how people make economic decisions—how everyday price experiences shape their expectations, and how uncertainty influences their spending. By combining rich data with carefully designed experiments, his work connects fundamental economic questions with issues that matter to businesses and society. We look forward to the fresh perspectives and opportunities for collaboration that his visit will bring to our faculty and students at NUS Business School.”

5 Mr Edward Robinson, Deputy Managing Director (Economic Policy) and Chief Economist, MAS, said, “Professor Weber’s research offers important insights into how households perceive inflation, form expectations and make everyday economic decisions. His work is particularly relevant to central banks which seek deeper understanding into expectation formations and effective communications with the public. We are pleased to engage with Professor Weber again following his participation in the 10th Asian Monetary Policy Forum in 2023, and look forward to further exchanges on the implications of his research for monetary policy. It is our great privilege to welcome him as the 27th MAS Term Professor.”

6 Professor Weber will deliver a public lecture at NUS on 17 November 2026 titled, "Subjective Expectations: Models meet Reality”. He will also give a seminar at MAS and engage senior policymakers and economists on issues in household inflation expectations, monetary policy and central bank communication.

item.title: ASIC And APRA Release Final Guidance To Streamline FAR Reporting
item.content:encoded:
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) and the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) have finalised changes to simplify reporting under the Financial Accountability Regime (FAR).  

The changes follow strong industry support for reducing unnecessary administration. Following consultation, the regulators have finalised the removal of: 

  • the requirement to report key functions for the FAR register; and 
  • the need for accountability maps to identify who reports directly to an accountable person. 

Together, these changes provide meaningful relief to regulated entities, with APRA and ASIC estimating they will reduce reporting requirements for all accountable entities and approximately 4,500 accountable people, while halving the number of updates to accountability maps. 

The changes will take effect from today. The accountability obligations of FAR-regulated entities and accountable persons will remain unchanged.  

ASIC Commissioner Kate O’Rourke said the feedback reinforced the benefits of simplifying FAR administration.  

“Industry strongly supported these changes, which will reduce unnecessary reporting while maintaining clear accountability,” Ms O’Rourke said.  

“We are proceeding with the reforms as proposed, delivering on our commitment to simpler regulation and making it easier for industry to meet its obligations.” 

APRA Deputy Chair Therese McCarthy Hockey said the reforms formed part of APRA’s broader body of work to reduce regulatory burden while continuing to receive the information it needs, ensuring APRA’s regulation strikes the right balance. 

“These straightforward reforms cut unnecessary reporting, freeing entities to focus on their work,” Ms McCarthy Hockey said. 

Some submissions also called for broader changes, including clearer thresholds for notifying APRA and ASIC of changes in accountability. These changes fall outside the current reforms but may inform future regulatory or legislative changes.  

The reforms complement other work to streamline requirements:  

  • APRA has recently consulted on removal of reporting requirements under its fit and proper regime to remove duplication with FAR reporting. 
  • ASIC has reduced requirements for Australian financial services licensees to submit evidence of competence for their responsible managers who are also accountable persons. These changes took effect in October 2026 and will benefit approximately 2,000 existing licensees.  

Entities should review the final guidance and update their reporting processes to reflect these changes. The final documents can be found at Streamlining FAR administration | APRA. 

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) is Australia's corporate, markets, financial services and consumer credit regulator. In administering the FAR, ASIC’s role is to focus on impacts to market integrity and consumer protection in the financial and payments systems. 

The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) is the prudential regulator of the financial services industry. It oversees banks, mutuals, general insurance and reinsurance companies, life insurance, private health insurers, friendly societies, and most members of the superannuation industry. APRA currently supervises institutions holding around $9.8 trillion in assets for Australian depositors, policyholders and superannuation fund members. 

Related links

Consultation page: Consultation on streamlining FAR administration | APRA 

RG 279 Financial Accountability Regime: Information for accountable entities | ASIC
