item.title: US Office Of The Comptroller Of The Currency’s Semiannual Risk Perspective Highlights Key Risks In Federal Banking System
item.content:encoded:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today reported the key issues facing the federal banking system in the Semiannual Risk Perspective for Fall 2026.

The OCC highlighted credit, market, compliance, and operational risks, as key risk themes in the report. Highlights from the report include:

  • Interest rate developments could affect both the net interest margin (NIM) and the valuation of securities held by banks. Higher interest rates could also increase commercial refinancing risk.
  • Credit risk in the loan portfolios of OCC-supervised banks remains modest overall.
  • Banks of all sizes are continuing to explore ways to leverage Super Intelligence (SI). The growing availability and advancement of SI create opportunities to enhance efficiency and internal controls as well as to improve analytics and customize services.
  • Employed by threat actors, advanced SI amplifies cybersecurity and fraud concerns.

The OCC reported that profitability for both the federal banking system and banks with assets less than $30 billion (community banks) increased to levels not seen in more than two decades during the first half of 2026. Loan growth, modest expansion of NIM and expansion of non-interest income contributed to robust revenue growth. Lower provisioning for credit losses further supported net income and profitability.

Since the release of the previous SARP, the OCC has continued to reset the OCC’s risk tolerance and enhance the risk-based nature of its supervisory policies and practices. Specific actions include the codification of unsafe or unsound practices and expanded eligibility for an 18-month exam cycle for community banks with up to $6 billion in assets. These and other changes aim to focus supervision on material financial risk and reduce exam burdens, especially for community banks.

Related Link

  • OCC Semiannual Risk Perspective, Fall 2026 (PDF)

item.title: New York State Department Of Financial Services Issues New Guidance Regarding Virtual Currency Advertising And Marketing Requirements - Guidance Emphasizes Department’s Expectation For Comprehensive Disclosure And Review Practices For Licensed Entities
item.content:encoded:
New York State Department of Financial Services (DFS) Acting Superintendent Kaitlin Asrow today issued guidance outlining expectations DFS-regulated virtual currency entities to maintain and implement comprehensive policies and procedures on advertising and marketing materials for virtual currency products, services, and activities. The guidance emphasizes the Department’s expectations for accurate content, clear disclosures, and an established governance and review process.   

“For more than a decade, DFS has set the global standard for virtual currency oversight and consumer protection,” said Department of Financial Services Acting Superintendent Kaitlin Asrow. “Today’s guidance reinforces our commitment to protecting New Yorkers and ensures advertising and marketing practices in the virtual currency space are clear, comprehensive, and accessible.”    

The guidance applies to virtual currency entities licensed or chartered by the Department (“VCEs”). VCEs are expected to update their policies and procedures for advertising and marketing consistent with this guidance by May 10, 2027, review those policies at least annually, and maintain records of the policies and procedures for Departmental review. Through examinations and supervisory monitoring, the Department will assess the application of these policies and procedures as well as their efficacy. 

The Department outlines commonly effective policies and procedures, including: 

  • Avoiding False, Misleading, or Deceptive Content: VCEs are expected to review claims made in marketing materials to ensure they are a fair portrayal of the products, services, or activities and are evidence-based and verifiable, and do not include exaggerated or false representations of performance or regulatory status.   

  • Disclosures: VCEs are expected to review customer disclosures to ensure they are clear, prominent, and easy for a general audience to understand.  The VCE providing the product, service, or activity must be clearly identified. 

  • Governance and Review Process: VCEs are expected to establish a governance process for review of advertising and marketing materials; specify the individual or individuals responsible for advertising and marketing processes and materials; ensure due diligence for third party-promoters; and have a process to monitor for and address on a timely basis the potentially fraudulent or otherwise wrongful use of the VCE’s name or brand. 

A copy of this guidance can be found on the Department’s website.

item.title: Federal Reserve Board Announces Pricing, Effective January 1, 2027, For Payment Services The Federal Reserve Banks Provide To Banks And Credit Unions, And Changes To Streamline And Adjust Their Check Services
item.content:encoded:
The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday announced pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, such as the clearing of checks, automated clearing house (ACH) transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services.

By law, the Federal Reserve must establish fees to recover the costs, including imputed costs, of providing payment services over the long run. The Federal Reserve expects to recover 101.5 percent of actual and imputed expenses in 2027, including the return on equity that would have been earned if a private-sector firm provided the services. Overall, price changes for 2027 will result in an estimated 1.4 percent average price increase for established, mature services.

In addition, the Federal Reserve Banks announced changes to streamline and adjust their check services. As described in the request for information on check services issued last year, the volume of checks processed by the Federal Reserve Banks is declining, but checks remain an important payment instrument for many consumers and businesses. The changes were informed by public feedback and ensure that the Federal Reserve Banks continue to provide check services efficiently. The adjustments include optimizing check processing windows during low-volume periods, increasing fees that banks and credit unions pay to process checks, and other operational updates. These changes do not impact consumers' and businesses' ability to pay with or receive checks and only impact how banks and credit unions process checks with Federal Reserve Banks.

The entire 2027 fee schedule for all of the Federal Reserve's payment services is published on FRBservices.org®. Additional information on the Federal Reserve's payments services, including service usage statistics, is available on the Board's website.

item.title: Ontario Securities Commission Highlights The Importance Of Governance And Oversight In AI Adoption
item.content:encoded:
Today, the Ontario Securities Commission (OSC) published Staff Notice 33-763 Focused Compliance Examination of Artificial Intelligence Systems Use and Governance (OSC SN 33-763) that provides the observations and findings from the Registration, Inspections and Examinations Division’s (RIE) Artificial Intelligence compliance initiative (OSC AI Initiative).

The OSC AI Initiative observed that most registered firms remain in the early stages of AI adoption, although some reported more advanced use in specific areas. The OSC AI Initiative covered a range of areas, including governance of AI system use, employee training, risk assessments and controls, oversight of third-party service providers and client disclosure.

The OSC expects registered firms to apply a proportionate, risk-based approach and oversight to the nature, scale and complexity of the risks each AI system use case presents. Registered firms remain accountable for their use of AI and its outputs.

“Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping our capital markets, from enhancing client service to improving efficiencies,” said Matthew Onyeaju, Senior Vice President, RIE, at the OSC. “Effective governance and thoughtful oversight are essential to realizing its benefits responsibly and in the public interest.”

The Notice highlights the key findings from the OSC AI compliance examination and reinforces existing guidance on the use of AI systems. The guidance reflects current securities law requirements and does not create any new rules or modify existing ones.

The mandate of the OSC is to provide protection to investors from unfair, improper or fraudulent practices, to foster fair, efficient and competitive capital markets and confidence in the capital markets, to foster capital formation, and to contribute to the stability of the financial system and the reduction of systemic risk. Investors are urged to check the registration of any persons or company offering an investment opportunity and to review the OSC investor materials available at www.osc.ca.

Note to editors:

  • OSC Staff Notice 33-763 – Focused Compliance Examination of Artificial Intelligence Systems Use and Governance was developed to assess registrants’ compliance with applicable securities laws requirements when using AI systems, informed by the guidance provided under CSA Staff Notice and Consultation 11-348 - Applicability of Canadian Securities Laws and the use of Artificial Intelligence Systems in Capital Markets.
  • In November 2025, OSC Staff surveyed 787 registered firms in Ontario, and achieved an 86% response rate.

item.title: IOSCO Board Announces New Structure For Standing Committees And Discusses Strategic Work Program For 2027
item.content:encoded:
The Board of the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) met over two days, 11 and 12 November 2026, at the organization’s headquarters in Madrid.

The Board discussed the 2027 Work Program, the emerging risks landscape outlined in the 2027 Risk Outlook report, and issues on the global regulatory agenda. Discussions focused on assessing the regulatory and supervisory implications of rapid financial innovation, notably artificial intelligence, tokenisation, and quantum computing technology in capital markets.

Board Members also examined vulnerabilities facing market intermediaries from increasingly sophisticated fraudulent schemes, and discussed developments in the audit and accounting sector, with particular reference to private equity investments in audit firms, and considered new initiatives to bolster capacity building.

The Board approved the publications of several statements and reports, which will be released in the coming weeks. Board members also had a constructive exchange of views with Erkki Liikanen, the Chair of the Trustees of the IFRS Foundation, on key developments within the IFRS Foundation.

A new structure for IOSCO’s standing committees takes effect on the day following the board meeting, on 13 November 2026, reflecting the evolutions of financial markets and of the current global regulatory agenda. The new structure includes the following standing committees:

  • Accounting, Disclosure, and Auditing (ADA) Committee chaired by Koichiro Kuramochi, Financial Services Agency (FSA) Japan and vice-chaired by Yu Cai, China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC)
  • Derivatives and Secondary Markets (DSM) Committee chaired by Martina Tambucci, Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa (CONSOB) Italy and vice-chaired by Carol M. McGee, US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
  • Enforcement and Cooperation Committee (ECC) chaired by Eric Jacob, Autorité des Marchés Financiers (AMF) Québec, and vice-chaired by Raffaella Panrano, CONSOB Italy
  • Financial Education and Retail Conduct (FERC) Committee chaired by Ali Sulaiman Aldakheel, Capital Markets Authority (CMA) Saudi Arabia and vice-chaired by Camille Beaudoin, AMF Québec
  • Investment Management Committee (IMC) chaired by Raymond Chan, Ontario Securities Commission (OSC), Canada and vice-chaired by Mhairi Jackson, Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) United Kingdom
  • Wholesale Market Conduct and Intermediation (WMCI) Committee chaired by Maria José Gomez Yubero of Comisión Nacional del Mercado de Valores (CNMV) Spain and vice-chaired by Yasumune Kano of FSA Japan
  • Financial Stability Engagement Group (FSEG) co-chaired by Marie-Anne Barbat-Layani, Autorité des Marchés Financiers (AMF) France and Nikhil Rathi, UK FCA
  • Assessment Committee (AC) chaired by Laurent van Burik, Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF) Luxembourg and vice-chaired by Antonio Mas, CNMV Spain
  • Committee on Emerging Risks (CER) chaired by Igor Kozhanov, US SEC and vice-chaired by Christophe Majois, Financial Services Market Authority (FSMA) Belgium
  • Screening Group (SG) chaired by Dominik Leimgruber, Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) and vice-chaired by Marlee B. Miller, US SEC

“I want to thank all colleagues at the Board for the fruitful and insightful exchange of views over the last two days during which we made significant progress on some of the most topical issues facing financial markets. I also want to congratulate the new Chairs and Vice-Chairs of the standing committees and FSEG Co-chairs, whom I thank for their commitment for the 2026-2028 term.”

Jean-Paul Servais, IOSCO Board Chair

item.title: ISDA derivatiViews - 2026 FX Definitions: Act Now
item.content:encoded:
On November 22, 2027, the 2026 FX Definitions will come into effect. From that point, these definitions will become the market standard for all cleared and new non-cleared FX derivatives, and the Swift messaging service will halt its support of the 1998 version. To put that another way, firms have a little over 12 months to prepare for the switch, and those that don’t will no longer be able to use Swift to confirm their trades. That’s why we’re urging market participants to sit up, take notice and start working on this now.

The 2026 FX Definitions were published in March to replace the 1998 FX and Currency Option Definitions, reflecting the changes in FX markets over the past 28 years. Published jointly by ISDA and EMTA, they retain everything that has worked well, while updating the framework to reflect current market practices, regulation and technology. Among the changes are revised disruption events and fallbacks for deliverable transactions, incorporation of EMTA template terms and market practices for non-deliverable FX transactions, a new fully automated exercise method for deliverable FX options and new provisions covering calendar adjustment events. They also modernize the calculation agent standard, bringing it in line with other ISDA product definitions and promoting consistent application across different governing laws.

The new definitions also bring together the various supplements and provisions published since 1998 into a single, integrated framework and remove the need for separate master confirmation agreements (MCAs). Available digitally through the ISDA MyLibrary platform, the definitions will be republished in full whenever future updates are made, making it much easier for users to navigate the document, find the provisions they need and understand the changes made in each publication.

While this isn’t a wholesale overhaul of the definitions, we recognize it will still take time for market participants to prepare for the switch. Firms need to understand how and where the changes affect their confirmation processes, systems and data, and determine how bespoke terms in existing master agreements or master confirmation agreements will be treated. They also need to engage with Swift, clearing houses and settlement systems to understand their implementation timelines and identify any dependencies. That will require coordination across legal, operations, technology and front-office teams. Firms should also reach out to their clients and counterparties to ensure they are aware of the initiative, the upcoming changes and the implementation timelines.

The clock is already ticking. These changes cannot be built and tested in a matter of weeks, so firms need to be working on implementation now. ISDA has published a range of resources to support implementation and outreach efforts, including an introductory brochure, implementation roadmap, redlines and mapping materials, annotated confirmation templates, FAQs and an introductory webinar.

There is a hard deadline and real consequences for missing it. From November 22 next year, the 2026 FX Definitions will become the market standard and Swift will no longer support electronic confirmations using the 1998 definitions. Firms that are not ready will therefore lose the ability to use Swift for those confirmations. That would be a major reversal for a market that has spent decades becoming more standardized, automated and efficient. ISDA will support implementation efforts where we can but there are no shortcuts – firms need to start work on this now.

item.title: American Inequality And The Future Of AI, Federal Reserve Governor Michael S. Barr, At Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut
item.content:encoded:
Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today.1 In a speech earlier this year, I explored scenarios in which artificial intelligence (AI) could affect economic inequality, for better or for worse.2 My focus in those remarks was on the AI side of this relationship, and today I would like to return to this topic by first providing some important context about inequality in the United States.

Inequality is an aspect of every economy, and understanding the extent and evolution of inequality in the United States can help in forming a clear view of the economic outlook and how the economy is likely to react to new developments. Widening inequality may also, depending on many factors, reflect a decline in economic opportunity for many people, which can limit the economy's productive capacity.

Today, I will begin by summarizing the current state of economic inequality in the United States, assisted by new results from a long-running survey of households conducted by the Federal Reserve, and then show where this fits into the history of inequality over the past century or so. I will explore some of the forces that have shaped inequality, and what these forces may indicate about how AI is likely to affect the way wealth and income are distributed.

Wealth and Income Inequality Today
Up-to-date and detailed information about inequality in the United States comes from the latest edition of the Federal Reserve's triennial Survey of Consumer Finances, conducted in 2025 and published just last month.3 The survey confirms that both wealth and income are highly concentrated and that inequality is greater for wealth. The top 10 percent by income of households receive almost one-half of all income in the United States and the top 1 percent receive about one-fifth of income.4 As for wealth, the wealthiest 10 percent of households hold nearly three-fourths of all wealth, and the top 1 percent hold about one-third. By contrast, the entire lower half of households, as measured by wealth holdings, have only 2 percent of wealth. Low wealth means it's also harder to get by every day. Another Fed survey of household finances conducted each year, the Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking, finds that 31 percent of respondents in 2025 didn't have the cash to cover an emergency expense of $500 or more.5

Wealth is even more highly concentrated among the very wealthiest. One-third of wealth is held by the upper 1 percent—that's nearly $60 trillion. There is even more concentration at the very top. The households in the upper 0.1 percent, which is only 135,000 individuals and families, own one-sixth of our nation's wealth. A household at the lower edge of the top 1 percent has 75 times as much wealth as the median household in the middle of the distribution—$16.3 million compared with $215,000 for a household in the middle. A household at the lower edge of the 0.1 percent of the wealthiest has 300 times as much wealth as the median household.

Wealth concentration has increased at the very top. Using Forbes magazine's tally of the 400 wealthiest individuals, together with data from the Survey of Consumer Finances, a rough estimate is that their share of total wealth rose from 3 percent in 2022 to 4 percent in the most recent survey. Forbes counts nearly 1,000 U.S. billionaires.6

Digging into the sources of widening inequality, the wealth of those at the top is primarily held in the form of business assets. Research using data from the Survey of Consumer Finances back to the 1940s shows that returns on business equity have been a major source of widening wealth inequality over the decades.7 Most of the income for these wealthy households is in capital income—interest, dividends, capital gains, and business profits—rather than wages and salaries. Unlike these higher-income or wealthier households, most income for middle-class households comes from their paychecks. And it's harder to build wealth that way.

Although the largest asset class for wealthy households is typically stocks and other financial assets, a substantial amount of their capital income also comes from ownership of private businesses. These private businesses come in two broad types: an actively managed business—such as a plumbing business, retail store, or manufacturing firm—and a passive investment in a business, commonly known as private equity. Owning and running a business has long been a way that households become wealthy. But private equity investments are passively run and are typically only open to the wealthiest individuals and families. These private investments have delivered returns to their owners higher than the typical mix of assets held by middle-income households. Private equity investments are 12 percent of the assets of the wealthiest 0.1 percent of households in the most recent Fed survey.

For households above the median but below the 90th percentile, the most prevalent assets are housing and stocks, but the value of housing equity has grown more slowly than that of business equity. About three-fourths of households in this group have stock holdings, mostly through retirement accounts. Although ownership of publicly traded companies has become more widespread across the income spectrum as 401(k) plans have become common over the past few decades, stock ownership by value remains highly concentrated among the wealthiest households. The group of households in the 50th through the 90th percentiles of wealth hold only 17 percent of all public stocks by value, underscoring how much wealth is concentrated.8

Finally, on net, households in the bottom half of the wealth distribution hold just over 2 percent of all wealth, an average of $52,000. About 40 percent of them have equity in homes, and nearly 40 percent own business equity, either through a retirement account or as their own business. But the values are low compared with the upper half of households.

The Evolution of Inequality
By many estimates, today's inequality levels are among the highest in the past 100 years.9 But wealth and income inequality in America have changed significantly over our history, widening and, at times, also narrowing, driven by a variety of factors, including booms and busts in financial assets, structural changes in the economy, and changes in tax and regulatory policy. In the Gilded Age, roughly 1870 to 1910, incomes rose strongly for most people, but it was also the era when large fortunes were accumulated by industrialists and their families. With no income tax or estate tax for the wealthiest and limited public education for everyone, the gap between those at the top and most others widened.10 But over the subsequent decades, especially during the New Deal, legal and institutional change strengthened worker power, and the introduction and broadening of progressive income and estate taxes helped limit the concentration of income and wealth.

Inequality narrowed in the decades after World War II, an era of fast economic expansion that benefited many households. There were improvements in public education, including the GI Bill, income tax changes that made rates more progressive, and growing unionization that raised wages for workers.11

Beginning in the late 1970s, however, wealth and income inequality began to increase again. This was a period of slower economic growth and sometimes high inflation. Top income tax rates declined, and fewer households were required to pay the estate tax. As in the 1910s and 1920s, business equity grew as a share of total assets, helping the wealthiest households become wealthier.12 The wealth generated from the typical middle-class asset—housing—increased but at a slower pace than business assets, exacerbated by the decline in housing wealth during the Global Financial Crisis. Over the same period, real wages grew slowly. Moreover, minimum wage laws failed to keep up with inflation and the growth of the economy.13

The lesson from this history is that the level of inequality in American society is not immutable—it changes over time. These historical patterns suggest that policy choices play a crucial role in shaping inequality levels. Economic growth, technological change, education, and globalization also play key roles.14

The Evolution of the Labor and Capital Shares of National Income
Some of these trends are most clearly seen in the decline in the share of national income going to labor over the past 25 years. Though individuals and families across the spectrum hold business equity from which they receive income, the main source of income for most households is wages and salaries—labor earnings. Since lower- and middle-income households depend heavily on wages, another useful way of exploring income and wealth inequality is to consider how the share of national income earned from labor has changed over time, compared with income earned from capital—dividends, interest, and private business earnings.

After World War II, the labor share of national income was fairly steady between 60 percent and 65 percent, but it began falling in fits and starts beginning in 2001. The decline accelerated after the pandemic and has been especially steep in the past year, reaching a record low of 52.8 percent in the second quarter of 2026.15 Some of this reflects measurement issues associated with how income has been allocated to labor and capital over time.16 But, even after adjusting for those factors, there is a clear downward trend.

Economic research suggests three causes of the decades-long trend in labor versus capital income, each highly relevant to the potential effects of AI on inequality. The first is technological innovations that have reduced demand for labor and decreased wages; the second is the concentration of market power in many industries with a small number of firms; and the third related cause is the reduction in the bargaining power of workers.

Technology replacing labor has been going on for centuries, but new technology can also augment the productivity of existing jobs and create new jobs, including those that are hard to envision when the technology is initially adopted, a point I have noted in a number of speeches.17 The internet and the businesses it created reduced employment in some occupations—such as travel agents—and eliminated others: Think video store workers. But the development of new technologies has expanded jobs in other areas. Consider that there are millions of full-time social media creators earning a living today in the United States, something unimaginable a decade ago.18

What matters for the focus of today's discussion is how returns to labor compare with those to capital from the adoption of new technology. The available evidence from across the globe suggests that advances in digital technology have lowered the price of investment in technology relative to labor. 19 If capital is cheaper relative to labor, firms use relatively more of it. Capital can substitute for labor, too—for example, through the adoption of automation and robots. 20 Some evidence shows that firms that adopt robots may also become more productive and expand their labor force. But in this expansion, labor is outpaced by the expansion in capital, seen in rising profits and equity appreciation, which widens inequality.21 It will be important to watch these developments closely given the immense capital investment going into the AI sector.

Another factor driving the decline in the labor share of national income is market concentration, which researchers estimate has increased significantly in three-quarters of U.S. industries since 2000. Since that time, wages have grown at a slower rate than labor productivity.22 Since larger firms are often more productive, these new technologies, in turn, can contribute to market consolidation, with so-called "superstar" firms as the result.23 Superstar firms also have lower labor shares of income because they can establish higher product markups—the difference between their costs and what they can sell their product for—because there may be less price competition and fewer alternatives for customers.24 At the same time, even with higher markups, their ability to deploy new technologies means these firms may be able to charge lower prices than before, which could serve to further increase their size and may result in lower costs for consumers.

These forces—technological change, market concentration, and declining bargaining power for workers—may have contributed to the declining share of labor income over time.25 All these changes have tended to favor those with the highest incomes and wealth, driving greater wealth inequality.

How Will AI Affect the Labor Share of Income?
The discussion of superstar firms probably brought to mind the handful of companies that are dominating AI: the hyperscalers and frontier AI labs. We have seen tremendous investment in the AI sector, with announced plans suggesting that capital deepening in this sector will escalate further. AI could be what some researchers call capital-biased innovation, in which the returns go primarily to capital rather than to labor.26 In previous remarks, I have explored scenarios for how AI could evolve as a technology and how it could affect labor markets. Key questions include the extent to which AI will substitute for human workers—or largely complement them—and the degree to which AI will create new jobs. Market competition and the bargaining power of workers will also affect the labor share of income. The nature of AI, particularly its ability to learn how to complete complex, nonroutine tasks that require extensive knowledge difficult for humans to achieve, raises the question of whether AI's effects on the labor market will be stronger than other technologies. 27 In previous speeches I have explored whether labor displacement could be larger than in the past, and today I consider the risk that the benefits of this technological revolution could be more narrowly shared than those that came before.28

There are questions also about the concentration of market power. Competition and distributed innovation could make AI a cheap and ubiquitous commodity, with gains widely shared. In this case, most businesses would have access to AI resources sufficient to support improved productivity and further innovation. AI could democratize access to skills and information needed for small businesses to thrive.

But some researchers believe that AI has characteristics that have, in past examples of high-tech advances, reinforced concentration of market power.29 AI depends on access to data, model improvements, and computing power, so it benefits from economies of scale and scope. AI itself is a powerful tool to train and accelerate the development of new AI models, including through self-reinforcement learning.

The extent of the advantage possessed by AI leaders may prove to be unprecedented. If a small number of AI firms dominate the market and receive the lion's share of investment returns, then the wealth of the managers and owners of these firms will surge. Large businesses could afford AI investments and continue to grow, while smaller firms would see declining market share. In this scenario, the vast majority of businesses and their employees would have limited access to ever-improving AI resources, which means they would see smaller returns. Overall, the labor share of income would decline, market concentration would increase, and inequality would go up.

So far, there has been relatively little displacement of workers by AI and some significant evidence that the transition to AI is enhancing the productivity of some workers, increasing demand in some sectors, and even creating new occupations. Vigorous competition among the AI firms so far has meant that access to AI remains fairly broad. Some believe that many businesses will find that most of their AI needs can be fulfilled by smaller-scale language models that will not need to be on the cutting edge of technology. And in that case, benefits would be more broadly shared.

As fast as AI has grown, its implementation is still limited so far, and no one knows the degree to which its benefits will be shared. We are already seeing signs that AI may be a labor substitute in some sectors, especially for younger, less-experienced workers. Some tasks that are easily automated with clear guardrails and predictable outcomes might see rapid labor substitution, while other tasks that require human judgment, management, coordination and relationships, creativity, or outputs that are hard to measure might see more labor augmentation.30 If labor market changes happen quickly, it will be hard for workers to adjust, and dislocations might be large, whereas a more gradual adoption might permit more orderly adjustments.

That said, we should be prepared for the possibility of serious short-term disruptions in the labor market that need to be managed effectively to ensure the benefits of AI are realized over the long term. If AI proves to be capable of work that displaces humans, the extent of the disruption to the labor market will depend in part on whether society undertakes the investments needed in new job creation and worker training, connecting workers to new jobs, and other efforts to mitigate adverse effects for the long term. The concentration of market power may help drive a widening of inequality that would strain the American Dream. In my judgment, now is the time for society to begin to consider how to address these potential challenges—while AI adoption is in its relatively early stages—so we can realize the long-term benefits for society.

1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Open Market Committee.

The sources of income collected in the survey include wages, self-employment and business income, taxable and tax-exempt interest, dividends, realized capital gains, unemployment insurance, food stamps and other related support programs provided by the government, pensions and withdrawals from retirement accounts, Social Security, alimony and other support payments, and miscellaneous sources. Note this survey gathers information from single-person households and families, referred to here simply as households.

This paper discusses how differential changes in equity and house prices shaped wealth dynamics in postwar America.

Revisiting Income Inequality in the United States, 1917–60," Economic Journal, vol. 132 (October), pp. 2366–91.

15. Some of the steep decline in the labor share for several years after the pandemic was due to the relative rise of less labor-intensive industries; see Richard Audoly, Miles Guerin, Srinidhi Narayanan, and Rachel Schuh (2026), "The Post-COVID Decline in the Labor Share," Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Liberty Street Economics (blog), June 24. But that decline has continued.

This paper estimates that the decline in the labor share between 1986 and 2017 is overstated by approximately one-third as a result of the shift to pass-through firms.

18. See Mark Schaefer (2023), "How Big Is the Creator Economy? Three Times Larger Than We Thought!" LinkedIn, November 14, https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/how-big-creator-economy-three-times-larger-than-we-thought-schaefer-pihac. 

19. See Loukas Karabarbounis and Brent Neiman (2014), "The Global Decline of the Labor Share," Quarterly Journal of Economics, vol. 129 (February), pp. 61–103. 

20. See Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo (2020), "Robots and Jobs: Evidence from U.S. Labor Markets," Journal of Political Economy, vol. 128 (June), pp. 2188–2244.

22. See Roc Armenter (2015), "A Bit of a Miracle No More: The Decline of the Labor Share," Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, Business Review,; also, see Gustavo Grullon, Yelena Larkin, Roni Michaely (2019), "Are U.S. Industries Becoming More Concentrated?" Review of Finance, vol. 23 (July), pp. 697–743. 

23. See Emin Dinlersoz and Zoltan Wolf (2024), "Automation, Labor Share, and Productivity: Plant-Level Evidence from U.S. Manufacturing," Economics of Innovation and New Technology, vol. 33 (May), pp 604–26. 

24. See David Autor, David Dorn, Lawrence F. Katz, Christina Patterson, John Van Reenen (2020), "The Fall of the Labor Share and the Rise of Superstar Firms," Quarterly Journal of Economics, vol. 135 (May), pp. 645–709. 

25. See Gene M. Grossman and Ezra Oberfield (2022), "The Elusive Explanation for the Declining Labor Share," Annual Review of Economics, vol. 14 (August), pp. 93–124; also, see Stansbury and Summers, "The Declining Worker Power Hypothesis" (in note 13). 

26. See Karabarbounis and Neiman, "The Global Decline" (in note 20); also, see Grossman and Oberfield, "The Elusive Explanation" (in note 26). 

27. See David H. Autor (2025), "Polanyi's Paradox and the Shape of Employment Growth," in Re-Evaluating Labor Market Dynamics: A Symposium Sponsored by the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (Kansas City: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, pp. 129–77). 

28. See, for example, Barr, "What Will Artificial Intelligence Mean," (in note 18).

NBER Working Paper Series 34986 (Cambridge, Mass.: National Bureau of Economic Research, March); Isabella Loaiza and Roberto Rigobon (2024), "The EPOCH of AI: Human-Machine Complementarities at Work," MIT Sloan Research Paper No. 7236-24 (Cambridge, Mass.: MIT, November; revised October 2025); Wilbur Xinyuan Chen, Suraj Srinivasan, and Saleh Zakerinia (2024), "Displacement or Complementarity? The Labor Market Impact of Generative AI," Harvard Business School Working Paper 25-039 (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard, December); and Kathryn Bonney, Cory L. Breaux, Emin Dinlersoz, Lucia S. Foster, John C. Haltiwanger, and Aditya A. item.title: Remarks At The 2026 Corporate Financial Reporting Insights (CFRI) Conference, Paul S. Atkins, SEC Chairman, Washington D.C., Nov. 12, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. And thank you, John [White], for your generous introduction. I should also like to thank Financial Executives International for inviting me to participate in today’s conference. Before I go any further, I must note that the views I express today are my own as SEC Chairman and do not necessarily reflect those of the Commission or my fellow Commissioner. 

There is much ground to cover and little time to spare. So, I will keep my remarks brief to allow maximum time for discussion with John [White]. But first, I would like to share a few thoughts on the priorities of the FASB and PCAOB in light of today’s ever-changing technological landscape. 

On the front lines of producing, auditing, overseeing, and using financial information, this group—perhaps more than most—understands that markets are rapidly evolving, business models are recalibrating, and technology is advancing at warp speed. In the face of such change, the institutions that support our financial reporting and auditing systems must remain strong—yet nimble, while staying tethered to their core responsibilities.

Of course, confidence in our capital markets depends on more than the quality of financial reporting and auditing. It also depends on trust in the oversight of those functions. Oversight should respond to marketplace developments, but it must remain focused on issues that are material to investors. Rigorous due process and meaningful stakeholder engagement can help achieve that goal. 

The institutions that the Commission oversees—namely the FASB and the PCAOB—must be able to respond to change, but they must do so with careful discipline. That means weighing costs and benefits, focusing on materiality, and achieving outcomes that serve both investors and the broader market. By addressing the right issues in a thoughtful and timely manner, these institutions can strengthen market confidence without imposing unnecessary costs or creating barriers to capital formation. Let me begin with accounting oversight.

Accounting Oversight

One of the FASB’s most important responsibilities, as the Commission’s designated accounting standard setter, is keeping its agenda centered on material issues. To that end, I applaud the addition of a Current Trends and Emerging Issues project to the FASB’s research agenda. This project monitors changes in the markets and evolving business practices, including current trends related to data infrastructure investments, non-traditional lending, and semi-annual reporting. I understand that it has already led to additions to the technical agenda based on stakeholder feedback, including the addition of the private credit disclosure project. Moving forward, I trust that it will continue to yield meaningful results for issuers and investors alike. 

By actively monitoring marketplace developments and seeking stakeholder input early in the process, the FASB is well positioned to identify areas where existing guidance may need to change, and to focus on the matters of greatest significance to the capital markets and to those who participate in them. 

Of course, evaluating potential changes makes up only half of the picture. The expected benefits of any change must also justify its costs. To be sure, meeting that objective requires more than broad, early stakeholder participation. It requires input that is thoughtful and meaningful. Indeed, detailed feedback from preparers regarding one-time versus ongoing costs, coupled with investor feedback on what information is material to investment decisions, is critical to the FASB’s success in developing standards that are both practical and effective. 

Auditing Oversight

The same principles must be applied to auditing oversight. Like the FASB, a strong auditing oversight institution should be able to respond appropriately as markets, businesses, and technology evolve. However, as it does, it should remain firmly grounded in its core statutory responsibility: protecting investors and furthering the public interest through informative, accurate, and independent audit reports.

For the PCAOB, that means getting back to basics. Specifically, registration, inspections, standard setting, and enforcement should each clearly tie back to the PCAOB’s mission. That starts with how projects are chosen. 

Before taking on a project, the PCAOB should plainly identify the problem that it seeks to address, evaluate the available evidence, and consider reasonable alternatives. At the same time, a rigorous cost-benefit analysis should inform the Board’s decisions from the beginning—assessing whether the anticipated benefits substantiate the imposed costs on audit firms, issuers, and ultimately shareholders. 

Meaningful stakeholder engagement is equally essential to that process, so I am encouraged to see the PCAOB’s openness to public input. This year, for example, the PCAOB invited comment on its strategic priorities and on proposed amendments to QC 1000, which the Commission approved earlier this month. It also completed its first-ever request for public comment on its standard-setting and research agenda. Seeking input early in this way can help uncover potential consequences, sharpen priorities, and ensure that the matters most consequential to audit quality are being addressed. I urge the PCAOB to make this engagement a regular part of its work, rather than an isolated exercise. 

Responsible Stewardship

Now, just as stakeholder engagement is essential to informed decisions, responsible stewardship is central to both the FASB’s and the PCAOB’s obligations. The accounting support fee that funds these institutions is borne in large part by issuers, and ultimately their shareholders. With that in mind, the FASB and PCAOB should begin with a clearly articulated strategy and connect their resources to measurable mission outcomes. They should also regularly evaluate whether programs remain both necessary and cost-effective. At the end of the day, high-quality accounting standards, improved audit quality, and greater confidence in audited financial statements should be the standard of success—not organizational growth, regulatory activity, and spending. 

Conclusion

Let me close by echoing the notion that I outlined at the beginning: strong institutions earn trust through disciplined action. If we let the principles that I have discussed today guide us—including engaging stakeholders and aligning costs with benefits—we can strengthen financial reporting, improve audit quality, protect investors, and uphold confidence in our capital markets for years to come. 

With that, thank you very much for your time and attention this morning. I look forward to the conversation ahead.

item.title: UK Financial Conduct Authority Proposes Greater Pension Investment Flexibility To Support Long-Term Value For Savers
item.content:encoded:
Workplace pension providers could have greater flexibility to invest for the long term under proposals from the FCA, helping them deliver better outcomes for savers while ensuring savers' interests remain protected.

The FCA is consulting on excluding certain performance-linked fees from the charge cap for default funds in workplace pensions it regulates.

Performance-linked fees are common in private markets, including private equity, venture capital and private credit. The proposed change would give providers greater flexibility to access a broader range of investments where this could help improve long-term returns and value for savers.

The FCA is clear that greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Providers should carefully weigh potential returns, risks and costs when making investment decisions, and any higher charges should be justified by the additional value delivered to savers.

Alongside the proposed flexibility, the FCA is proposing safeguards covering transparency, fair allocation of fees between savers and scrutiny of how private assets are valued. Providers and Independent Governance Committees would need access to the information necessary to assess whether performance-linked fees offer value for money.

Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market integrity at the FCA, said: 'People's pension savings should work hard for them. We want providers to have greater choice over how they invest for the long term where this can deliver better outcomes for savers.

'But greater flexibility is not a licence to charge more. Any higher charges must be justified by additional value, with firms carefully weighing returns, risks and costs when deciding what is in savers' best interests.'

The proposals would bring FCA rules more closely into line with the regime for trust-based pension schemes, where certain performance-linked fees have been excluded from the charge cap since 2023.

Greater alignment would support competition and choice and reduce unnecessary complexity for providers operating across both parts of the market.

The proposals would give providers an option, not an obligation, to use the exemption. Providers should do so only where it is in savers' interests, and they can meet the relevant protections.

The FCA is seeking responses by 14 January 2027 and currently expects to make final rules in summer 2027 following consideration of feedback. 

Background

  1. The consultation is open until Thursday 14 January 2027. Read CP26/40: Exempting performance fees from the workplace pensions charge cap.
  2. This work is a priority under the FCA's Pensions Regulatory Priorities (PDF) and forms part of the wider pensions reform.
  3. In 2023, the Government changed the rules so certain performance fees sit outside the limit on charges, with protections for members. The proposals build on changes made for trust-based schemes in 2023, while reflecting developments in private markets and strengthening protections in areas such as how investments are valued.
  4. The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA .

item.title: 76% Of Quant Finance Professionals Say Skills Gap Is Widening As AI Reshapes Quant Roles - More Than Half Of Professionals Say Hiring Quant Talent Is Difficult As AI Expands Job Demands Across Finance, According To A New CQF Institute Survey
item.content:encoded:
A survey by the CQF Institute, the global membership organization for quantitative finance, reveals that 76% of quantitative finance professionals believe the gap between required skills and available talent has grown in recent years, as AI expertise is increasingly expected to complement traditional quant skills.


“AI is raising the technical bar across quant finance,” says Dr. Randeep Gug, Managing Director of the CQF Institute. “Financial institutions are discovering that deploying advanced AI systems requires far more professionals with strong quantitative and computational foundations than the market currently produces. The result is a clear and growing shortage of talent capable of operating at the intersection of finance, data science, and machine learning.”

As new technologies become embedded within financial workflows, 58% of survey respondents say AI has expanded the scope of their responsibilities over the past two years, requiring deeper expertise in areas such as statistical modeling, programming, and machine learning. These changes are expected to continue, with 74% predicting that AI will drive major or complete transformation for quantitative roles within the next five years.

This rapid expansion of technical requirements is already translating into hiring challenges. More than half (55%) of respondents say that hiring strong quant professionals is difficult, pointing to a persistent shortfall of specialists with the mix of quantitative, computational, and AI skills needed to build, validate, and manage the increasingly complex models used across modern financial markets.

With 75% of professionals saying their current roles require capabilities they were never taught in university, many are relying on self-directed learning, on-the-job experience, and professional certifications, such as the Certificate in Quantitative Finance (CQF), to continuously upskill.

Overall, the findings suggest the quant finance skills gap is not a short‑term hiring challenge, but a structural issue shaped by rapid technological change. “As AI continues to reshape roles and expand job requirements, continuous reskilling is essential to keep pace with the industry’s demands,” Dr. Randeep Gug concludes.

The full CQF Institute “Careers in Quantitative Finance Survey” (2026), conducted among 135 quantitative finance professionals globally, is available here.

Survey: Fast Facts

  • 88% of quantitative finance professionals globally believe a skills gap exists across the industry.
  • 76% say the gap between required skills and available talent has grown in the past three years.
  • 58% say AI has expanded the scope of their responsibilities over the past two years.
  • 74% predict that AI will drive major or complete transformation for quant roles within the next five years.
  • 55% say that hiring strong quant professionals is difficult.
  • 75% say their current roles require capabilities they were never taught in university.
  • 84% say that continuous reskilling is vital for a successful career in quant finance.
  • 39% believe the greatest risk of the skills gap is increased reliance on automated systems without sufficient human oversight.

The findings build upon earlier CQF Institute research from 2025, which found that fewer than 9% of quantitative finance professionals believe new graduates are well equipped with the artificial intelligence and machine learning skills required for modern quant roles.

item.title: Exchange Data International Partners With Tallarium To Offer Real-Time OTC Energy Forward Curve Data
item.content:encoded:
Exchange Data International (EDI), a leading provider of global securities and financial market data, today announced a strategic partnership with Tallarium, a specialist provider of real-time forward curve data for off-exchange energy markets.

The collaboration combines EDI’s expertise in financial market data standardization with Tallarium’s expertise in structuring OTC energy market data, providing financial institutions and energy market participants with greater visibility into markets where reliable intraday pricing can be difficult to obtain.

Risk, valuation and product control teams covering OTC energy markets have traditionally relied on end-of-day assessments and lacked access to real-time pricing needed for timely PnL and having a clear view of portfolio impact during volatile markets, particularly for less liquid off-exchange energy.

Tallarium’s forward curves aggregate a wide range of price sources and are updated every five seconds throughout the trading day, providing an independent, timestamped reference that teams can use to verify and challenge marks.


“EDI through its partnership links has been expanding the range of data offered to take account of changed circumstances in the market. Oil markets have seen extreme volatility because of geopolitical events. Waiting until the end of the day to analyse data is no longer feasible or desirable, Tallarium fills this gap.” Jonathan Bloch, CEO, Exchange Data International

Through the partnership, EDI clients can access Tallarium’s independent & systematic forward curve data for major energy markets, more than 120 swap contracts across refined products, crude oil, natural gas and LNG, biofuels, wet freight and petrochemicals. The offering provides:

  • Intraday forward curves for independent price verification (IPV), mark-to-market and variation margin estimation;
  • Standardized data formats with API delivery for integration into existing risk, valuation, pricing systems and in-house AI tools to support institutional workflows;
  • Over 6 years of historical data for quantitative research, model calibration, back-testing and VaR analysis;


“Demand for intraday price visibility from financial institutions, corporate risk and product control teams is rising rapidly. Partnering with EDI allows us to bring independent intraday pricing and improved price discovery in OTC energy markets to EDI’s broad base of institutional clients,” Stanislav Ermilov, CEO, Tallarium

Learn more
For more information about OTC Energy Forward Curve Data or to request a demo, visit the product page or contact EDI at info@exchange-data.com.

About Exchange Data International (EDI)
Exchange Data International (EDI) is a leading provider of global securities data, delivering high-quality, comprehensive market intelligence to financial institutions worldwide. Specializing in pricing, corporate actions, reference data, EDI helps clients navigate complex markets with reliable, timely, and customizable data.

item.title: Helio Intelligence Appoints Andrew Rashbass As Chair
item.content:encoded:
Helio Intelligence, Europe’s leading provider of AI-enabled political and policy insights, has announced the appointment of Andrew Rashbass as Chair.

Andrew joins the business as Helio continues to build on more than 25 years of political expertise, serving over 1,100 customers across corporates, non-profit organisations, investment firms and public affairs consultancies. His appointment comes at a pivotal moment, following investment from growth-focused private equity firm ECI Partners in May 2026, as Helio accelerates the next phase of its journey, expanding its political coverage, with investment in high-quality human political judgement, augmented by advanced use of the latest AI technology.

Andrew brings an exceptional track record of executive leadership across world-class media and intelligence groups. As Chief Executive of The Economist Group, he spearheaded a remarkable digital transformation of The Economist, scaling global reader engagement, steering the iconic brand through a pivotal era of publishing innovation, and overseeing the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), a world-leading geopolitical intelligence provider. As Chief Executive of Euromoney, he led the global B2B information, intelligence and events group through strategic growth and business transformation, from a specialist news, media and events business into a world-class information, data and intelligence provider.

Alongside his executive career, Andrew is an Associate in the world-leading van der Schaar AI lab at the University of Cambridge, which develops cutting-edge machine learning and AI theory and methods that are transforming medicine, scientific discovery and other fields at the heart of human progress. 

This combination of large-scale transformation leadership in information services, strategic vision and hands-on engagement with cutting-edge AI research makes Andrew uniquely placed to support Helio’s next chapter of growth and innovation. 

Andrew Himsley, CEO of Helio Intelligence, comments: “We are thrilled to welcome Andrew to the board as Chair. His experience leading transformational change at The Economist Group and Euromoney, combined with his active involvement in frontier AI research at Cambridge, is exactly the blend of expertise Helio needs as we scale and continue to deliver best-in-market insight to our clients. His perspective will be invaluable as we move into our next phase of growth.” 

Andrew Rashbass, Chair of Helio Intelligence, comments: “Helio sits at the intersection of two things I care deeply about: world-class expert-led intelligence and the thoughtful application of AI to make that intelligence sharper, faster and more useful. The business has built a remarkable position in a market where quality and speed of insight really matter. I’m delighted to be joining Andrew and the team, alongside ECI, at such an exciting point in the company’s journey.”

Toby Fitzherbert, Investment Director at ECI Partners, comments: “Andrew has an outstanding record of leading data and intelligence businesses through major transformations. We look forward to working with him as the Helio team builds further on its standout position in the political intelligence market.”

item.title: Fourthline Expands Into Luxembourg With Banque Internationale à Luxembourg (BIL) As New Business Partner For Its Identity Verification Solution
item.content:encoded:
Fourthline, Europe's leading identity services provider, has been selected by Banque Internationale à Luxembourg (BIL), a leading player in Luxembourg’s financial market, as their Identity Verification Partner (IDV). The partnership marks Fourthline's first business partner in Luxembourg, a significant milestone in the company's continued European expansion.

BIL will use Fourthline's IDV services to support compliant, seamless onboarding for both domestic and international clients across its digital banking operations.

"We are delighted to welcome BIL as our first Luxembourg partner. As the oldest tier 1 bank in the Grand Duchy, BIL sets an exceptionally high bar for compliance and customer experience. This partnership is a strong validation of Fourthline's ability to meet that standard, and we look forward to supporting BIL's continued growth across domestic and international markets," said Fourthline CEO, Paul Stoddart.

Compliant onboarding will be delivered through a single API integration, encompassing identity document verification, biometric data analysis, and the application of Fourthline's advanced proprietary verification models, providing BIL's clients with a secure, frictionless experience.

"At BIL, we are committed to providing our clients with a secure, seamless and efficient onboarding experience while maintaining the highest standards of compliance. Fourthline's proven expertise in digital identity verification and deep understanding of the European regulatory landscape makes them a natural partner for us. Together, we are strengthening our onboarding capabilities and supporting the continued growth of our activities in Luxembourg and beyond," said Isa Scheunpflug, BIL Chief Operating Officer.

item.title: Samsung Securities Launches Two China Thematic ETNs Tracking Solactive’s KRW-Hedged China Rare Earth And Gaming Benchmarks
item.content:encoded:
Solactive is pleased to announce the expansion of its collaboration with Samsung Securities through the launch of two new exchange-traded notes (ETNs) track the Solactive China Rare Earth Top 5 Index Hedged to KRW Index and the Solactive China Game Top 3 Hedged to KRW Index. The two products provide exposure to distinct segments of the Chinese equity market through Solactive’s KRW-hedged thematic benchmark solutions.

Rare earths remain strategically important to global industrial and technology supply chains due to their role in a range of advanced technologies and broader industrial applications. As critical minerals have moved higher on policy agendas amid supply-chain constraints, price volatility, and geopolitical developments, the rare-earth segment has gained increased market relevance.

China’s gaming industry continues to combine a large domestic market with growing international reach. In the first half of 2026, China’s domestic gaming market generated RMB 188.45 billion in sales revenue, representing a 12.17% year-on-year increase, while the number of users reached 684 million. Overseas revenue from Chinese-developed games rose by 30.22% year on year to USD 12.37 billion, highlighting the sector’s continued expansion beyond the domestic market.1 

The Solactive China Rare Earth Top 5 Index Hedged to KRW Index is designed to capture the performance of five companies from China and Hong Kong with strong relevance to the rare-earth value chain. The eligible universe is drawn from the Solactive GBS Hong Kong All Cap Index and the Solactive GBS China All Cap Index, subject to listing, geographic, liquidity, and sector requirements. Using ARTIS®, Solactive’s proprietary natural language processing technology, the index identifies companies active in exploration and mining, processing and refining, and the production of oxides, metals, and compounds. Constituents are weighted by free-float market capitalization, subject to a 30% cap.

The Solactive China Game Top 3 Index Hedged to KRW Index is designed to provide concentrated exposure to leading Chinese gaming companies listed in Hong Kong. Starting from the Solactive GBS Hong Kong All Cap Index, the methodology focuses on technology companies that meet a minimum free-float market capitalization threshold. ARTIS® is then used to identify companies with strong relevance to online gaming ecosystems, digital distribution platforms, and gaming content and intellectual property creation. The three selected constituents are weighted by free-float market capitalization, subject to a 40% cap.

Both ETNs was listed on 12 November 2026, on the Korea Exchange (KRX) under the following name and ticker,

ETN NAMETICKER
Samsung Securities Samsung CHINA RARE EARTH COMPANY TOP5 TR ETN 530146.KS
Samsung Securities Samsung CHINA GAME TOP3 TR ETN 530147.KS

Timo Pfeiffer, Chief Markets Officer at Solactive, commented: “We are pleased to further expand our collaboration with Samsung Securities through the launch of these two China-focused thematic ETNs. The new benchmarks translate two distinct market themes into targeted and investable index solutions, offering differentiated access to the rare earth value chain and China’s gaming ecosystem through transparent and rules-based methodologies.”

Samsung Securities, commented: “With these two new ETNs, we aim to broaden access for Korean investors to two distinctive themes in the Chinese equity market: rare earths and gaming.”

  1. China Daily, citing the 2026 China Game Industry Report (January–June), 6 August 2026.

item.title: BMLL And Vola Dynamics Partner To Bring Market-Maker-Quality Options Analytics To Unified Historical Data In A Fully Managed Research Environment
item.content:encoded:
• Vola’s options analytics library is now integrated directly into BMLL Data Lab, allowing quant teams to fit volatility surfaces, price options and run scenario analysis without building a data pipeline or maintaining fitting and pricing infrastructure.

BMLL, the global market data and analytics platform provider, today announced a strategic partnership with Vola Dynamics, the options analytics provider that market makers, banks, and hedge funds use to price options, model volatility and manage risk. 

The collaboration integrates Vola’s options analytics library directly with BMLL’s historical market data within the BMLL Data Lab, combining BMLL’s deep, clean, historical options and underlying market data with Vola’s volatility and pricing library inside a single managed environment.  Quantitative hedge funds are able to run scenarios, market makers can reconstruct historical vol surfaces and validate hedging strategies, and asset managers can add  volatility fitting, pricing and scenario analysis to their historical market research without the need to build separate data or analytics workflows. 

Options and Volatility Research Infrastructure Challenges

Building and maintaining an in-house pipeline to clean options and underlying data, snapshot it, fit volatility surfaces, and compute risk is slow, expensive, and specialist work. Historically, quantitative research teams have faced significant technical barriers in assembling clean historical options data and market-maker-quality fitting, pricing, and risk workflows within the same research environment. This technical friction often forces quants to spend substantial development time managing data infrastructure and maintaining software libraries rather than focusing on core research.

Responding to Market Demand for Integrated Options Analytics

As options and volatility become a core research focus driven by increased listed options activity and the growth of volatility as an asset class, research teams increasingly want to reduce the lead time needed for systematic options research.

BMLL and Vola Dynamics significantly reduce this technical barrier by enabling research teams to apply Vola’s volatility surface fitting, theoretical pricing, Greeks and scenario analysis directly to BMLL options and underlying data within the BMLL Data Lab. Rather than managing two separate systems or operating complex data-cleaning pipelines, researchers can quickly move from historical market data to fitted volatility surfaces, theoretical prices, and risk metrics in minutes.

To access the capability, clients run Vola's library directly inside the BMLL Data Lab using their own Vola license. Under this structure, researchers can use BMLL’s underlying historical dataset, and the Vola library to transform raw data into arbitrage free volatility surfaces, clean valuations, and realistic scenarios. 

Paul Humphrey, CEO of BMLL, said: "As listed options activity grows and volatility becomes an increasingly vital asset class, quantitative teams need to move fast without getting bogged down by infrastructure. By integrating Vola’s options analytics directly within the BMLL Data Lab, we are removing the heavy plumbing work of cleaning data and maintaining the options analytics stack. Our clients can now seamlessly access BMLL’s deep historical data alongside Vola’s pricing and risk analytics within a unified, fully managed environment, enabling them to transform market data and analytics into research-grade insights in a matter of minutes."

Timothy Klassen, CEO of Vola Dynamics, added: "Over 50 of the most sophisticated options desks in the world run Vola on-prem. For the first time, with Vola available inside the BMLL Data Lab, research teams can fit surfaces, price options and run risk scenarios on BMLL's unified historical options and underlier data, without building or maintaining an options analytics pipeline of their own.”

The single managed solution is purpose-built for options and volatility research teams across systematic hedge funds, options market-makers, proprietary trading firms, asset managers, and bank quantitative research desks. Core use cases within the managed environment cover systematic research, backtesting, volatility analysis, and risk model validation.

item.title: HKEX Hosts ETF Summit 2026 As Market Sets New Records
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) today (Thursday) welcomed hundreds of distinguished speakers and guests at its ETF Summit 2026, marking a year of fresh records, new products, and continued vibrancy.

The event today brought together institutional and private wealth investors, asset managers, issuers and market participants to discuss the latest developments shaping the exchange-traded funds market, including growing institutional adoption, evolving investor needs, product innovation, cross-border opportunities and tokenisation.

HKEX Head of Markets, Gregory Yu, said: “This year’s ETF Summit brought many members of our market community together to look at how to capture the next phase of growth. Building a successful ETF market is about much more than just the products on our shelves. It requires an ecosystem where indices and benchmarks provide the building blocks for innovation, broader product choice attracts more investors and strategies, and deeper participation supports liquidity and scale. We at HKEX are bringing these elements together with Hong Kong’s unique connectivity, helping create a virtuous circle that makes the market more vibrant and delivers practical portfolio solutions for investors. We thank our entire ETF community for their staunch support over the past year, and we look forward to working together to propel our markets from strength to strength.”

Hong Kong’s ETP market has continued to demonstrate strong momentum. Assets under management of ETFs and leveraged and inverse (L&I) products reached HK$616.5 billion at the end of October 2026, while average daily turnover rose 23% year-on-year to a record HK$46.5 billion.

The product ecosystem has also continued to expand. As of end-October, Hong Kong had 246 ETFs and 29 L&I products, while three new ETFs were listed in October. Trading of ETFs through Stock Connect also continued to grow, with Northbound and Southbound ETF average daily turnover reaching RMB5 billion, up 48 per cent from a year earlier, and HK$4.6 billion, up 8 per cent year on year, respectively, in the first 10 months of 2026.

HKEX will continue to work with the industry to further develop Hong Kong’s ETP ecosystem, expand investor choice and reinforce the city’s role as a leading international ETF marketplace. For more data and insights, please refer to our latest HKEX Insights article.

item.title: TOPPAN And BitGo Conduct Proof-of-Concept for Decentralized Key Management Scheme To Securely And Seamlessly Manage Digital Assets - Verifying A Scheme Combining 3-Party Decentralized Management Of Private Keys With Corporate Identity Verification Via vLEI To Reduce Single Points Of Failure And Strengthen Transaction Security
item.content:encoded:
TOPPAN Inc. (TOPPAN), a TOPPAN Group company and wholly owned subsidiary of TOPPAN Holdings Inc. (TYO: 7911), and digital asset infrastructure provider BitGo Holdings, Inc. (NYSE: BTGO) (BitGo) conducted a joint proof-of-concept (PoC) experiment from August to October 2026 for a Decentralized Key Management Scheme designed to manage digital assets securely and seamlessly.

In this PoC, TOPPAN combined sophisticated private key (undisclosed digital keys used for encryption, digital signatures, etc.) management infrastructure and operational expertise cultivated in its card issuance business with BitGo’s operational management expertise for digital assets. Together, they constructed an environment to manage private keys across three parties, conducting technical verification of decentralized private key management and operation among the client, TOPPAN, and BitGo. Furthermore, by integrating with TOPPAN’s vLEI-Gateway™—a service for issuing global verifiable Legal Entity Identifiers (vLEI)1 —the scheme leveraged vLEIs to strictly verify the identity and authority of target corporations and corporate representatives when private keys are used or when registering destinations to digital asset transfer whitelists.2

This scheme is designed to eliminate Single Points of Failure3 (SPOF) while preventing unauthorized transactions via approvals by other parties and ensuring robust corporate identity verification, thereby supporting security and governance in private key operations.

Background of the PoC

In recent years, while the utilization of digital assets has expanded rapidly both in Japan and internationally, there have been numerous occurrences of unauthorized leaks and cyberattacks exploiting vulnerabilities in management systems. Furthermore, as external attacks become increasingly sophisticated and diverse through the exploitation of AI, strengthening governance environments—such as preventing internal fraud and ensuring strict identity verification (KYC/AML) of transaction partners—has become an urgent priority. However, building and maintaining a strict private key management environment and an advanced corporate authentication environment in-house requires substantial cost and specialized expertise, which may limit adoption to a limited number of large enterprises. These aspects may pose barriers to adoption for regional banks, municipalities, and corporations seeking to enter the digital asset space.

In addition, traditional operations where a single party manages private keys alone carry the risk of concentrated cyberattacks, while also being vulnerable to SPOF risks such as data loss or system outages during natural disasters. Therefore, there has been strong demand for establishing a new, secure, and sustainable key management infrastructure, not only for security assurance but also from a business continuity perspective.

Overview of the PoC

To solve the aforementioned issues, TOPPAN and BitGo jointly developed and verified a new Decentralized Key Management Scheme by combining their respective strengths.

By combining TOPPAN's long-cultivated sophisticated key management infrastructure and operational expertise with BitGo's advanced multi-signature key distribution technology, this scheme is designed to support secure decentralized management of private keys and signature execution. Furthermore, by integrating strict corporate verification via vLEI, an end-to-end defense mechanism—from decentralized storage of private keys to identity/corporate verification during transactions—was established to strengthen security and governance.

・Enhanced Resistance to Cyberattacks
Signature authority is decentralized across three parties: the Client (main signature) executing the transaction, BitGo (countersignature) disallowing unilateral execution, and TOPPAN (backup key) storing a backup in a secure environment. Even if one party’s access authority or management environment is compromised by increasingly diverse cyberattacks, the transaction cannot be completed without approval from the other keys, helping to reduce the risk of unauthorized asset transfers.
・Rigorous Corporate Verification via vLEI
Automated digital corporate verification via vLEI is conducted when registering on the digital asset transfer whitelist or executing transactions. By verifying the existence and authority of transaction counterparties, the system is designed to help reduce the risk of spoofing or accidental transfers to unauthorized addresses, demonstrating financial-institution-grade governance.
・Prevention of Internal Fraudulent Transactions
Transactions cannot be completed solely through the client’s unilateral authority; requiring BitGo’s countersignature (multi-approval) combined with rigorous corporate verification via vLEI can help to reduce the risk of internal abuse of authority and fraudulent transactions.
・Strengthened Business Continuity (BC)
Even if the keys of a client or BitGo become unavailable due to natural disaster or system failure, using the backup key stored by TOPPAN in a secure environment such as an HSM4 demonstrates that assets do not need to be frozen, and that continuous business operations are possible.

Implementation Period August – October 2026
Scope ・Wallet/Certification Infrastructure Construction: Created wallets supporting 3-party decentralized management and implemented system integration with vLEI-Gateway™.
・Storage/Authentication Environment Construction: Established physically and systematically secure storage for private keys and integrated vLEI-based corporate verification processes.
・Standard Transaction/Verification: Conducted corporate verification during whitelist registration and performed digital asset transfer tests using the created wallets.
・Failure Scenario Verification: Conducted digital asset transfer tests assuming a scenario where one key is lost or rendered unusable.
Verification Results & Achievements Through this PoC, the following items were confirmed to function and operate as designed:
・Key Generation / Decentralized Management: Private keys designed for 3-party decentralized management were correctly generated and managed.
・Corporate Verification via vLEI: Accurate corporate verification was performed during whitelist registration and asset transfers, enabling safe transaction execution.
・Normal Transfer Operations: Digital assets were transferred and traded without issues following the prescribed multi-approval workflow and corporate verification.
・Business Continuity During Failures: By using two of the three decentralized private keys, digital assets were safely transferred and protected even when one key was unavailable (verifying business continuity plan effectiveness).

Future Objectives

Based on the results of this PoC, TOPPAN and BitGo will further advance the operational sophistication of their Decentralized Key Management Scheme, aiming for a service launch as early as 2028. Any launch remains subject to, among other things, definitive agreements, regulatory requirements, and technical and commercial readiness.
