TOPPAN and BitGo will provide a secure digital asset management and operation platform to regional banks, municipalities, and corporations facing challenges in private key management and compliance, contributing to the healthy expansion of the digital asset market.

  1. vLEI (verifiable LEI): A verifiable credential that combines an LEI (Legal Entity Identifier)—a globally standardized corporate ID based on the international standard 
  2. Whitelist Registration: A mechanism to pre-screen, approve, and authorize only safe addresses (counterparties) for digital asset transfers and transactions, reducing the risk of unauthorized leaks or accidental transfers to unapproved destinations in advance.
  3. Single Point of Failure (SPOF): A single component or location within a system that, if it fails or stops working, causes the entire system to stop functioning.
  4. HSM (Hardware Security Module): A dedicated security hardware device that physically and securely performs cryptographic key generation, storage, and processing. It is designed to provide strong resistance against unauthorized external access and physical tampering attacks, executing secure encryption and signature processes without exposing private keys outside the device.

item.title: SET Market Report For October 2026
item.content:encoded:
The SET Index closed October 2026 at 1,518.59 points, down 2.6 percent from the previous month, in line with the broader decline across regional markets, but still 20.6 percent higher than at the end of 2025. Global equity markets experienced heightened volatility, particularly a sell-off in technology and AI-related stocks, amid concerns over valuations, returns on substantial investments in AI and data centers, and regulatory uncertainty. These developments prompted investors to increasingly rotate from growth stocks toward value stocks. Despite pressure from AI supply chain-related stocks, the SET Index declined less than many regional peers, while net foreign selling remained relatively limited.

The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) Executive Vice President and Head of Research Department, Chatchai Thisadoldilok, CFA, FRM, said that despite the market correction driven by the technology sector sell-off in October, high-dividend stocks, particularly in the banking and energy sectors, as well as ESG-related stocks, demonstrated relative resilience amid market volatility. Domestic economic fundamentals also continued to provide support. The Bank of Thailand raised its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 2.4 percent, supported by strong exports and investment, particularly in technology and AI-related industries, alongside a substantial increase in applications for the Board of Investment (BOI) promotion during the first nine months of the year. Meanwhile, revisions to the Manufacturing Production Index (MPI) have improved its coverage of activity in emerging industries. Other key developments to watch include the ongoing release of listed companies' third-quarter earnings, which will provide greater clarity on the full-year earnings outlook; the recovery of tourism during the high season; U.S. inflation trends and the Federal Reserve's interest rate policy; as well as geopolitical risks and potential shifts in U.S. fiscal and trade policies following the midterm elections.

Key highlights for October 2026

  • The SET Index ended October at 1,518.59 points, down 2.6 percent from the previous month but up 20.6 percent from the end of 2025.
  • Resources and Financials outperformed other industry groups in October, while Industrials, Resources, and Financials outpaced the market year-to-date.
  • Combined SET and Market for Alternative Investment (mai) average daily trading value in October 2026 jumped 68.2 percent year-on-year to THB 66.39 billion. For the first 10 months, average daily trading value surged 63.2 percent year-on-year to THB 69.61 billion.
  • Foreign investors were net sellers of THB 6.67 billion in October, reducing their net buying to THB 18.19 billion for the first 10 months.
  • Foreign investors represented 58.7 percent of total trading value, followed by local retail investors at 27.4 percent, proprietary trading by securities companies at 7.0 percent, and local institutional investors at 6.9 percent.
  • Two companies were newly listed in October: Thai Packaging Industry pcl (TIPAK) on SET and Quick Transformation pcl (QUICK) on mai.
  • SET’s forward P/E ratio at the end of October 2026 was 13.3 times, above the Asian stock market average of 12.1 times. Its historical P/E ratio was 14.4 times, on par with the Asian stock market average.
  • SET’s dividend yield at the end of October 2026 was 4.6 percent, above the Asian stock market average of 3.1 percent.

Derivatives Market for October 2026

  • Thailand Futures Exchange’s (TFEX) average daily trading volume in October 2026 was 366,065 contracts, down 33.0 percent from the previous month, mainly attributable to lower trading in SET50 Index Futures and Single Stock Futures. For the January-to-October period, TFEX average daily trading volume increased 24.7 percent year-on-year to 526,527 contracts.

item.title: Moscow Exchange: Changes In Trading And Clearing Reports On The Securities Market
item.content:encoded:
We have clarified the scope of changes to the trading and clearing reports on the Securities Market, which was announced in Developer Newsletter No. 156. Please note that in reports SEM21 and SEM21D, the attributes RegNumber, FaceUnit, Volume, and IssueSize remain mandatory. They will not be populated for digital currencies: empty value – for attributes RegNumber and FaceUnit, value 0 – for Volume and IssueSize. The announcement on the website has been updated: https://www.moex.com/n105622.

The full list of changes to the reports is provided below.

Changes in trading reports

  1. In the SEM21 (General Market Data) and SEM21D (General Intraday Market Data) reports:
    • The description of the attributes BoardType, SecurityId, SecuryType, PriceType, EngType, LowOffer, TrendClose, MP2ValTrd, and MarketPrice2 is changed;
    • The mandatory attributes RegNumber and FaceUnit for digital currencies are not populated – empty value;
    • The mandatory attributes Volume and IssueSize for digital currencies are not populated – value is 0.
  2. New reports are introduced:
    • SEM27 (Compliance with the REPO_CI Tariff Plan Condition);
    • SEM02DC (Orders for digital currency register);
    • SEM03DC (Digital currency trades register).
  3. In the SEM02C (Cancelled orders register) report:
    • The description of the SecurityId field is changed;
    • A decimal places value (8) is added to the Quantity and QuantityVisible attributes.

Updated specifications for report formats are available on the MOEX website: https://www.moex.com/en/documents/13896.
Schemas and styles for printed report forms are available on the MOEX FTP server: https://ftp.moex.com/pub/Reports/Equities.
Trading reports for digital currencies are available on the test environment. Reports from the test environment are prepared upon request; please contact support.
Changes in clearing reports

  1. In the EQM20 (Report on trading/clearing accounts) and EQM28 (Report on additional divisions on trade accounts open for the clearing member operations) reports:
    • The description of the attributes DepAccId and DepUnitId is changed;
    • New attribute, DepositoryId - Depository code / digital depository code, is added to the node RECORDS:
      • N - a trading Securities Sub-account for recording securities, opened at the depository of NKO JSC NSD.
      • R - a trading Sub-account of a digital account for recording digital currencies and foreign digital instruments, opened at the Settlement Digital Depository.
  2. In the EQM06 (Trades included into clearing (EQM06/EQM06P/EQM06R)*) report:
    • The description of the attributes InstrType, Price, Quantity, Amount, Balance, ClientDetails, DueDate, and Type is changed;
    • New attribute, TradeType - Type of trade in foreign currency / digital currency / foreign digital instrument (InstrType=C):, is added to the node RECORDS:
      • S - Swap trade.
      • T - Buy/sell trade.
    • The number of decimal places in the Quantity and Balance attributes is changed from 2 to 8.
  3. In the EQM6C (Trades included into clearing (client trades)) report:
    • The description of the attributes InstrType, Price, Quantity, Amount, Balance, ClientDetails, DueDate, and Type is changed;
    • New attribute, TradeType - Type of trade in foreign currency / digital currency / foreign digital instrument (InstrType=C), is added to the node RECORDS:
      • S - Swap trade.
      • T - Buy/sell trade.
    • A decimal places value (8) is added to the Quantity and Balance field.
  4. In the EQM6D (Trades included into clearing (for holders)) report:
    • The description of the attributes InstrType, Price, Quantity, Amount, Balance, ClientDetails, and Type is changed;
    • New attribute, TradeType - Type of trade in foreign currency / digital currency / foreign digital instrument (InstrType=C):, is added to the node RECORDS:
      • S - Swap trade.
      • T - Buy/sell trade.
    • A decimal places value (8) is added to the Quantity and Balance field.
  5. In the EQM13 (Report on net liabilities and net claims) report:
    • The description of the attributes GuarDepUnitId, SecurityId, and SecShortName is changed;
    • New value for the attribute PosType in the node POSTYPES is added:
      • D - information on digital currencies / foreign digital instruments.
    • New value for the attribute DataType in the node RECORDS is added:
      • DISCH_OBLIG - Net claim / Net liability terminated as a result of interim clearing settlement sessions.
    • The number of decimal places in the NettoSum, Debit, and Credit attributes is changed from 2 to 8.
  6. In the EQM23 (Report on obligation under T+ trades) report:
    • The description of the attributes GuarDepUnitId, SecurityId, and SecShortName is changed;
    • New value for the attribute PosType in the node POSTYPES is added:
      • D - information on digital currencies / foreign digital instruments.
    • The number of decimal places in the Debit and Credit attributes is changed from 2 to 8.
  7. In the EQM84 (Collateral valuation report) report:
    • The description of the attributes CurrencyId, CurrencyName, SecurityId, SecShortName, Quantity, LockQuantity, and FreeQuantity is changed;
    • The number of decimal places in the Quantity, LockQuantity, and FreeQuantity attributes is changed from 2 to 8.
  8. In the EQM91 (Report on net liabilities that will be terminated) report:
    • The description of the attributes CurrencyId, CurrencyName, SecurityId, SecShortName, FixBalanceTime, and Balance is changed;
    • The number of decimal places in the Balance, Netto, and UnsecuredLiabilities attributes is changed from 2 to 8.
  9. In the EQM99 (Report on collateral) report:
    • The description of the attributes SecurityId and SecShortName is changed;
    • New value for the attribute PosType in the node POSTYPES is added:
      • D - information on digital currencies / foreign digital instruments.
    • The number of decimal places in the OpeningBalance, ClosingBalance, DebitSum, CreditSum, NettoSum, Debit, Credit, and Netto attributes is changed from 2 to 8.


Updated specifications for report formats are available on the MOEX website: https://www.moex.com/en/documents/13900.
Schemas and styles for printed report forms are available on the MOEX FTP server: https://ftp.moex.com/pub/Reports/Equities.

The full list of planned changes has been updated: https://www.moex.com/media/version-2026-4.pdf.
The document describing technical implementation of digital currency trading in the Securities Market system has been updated: https://www.moex.com/media/tsifrovye-valyuty-v-sisteme-fondovogo-rynka.pdf.

item.title: UK Retail Payments Infrastructure: Moving From Vision To Design − Speech By Victoria Cleland, Bank Of England, Senior Advisor To The Governors, Given At The FTT Fintech Festival, Published On 11 November 2026
item.content:encoded:
The UK’s next-generation retail payments infrastructure is being designed to meet evolving needs of the whole ecosystem. It must enable different payment journeys and forms of money and provide a platform for innovation. Victoria Cleland explains how industry inputs are shaping the Blueprint for the new core infrastructure. She also explains why collaboration remains essential, throughout the process.

Victoria Cleland

Senior Advisor to the Governors


Speech

It is a pleasure to join you this morning at the FTT Fintech Festival, with an exciting update on our journey to create a next generation retail payments infrastructure for the UK. And when I say “our journey”, I do not just mean the Bank of England. I do not just mean the other authorities. I mean everyone in this room, and the whole payments ecosystem. To design and deliver an infrastructure that is well used, trusted and truly valued requires strong collaboration between the public and the private sectors, between incumbents and fintechs, and between providers and users.

Payments are a key part of all our lives, and the lifeblood of the economy and of the financial system. And we need to keep them relevant in an ever-changing landscape. Technology, about which we are hearing so much at today’s Festival, is reshaping how payments are initiated and authorised. And demand is changing, with expectations of speed and functionality increasing as payments respond to our "always on" world.

So, what is our destination?

Last year the Payments Vision Delivery Committee (PVDC) footnote[1] outlined five key outcomes for a next generation infrastructure:

  • greater choice of innovative and cost-effective payment options;
  • interoperability across a multi-money ecosystem;
  • protection from fraud and wider financial crime;
  • fair and transparent access that supports competition and innovation; and
  • an operationally and financially resilient payments ecosystem.

Together these will make a real difference for consumers and businesses, enhance resilience and support competition and innovation.

To help realise this ambition, the Retail Payments Infrastructure Board (RPIB) was established. I chair the RPIB, which brings together a range of industry experts, with the FCA/PSR participating as an observer, to translate these PVDC outcomes into a high-level design for the core clearing and messaging infrastructure. Next Spring the Blueprint will be handed over to the industry led Delivery Company to deliver the new infrastructure.

We took an important step towards this in June this year when the RPIB issued a public consultation inviting respondents to help shape the design of the new infrastructure. The consultation asked what payment journeys the infrastructure should support; the principles and characteristics that should guide its design; and the role of the core infrastructure as a platform for innovation across the wider payments ecosystem.

Today, I want to explain what we heard, how that feedback is helping us on our journey from vision to design, and the next steps.

Respondents

First, I would like to say an enormous thank you to everyone who contributed to the consultation. I was really encouraged by the diversity of organisations responding and by the insightful feedback in the 121 responses. We received responses from: financial institutions, payment firms, technology firms, merchants, consumers as well as trade bodies, consultants and individuals. This feedback has been supplemented by a variety of roundtables, forums and discussions, with the high level of engagement underlining how important payments are to so many players.

Feedback demonstrated broad support for the direction of travel, and for moving at pace. Respondents saw the payment journeys, design principles and conceptual architecture as a strong basis for the next stage.

Of course, broad support does not mean that every detail has been agreed and every question has been answered. Important choices remain: where the boundary of the core should sit, how interoperability should work in practice, and how migration should be managed safely. But we have strong buy-in for the overall destination and we know the big questions that need to be addressed.

From feedback to design

I cannot do justice to all of the feedback this morning - there is far more detail in our published consultation response - but I would like to focus on a few of the key points that will be front of my mind as we move into the co-creation phase.

There was strong support for the proposed payment journeys: both the existing journeys and the new and emerging journeys including A2A at point of sale, payments between different forms of money, instant payments using aliases, advanced delegated payments, programmable and deferred payments. This endorsement was very good news, as ultimately payments need to meet users’ needs. And importantly the new infrastructure will enable not just different types of payments but also different types of money, with a core infrastructure that can support many different products. I sometimes refer to this as being able to plug and play products, be they faster payments, stablecoins, programmable payments and much more, into an infrastructure that supports future developments such as those being discussed at the Festival today.

Interoperability between these different forms of money, allowing a payer to initiate a payment in one form of money and a payee to receive it in another form of money frictionlessly and at par, was welcomed. This will be a crucial feature of the new infrastructure and will greatly enhance choice for consumers and scope for Fintechs to develop new solutions.

An ecosystem that prevents fraud and financial crime was a priority for respondents. While some features will be included in layers above the core, it is essential that the new infrastructure can support and enable effective controls across the ecosystem. They need to be designed in from the start.

Respondents were supportive of a ‘layered’ architecture footnote[2] for the wider payments ecosystem where the core infrastructure can act as a platform for innovation. They also welcomed the proposed modular and extensible approach, footnote[3] designed around common capabilities, rather than around each product in isolation. This should support existing payment journeys and provide a foundation to enable new products and forms of money to be included in the future. And extensibility will be key as the new infrastructure will need to be able to scale as payment volumes grow.

As we reflect on these responses, we will be considering that there was a preference for a relatively thin core, footnote[4] that is the element that will be common to all products. However, there was a range of views as to precisely how thin the core should be, and where certain capabilities should sit. Respondents placed varying levels of emphasis on the role shared services and common capabilities should play, and whether these should sit within the core.

There was little disagreement though on the crucial importance of security, resilience and cyber security, in particular, in the context of AI and developments in frontier technologies. Respondents emphasised secure, resilient, and adaptable infrastructure, with sufficient flexibility to support future requirements. We envisage a system that will be designed to exacting levels of operational resilience. And the core infrastructure will connect to the Bank’s RTGS service for settlement in central bank money, supporting confidence and financial stability by providing a safe and final means of settlement.

Respondents highlighted common messaging, interfaces and technical standards as important foundations for the new infrastructure. And these, together with ISO20022 messaging, a consistent implementation of standards, and strong governance would be important to support interoperability in its broadest sense.

There were many comments emphasising the importance of a smooth and safe transition to the next generation infrastructure. Planning the transition will be crucial and will need to draw on the input from many players, but it can only be planned once we have a clearer idea of what is being built and hence what is being transitioned to.

The core infrastructure is only part of the ecosystem

The next-generation infrastructure will be a critical layer of the UK retail payments ecosystem. But it is only one layer. It cannot deliver successful payment journeys on its own. Product and scheme arrangements, payment services providers, consumer protection, liability, merchant acceptance, commercial incentives, financial inclusion and access will all need to develop alongside the core. For the core we need to ensure that it can enable what is needed in the product layers that sit above it. And there is also a strong complementary role for the payments industry and financial institutions to leverage the core infrastructure to develop their product offerings to provide open, transparent and accessible payments. This an exciting opportunity to innovate, for all types of customers including the most vulnerable.

The PVDC set out its thinking on this wider picture in its July 2026 update on Roles and Responsibilities in the future Retail Payments EcosystemOpens in a new window . It is important now that the industry maintains momentum and stays focused, with Pay.UK continuing its vital role as Payment System Operator of the current systems, and the Delivery Company preparing to take forward the Blueprint for the next generation infrastructure.

What happens next

The valuable consultation responses, combined with insightful feedback from wider engagement, provide a strong foundation from which to develop the Blueprint for the next-generation infrastructure. This will set out the high-level design proposals to enable the Delivery Company to take forward the detailed design and delivery of the core.

We are now entering a period of co-creation, bringing together public and private sector expertise. This will enable the golden thread of public policy objectives to run through a design, with industry helping to shape the requirements in a way that will enable them to operate effectively. RPIB, the Design Authority, representatives from the Delivery Company, and industry experts will work together and incorporate feedback from this and our future outreach activities.

The Blueprint will then be handed over to the Delivery Company in Spring 2027, so that they can take forward detailed design, procurement, build and implementation. Ongoing public and private sector engagement will be important in ensuring that the design supports delivery of RPIB’s vision for the new infrastructure and can adapt to the changing technological and demand landscape.

This work does not mean that other innovation should stop and wait. We want it to continue, and we look forward to working with innovators so that it can align with the overall vision.

This is an exciting journey, and we need to keep up momentum. Our destination is a core infrastructure that enables: greater choice, more innovation, and a payments ecosystem that is operationally and financially resilient. The feedback from the consultation has added more detail to our map. And we have a route from high-level design to industry led delivery. I would encourage everyone to move in the same direction together, to point out safe short cuts, and to encourage other passengers to join along the way. The destination is one where we can all thrive.

I would like to thank Katie Britton and Sofia Edrihen Ruiz for helping with the preparation of these remarks.

  1. On 7 November 2025, the PVDC published its strategic outcomes for the future UK retail payments infrastructure, building on the ambitions set out in the government’s National Payments Vision.

  2. Layered models are commonly used to represent complex payment systems and are not specific to this work.

  3. Modular and extensible approach – designing the core infrastructure as a combination of discrete, self-contained components that can be upgraded independently over time, while allowing new functionality and capabilities to be added without requiring fundamental redesign or replacement of the entire core.

  4. Thin core – a core that operates core messaging, clearing, shared services, and settlement coordination services while leaving sufficient room for private sector innovation and competition.

item.title: Policy paper: Joint EU-UK Financial Regulatory Forum - November 2026
item.content:encoded:
The sixth meeting of the Joint EU-UK Financial Regulatory Forum (the Forum) between the European Union (EU) and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (UK) took place in Brussels on 10 November 2026.

The meeting was co-chaired by the Director General of the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union (DG FISMA) and the Director General for Financial Services at HM Treasury (HMT). Participants also attended from the European Central Bank (ECB), the European Supervisory Authorities (EBA, ESMA, EIOPA), the EU Single Resolution Board (SRB), the Bank of England (BoE) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).  

Building on their shared objectives of safeguarding financial stability, ensuring market integrity, and protecting investors and consumers, the EU and the UK reaffirmed the value of a strong and structured dialogue to support cooperation on financial services and regulatory matters. Both sides welcomed recent technical exchanges and reaffirmed their commitment to take forward cooperation on emerging challenges including the green and digital transitions and to reduce burdens for firms on transaction reporting. Beyond the Forum, both sides also noted the importance of continued cooperation in other areas, such as anti-money laundering and sanctions.

The Forum agenda covered six broad themes of mutual interest: (i) the macroeconomic and financial stability outlook; (ii) the policy outlook; (iii) banking and insurance; (iv) digital finance; (v) markets reform; and (vi) sustainable finance.  

Participants exchanged views on the macroeconomic and financial stability outlook. While the EU and UK financial sectors remain resilient, global uncertainty remains elevated. Both sides noted evolving cyber and operational risks including Artificial Intelligence (AI) and emphasised the importance of continued engagement. Participants discussed the 2027 Financial Stability Board (FSB) work programme, and the UK provided an update on planning for its 2027 G20 Presidency. Both parties reaffirmed their commitment to cooperation and dialogue in multilateral fora, welcomed the opportunity to continue that cooperation under the UK’s G20 Presidency, and agreed that maintaining high standards of financial regulation is essential to safeguarding financial stability and market integrity and ensuring an international level playing field

Participants exchanged views on their respective policy priorities to support economic growth and competitiveness while maintaining resilience. The European Commission provided an update on the implementation of the Savings and Investments Union (SIU) strategy, including the Market Integration and Supervision Package. This package is a key pillar of the SIU and the EU’s wider competitiveness agenda, aiming to eliminate barriers to integrated capital markets. The UK provided an update on the implementation of the Financial Services Growth and Competitiveness Strategy and the Financial Services and Markets Bill.

The EU and the UK exchanged views on developments in their respective banking sectors and prudential frameworks. The EU highlighted the adoption, in July 2026, of its Communication on the competitiveness of the EU banking sector, another key pillar of the SIU strategy, and noted the intention to present a legislative package in early 2027. Both sides also reflected on reforms to their respective securitisation frameworks, with the Commission noting the recent political agreement reached between the Parliament and the Council on the review of the EU Securitisation Framework. Both sides also exchanged views on the implementation of Basel standards. They noted the importance of maintaining robust regulatory standards and of preserving banking sector resilience to support economic growth, as well as frameworks that are forward-looking and supportive of innovation and evolution in the financial system.

The parties also exchanged views on the importance of effective cross-border resolution frameworks. Both sides welcomed continued cooperation in international fora, including the FSB, to support the operationalisation of open bank bail-in.

Participants held a discussion on structural shifts in the insurance sector and the appropriate regulatory responses. 

The EU and the UK exchanged views on recent developments in digital innovation in the financial sector including the opportunities and risks associated with AI, stablecoins, cryptoassets and broader tokenisation in financial markets. Participants noted the potential that digital finance has to drive innovation, improve market efficiency and strengthen the competitiveness of the UK and EU economies. Recognising the common policy challenges, both sides committed to continue exchanges on the digital transition including on digital assets. The EU and the UK will also continue to cooperate closely in multilateral fora with a view to supporting digital innovation while addressing risks to financial stability, market integrity and consumer protection.

The EU and the UK welcomed the positive recent exchanges on transaction reporting and consolidated tape and committed to continue engagement to explore opportunities for future cooperation. On accelerated settlement (T+1), while acknowledging that each jurisdiction is following its own independent implementation processes, the EU and UK agreed to continue to maintain close coordination as work progresses towards the implementation date of 11 October 2027.

The European Commission provided an update on efforts to enhance the competitiveness of EU venture capital and growth capital fund managers, including by enabling them to operate more efficiently across the EU single market and achieve greater scale. The UK noted progress on its reforms to its Alternative Investment Fund Managers Regulations (AIFMR). Alongside this, participants discussed their respective workstreams relating to fund reporting frameworks. Moreover, participants exchanged views on ongoing efforts to strengthen Money Market Funds’ (MMFs) resilience and welcomed the close and constructive cooperation between EU and UK authorities in this area. The UK also updated participants on progress regarding the extension of the Temporary Marketing Permissions Regime (TMPR), confirming that there will be no cliff-edge for EU MMFs, as well as on the next steps for their recognition under the Overseas Funds Regime (OFR) to establish a longer-term solution on market access.  

Participants also exchanged views on private markets, including potential vulnerabilities, as well as ongoing work in both jurisdictions to assess risks in market-based finance. Participants recognised the role transparency can play in strengthening market participants and authorities’ ability to monitor vulnerabilities and manage risks in the non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI) sector. Both the EU and UK remain engaged within international fora to promote more analytical work and data sharing on private markets. The European Commission provided an update on ongoing work on private credit markets and the recent call for advice to the ESAs. The Bank of England gave an update on the ongoing system-wide exploratory scenario on private markets. 

Participants recognised the role of sustainable finance in mobilising private investment to support the transition towards more sustainable, competitive and resilient economies. In this context, participants exchanged updates on developments in sustainable finance in their respective jurisdictions and discussed a range of common policy priorities including sustainability disclosures for financial products, sustainability reporting standards, and transition finance. Both sides welcomed positive recent exchanges and committed to continue engagement on the green transition.  The EU and UK also reaffirmed their support for continued dialogue and cooperation on sustainable finance at international levels.

The EU and the UK underlined the importance of continued engagement on issues of common interest, reflecting the interlinkages between the EU and UK financial sectors, and agreed to remain in contact ahead of the next meeting of the Forum.

item.title: Principals And Agents – Speech By Jonathan Hall, Bank Of England, External Member Of The Financial Policy Committee, Given At CFM-Imperial Workshop On Quantitative Finance (Hosted By Deutsche Bank)
item.content:encoded:
In his final speech as an external member of the Financial Policy Committee, Jon Hall considers the growing use of AI agents in finance and the potential implications for financial stability. Drawing on principal-agent theory and the Bank of England’s own institutional framework, he discusses how access controls, monitoring and other safeguards could help manage the risks as AI agents become more capable.

Jonathan Hall

External member of the Financial Policy Committee

Speech

This will be my final speech as a member of the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee (“FPC”). Naturally, that makes me want to reflect on the lessons learned whilst working as a public servant at the Bank. But I also want to look forward and discuss one of the challenges the FPC is likely to face in the years ahead – the growing use of AI agents in finance. 

Fortunately, I can do both, as there is a common denominator: the Bank and an AI agent are both delegates in a principal-agent relationship. The Bank of England provides not only proof that delegating authority to powerful agents is not a new issue, but also a framework for how to ensure an “agent” remains transparent, accountable and subject to appropriate constraints.

Of course, AI adoption also brings new challenges, not least the speed and scale at which agents can act and interact. Some guardrails will need to evolve. But by managing risk through both top-down supervision and bottom-up model control, our regulatory framework should be resilient to the adoption of AI technologies.

My remarks will focus mainly on how to mitigate the risks of misalignment between principal and agent as AI becomes more capable. There is, of course, another possible future in which those capabilities fall significantly short of current expectations. That might bring a different set of financial stability risks, particularly given the degree of optimism reflected in market prices. That is a live market issue but not my focus today.

Click here for full details.

item.title: UK Government Guidance - Money Laundering Advisory Notice - October 2026 - HM Treasury Advisory Notice: Changes To The Financial Action Task Force’s Public Lists
item.content:encoded:
The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 (“the MLRs”) require the UK regulated sector to apply enhanced customer due diligence in relation to countries identified as high-risk jurisdictions by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). This obligation is in addition to the requirement to apply enhanced customer due diligence where there is an assessed high risk of money laundering or terrorist financing, including geographic risk based on credible sources (for example the UK’s National Risk Assessment).

Regulation 33(1)(b) of the MLRs requires regulated businesses (“relevant persons”) to apply enhanced customer due diligence measures and enhanced ongoing monitoring in any business relationships with a person established in a FATF call for action country or in relation to any relevant transaction where either of the parties to the transaction is established in a FATF call for action country, where a FATF call for action country is defined as a country named on the FATF’s list of “High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call to Action”.

For these purposes, regulation 33(3) explains that:

  • a relevant transaction means a transaction in relation to which the relevant person is required to apply customer due diligence measures under regulation 27;
  • being established in a country means:
    • in the case of a legal person, being incorporated in or having its principal place of business in that country, or, in the case of a financial institution or a credit institution, having its principal regulatory authority in that country; and
    • in the case of an individual, being resident in that country, but not merely having been born in that country.

In order to keep abreast of which countries are FATF call for action countries, relevant persons should refer directly to the list published by the FATF of “High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action”. This list is updated three times a year, on the final day of each FATF Plenary meeting, held every February, June and October. The dates of these meetings are published several months in advance, in the events calendar on the FATF website. The FATF lists of countries are updated and published in full, and can be found via the High-risk and other monitored jurisdictions page on the FATF website. Please see below a copy of the current jurisdictions on these lists.

Applying Enhanced Due Diligence on new and existing customers established in high-risk third countries

Regulation 33(1)(b) requires businesses to apply enhanced customer due diligence and enhanced ongoing monitoring in any business relationship with a person established in a FATF call for action country or in relation to any relevant transaction where either of the parties to the transaction is established in a FATF call for action country. This means that relevant persons are obliged to carry out enhanced customer due diligence and enhanced ongoing monitoring on all customers, new and existing, established in FATF call for action countries. Relevant persons should refer to their sector-specific guidance, approved by HM Treasury, for further advice on meeting their obligations under regulation 33.

Group wide controls

Regulation 20(3) requires relevant persons to ensure third-country branches and subsidiaries in countries with weaker AML/CTF requirements than the UK apply measures equivalent to those in the UK. Regulation 33(1)(b) and 20(3) taken together create a requirement for UK relevant persons to ensure any of their branches or subsidiaries based in FATF call for action countries apply measures equivalent to the enhanced customer due diligence measures set out in regulation 33(3A) that the branch or subsidiary would be required to implement were they based in the UK.

When considering what measures are necessary to fulfil these obligations, firms should also consider where customers of branches or subsidiaries have already been subject to measures equivalent to enhanced due diligence as a result of increased geographical risk in line with regulation 33(6)(c).

The Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Regulations 2026

On 30 June 2026, the Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (‘the amendment regulations’) took effect. Regulation 19 of the amendment regulations amended the previous requirement in regulation 33 of the MLRs for enhanced due diligence on “high risk third countries”. Enhanced due diligence and enhanced ongoing monitoring is now only required for business relationships with a person established in a jurisdiction listed by FATF as a High-Risk Jurisdiction subject to a Call for Action or in relation to relevant transactions where either of the parties to the transaction is established in a jurisdiction listed by FATF as one of the High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action.  

Relevant persons continue to be required to take FATF mutual evaluations into account as a relevant geographical risk factor in line with regulation 33(6)(c) and must apply enhanced due diligence and enhanced ongoing monitoring where they identify a high risk of money laundering or terrorist financing.

FATF public statement

On 30 October 2026, the FATF published the most recent update to its lists of jurisdictions identified as having strategic deficiencies in their AML/CTF regimes, of “Jurisdictions Under Increased Monitoring” and “High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action”.

Inclusion on FATF’s list of Jurisdictions Under Increased Monitoring does not, of itself, trigger the requirements in regulation 33(1)(b), but remains relevant to the assessment of geographical risk under regulation 33(6)(c).

Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring

  • Angola
  • Bolivia
  • Bosnia and Herzegovina
  • British Virgin Islands
  • Cameroon
  • Haiti
  • Iraq
  • Kenya
  • Kuwait
  • Lao PDR
  • Lebanon
  • Nepal
  • Papua New Guinea
  • South Sudan
  • Syria
  • Venezuela
  • Vietnam
  • Yemen

High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action

  • Democratic People’s Republic of Korea
  • Iran
  • Myanmar

The following are also subject to financial sanctions measures at the time of publication of this notice, which require firms to take additional measures:

  • Bosnia and Herzegovina
  • Democratic People’s Republic of Korea
  • Haiti
  • Iran
  • Iraq
  • Lebanon
  • Myanmar
  • South Sudan
  • Syria
  • Venezuela
  • Yemen

Details on financial sanctions targets by regime can be found here.

Background Information

1. This advice replaces all previous advisory notices issued by HM Treasury on this subject.

2. The Financial Action Task Force is an inter-governmental body established by the G7 in 1989 and today includes as members 38 jurisdictions and two regional organisations (the European Commission and the Gulf Co-operation Council). It is the global standard setter and monitoring body for anti-money laundering and counter terrorist financing.

3. The Government’s strategy is to use financial tools to deter crime and terrorism, detect it when it happens, and disrupt those responsible and hold them to account for their actions. The FATF is central to the UK’s international objectives within this strategy.

4. The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 require firms to put in place policies and procedures in order to prevent activities related to money laundering and terrorist financing. Regulated businesses are also required to apply enhanced customer due diligence and enhanced ongoing monitoring on a risk-sensitive basis in certain defined situations and in any other case which by its nature can present a higher risk of money laundering or terrorist financing.

5. Other restrictive measures are applicable in the UK in respect of some of the jurisdictions listed in the content of this advisory notice.

6. Further information about what HM Treasury is doing to combat financial crime, and how to subscribe to financial crime alerts.

item.title: CME Group Sets New Volume Record In Lean Hog Futures And Options
item.content:encoded:
CME Group, the world's leading derivatives marketplace, today announced that its Lean Hog futures and options reached a new daily volume record of 209,363 contracts on November 9, 2026, surpassing the previous record of 204,948 contracts traded on November 10, 2025. 

"Steady supply and contracting demand have pushed Lean Hog prices to six-year lows, and market participants are turning to CME Group in record numbers to manage their risk," said John Ricci, Global Head of Agricultural Products at CME Group. In addition, CME Group's Livestock options reached a new daily volume record for options on November 5, 2026, with 136,923 contracts.

item.title: ADI Foundation And The Vault Partner To Strengthen Institutional Custody Technology And Advance Post-Quantum Security On ADI Chain
item.content:encoded:
• The Vault will bring its multi-party computation custody technology to ADI Chain and lead joint research into quantum-resistant security, as tokenized real-world assets reach a record US$32.1 billion globally.

ADI Foundation, the organization behind the institutional blockchain network ADI Chain, and The Vault, an institutional digital asset infrastructure platform, have announced a strategic partnership to strengthen digital asset custody infrastructure and advance research into post-quantum security.

As financial institutions increasingly adopt stablecoins and tokenized real-world assets, technology that secures these assets against both current and emerging threats is becoming a critical requirement. The value of tokenized real-world assets reached a record US$34 billion in September 2026, while the total stablecoin market stood at US$313 billion. The partnership brings together ADI Chain's institutional blockchain infrastructure and The Vault's expertise in digital asset custody technology and advanced cryptography to strengthen the security infrastructure supporting institutional participation in on-chain financial markets.

Under the partnership, The Vault plans to integrate ADI Chain into its institutional custody platform, enabling support for the ADI token and assets issued on the network, including DDSC, the UAE dirham-backed stablecoin. Once implemented, the integration is intended to allow institutions using The Vault's platform to manage supported ADI Chain assets through established security controls, transaction authorization policies and multi-party computation (MPC) technology.

The Vault will also make its custody infrastructure and proprietary MPC technology available to ADI Foundation. Its technology distributes transaction-signing authority across multiple parties, reducing reliance on any single individual or device to authorize asset transfers. The Vault's cryptographic library has undergone independent security review by Halborn.

The partnership will also explore post-quantum security to help protect digital assets against future threats from quantum computing. The Vault will lead research into quantum-resistant signing technology for MPC wallets, building on ML-DSA, a cryptographic standard published by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). ADI Foundation will contribute expertise on integrating these capabilities with ADI Chain, with the goal of strengthening the long-term security of institutional digital assets.

Andrey Lazorenko, CEO of ADI Foundation, said:

“Secure custody is a fundamental requirement for bringing institutional finance on-chain. As stablecoins and tokenized assets become more widely adopted, institutions need confidence that their assets can be securely managed and protected over the long term. Our partnership with The Vault strengthens the infrastructure supporting ADI Chain today, while helping us explore the next generation of security capabilities needed for institutional digital finance.”

Artem Stopnevich, CEO of The Vault, said:

"The UAE has been one of the earliest jurisdictions to put regulated digital money into real use, and networks such as ADI Chain are being built to carry it at institutional scale. As a technology provider, our role is to give institutions robust control over how their digital assets are held, managed and transferred, with the same confidence they place in the traditional financial system, today and in ten years' time. Bringing our MPC custody technology to the ADI ecosystem addresses the first part of that, and our post-quantum research with ADI Foundation is how we intend to prepare for the challenges of the quantum era."

The partnership will also include joint technical research, industry engagement and ecosystem development initiatives to support institutional adoption of ADI Chain.

The organizations plan to establish a joint working group to define the custody integration timeline and post-quantum research roadmap, with further milestones to be announced as the collaboration progresses.

item.title: FSB Recommends Türkiye Further Strengthens Its Regulatory Framework For Crypto-Assets And Stablecoins
item.content:encoded:
• Peer review finds Turkish authorities have made meaningful progress in enhancing the regulation, supervision and oversight of crypto-assets.
  • Further steps are warranted to reinforce Türkiye’s framework and improve alignment with the FSB Global Regulatory Framework for Crypto-asset Activities.
  • The FSB recommends Türkiye operationalises a financial stability monitoring framework, establishes a regime for stablecoins, strengthens supervision and enforcement, and promotes cross-border cooperation and information sharing.

The Financial Stability Board (FSB) today published its second Peer Review of Türkiye, examining the country’s progress in implementing the FSB recommendations for the regulation and supervision of crypto-asset activities, including stablecoins.

Since the publication of the Thematic Review on the FSB Global Regulatory Framework for Crypto-asset Activities in 2025, the Turkish authorities have made meaningful progress in strengthening the regulation, supervision and oversight of crypto-asset markets and activities. Authorities have brought a large part of the crypto-asset market within the regulatory perimeter, introducing registration and licensing requirements for crypto-asset service providers (CASPs). Moreover, structural safeguards, such as strict custody separation, and the prohibition on the use of crypto-assets for domestic payments, limit some of the risk transmission channels into payments and banking.

This regulatory framework allows authorities to better understand the business models of CASPs and the channels through which financial stability risks could arise. Authorities have also operationalised a centralised data platform for monitoring crypto-asset activities.

However, further steps are warranted to reinforce the country’s regulatory framework and improve alignment with the FSB Global Regulatory Framework for Crypto-asset Activities.

Building on these achievements, the FSB recommends that Turkish authorities further enhance crypto-asset and stablecoin regulation and supervision by operationalising a framework for financial stability monitoring, establishing a dedicated regime for stablecoins, strengthening supervision and enforcement, and promoting effective cross-border cooperation and information sharing.

Background

At the G20’s request, the FSB has led international work on the financial stability risks of crypto-assets since 2018. In July 2023, it finalised a global regulatory framework made up of two sets of recommendations: one for crypto-asset activities and markets, and a revised one for global stablecoin arrangements. The FSB’s 2025 thematic peer review found welcome progress in putting the framework into practice, but also highlighted significant gaps and inconsistencies across jurisdictions, and called on them to prioritise full and consistent implementation.

FSB member jurisdictions have committed to undergo periodic peer reviews to evaluate their adherence to international financial standards. To fulfil this responsibility, the FSB has established a regular programme of country and thematic peer reviews of its member jurisdictions. As part of this commitment, Türkiye volunteered to undergo a peer review in 2026. A schedule of country peer reviews, as well as all completed peer review reports, are available on the FSB website.

The FSB coordinates at the international level the work of national financial authorities and international standard-setting bodies and develops and promotes the implementation of effective regulatory, supervisory, and other financial sector policies in the interest of financial stability. It brings together national authorities responsible for financial stability in 24 countries and jurisdictions, international financial institutions, sector-specific international groupings of regulators and supervisors, and committees of central bank experts. The FSB also conducts outreach with approximately 70 other jurisdictions through its six Regional Consultative Groups.

The FSB is chaired by Andrew Bailey, Governor of the Bank of England. The FSB Secretariat is located in Basel, Switzerland and hosted by the Bank for International Settlements.

Publication

11 November 2026

Peer Review of Türkiye

Peer review assesses Türkiye’s progress in implementing the FSB recommendations for the regulation and supervision of crypto-asset activities, including stablecoins.

item.title: This Morning, Representatives Of The Hedge Fund Association (IHFA) Opened Trading On The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange
item.content:encoded:
This morning (November 11, 2026), the CEO and board members of the Israel Hedge Fund Association (IHFA) opened trading on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange (TASE) in a opening  bell ceremony marking the the Association's 13th Annual International Conference.

More than 100 hedge fund managers from Israel and abroad attended the ceremony, including CEOs and founders of some of the largest and most influential hedge funds in the world. Their participation reflects the importance of the linkage between the Israeli investment industry and the international financial community. Alongside senior industry figures, new immigrants from the investment field who chose to join the Israeli industry also took part.

The ceremony was accompanied by Agam Berger, a former hostage in captivity, playing the violin in a moving moment that carried a message of unity, hope and faith in a better future.

After the ceremony, the 13th Annual International Conference of the Association opened at the TASE conference center, with hundreds of representatives from the hedge fund industry and from the Israeli and international capital markets. Participants included managers of local and international hedge funds, institutional investors from Israel and abroad, representatives of multi-family offices, law and accounting firms, local and foreign banks, investment houses, trustees, administrators and other professionals in the industry.

The conference was opened by Bank of Israel Governor Prof. Amir Yaron, with a lecture on "The Israeli Economy – Challenges and Opportunities".

Natalie Raz, CEO of the Israel Hedge Fund Association, said: "The hedge fund industry in Israel continues to develop, innovate and create value, even in a complex economic and security reality. Today, about 260 hedge funds operate in Israel, managing together about NIS 65 billion. The industry relies on professional human capital, knowledge and experience, and is an important part of the development of the Israeli capital market.

We see great importance in deepening ties and cooperation with the global hedge fund industry. The participation at the conference of managers of leading funds from around the world, alongside professionals who chose to immigrate to Israel and join the local industry, reflects the growing connection between Israel and the world's investment centers, and the confidence in the ability of the Israeli hedge fund industry to continue to develop, renew itself and grow.

Hedge funds bring to the capital market expertise, managerial flexibility and diverse investment strategies. They contribute to the development of an advanced capital market, to encouraging innovation and to job creation. I believe that the continued development of the industry is of great importance for strengthening the Israeli capital market and expanding financial activity in Israel.

We are proud of the Israeli hedge fund industry and of the people who lead it. We will continue to work in cooperation with the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange and with all parties in the capital market to advance initiatives that will strengthen the industry and contribute to the growth and resilience of the Israeli economy."

Ittai Ben Zeev, TASE : "The current period requires, more than ever, deepening the cooperation between TASE and the hedge fund industry. The funds are key partners in developing the Israeli capital market and connecting it to international markets, thanks to the expertise, diverse investment strategies and connections they bring with them. Over the past year, the TASE has become more attractive to international investors, among other things following the successful transition to trading Monday through Friday, in line with the standard accepted in global markets. Deepening the relationship with hedge funds in Israel and abroad is an essential part of expanding the participation of international investors in the local capital market, broadening the investor base and deepening liquidity. We view the hedge fund industry as a long-term partner, and we will continue to work together to strengthen the Israeli capital market and deepen its connection to international markets."

In the photo: Natalie Raz, CEO of the Israel Hedge FundAssociation; Max Krapel and Lior Segev, representing the Association's board members; Agam Berger, a former hostage in captivity; Ittai Ben Zeev, CEO of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, and members of the Association's board.

Credit: Erez Uzir, free of charge.

item.title: Western Exchanges Surge As Emerging Market Venues Slump In October: FTSE Mondo Visione Index
item.content:encoded:
Global exchange stocks split sharply in October 2026, with performance determined by geographic footprint and asset specialisation, according to the FTSE Mondo Visione Exchanges Index.

Western exchanges lead

  • Cboe Global Markets topped the sector with a 21.9% return in USD terms. 
  • It was followed by:- London Stock Exchange Group: +17.4%
  • MX Group: +16.9%
  • CME Group: +15.7%
  • Nasdaq: +15.5%

Investors favoured platforms with strong derivatives clearing businesses and recurring data subscription income.

Emerging markets and Asia lag

  • Brazil's B3 SA was the weakest performer, down 30.2%. Others posted steep falls:
  • Boursa Kuwait: -10.8%
  • Singapore Exchange: -10.1%
  • Dubai Financial Market: -9.4%

Shifting institutional capital flows and weaker local currencies hit venues that rely mainly on cash-equity trading.

Index performance

The FTSE Mondo Visione Index closed October at 104,360.3 points, up 8.7% from its September close of 95,998.56. It set a closing all-time high of 105,656.17 on 30 October 2026.

Top five exchanges by market capitalisation, end of October

Exchange

Market Cap (USD bn)
CME Group 109.84
Intercontinental Exchange   95.49 
Deutsche Boerse    65.15
London Stock Exchange Group    62.13
Nasdaq    59.38

 

Comment

Herbie Skeete, Managing Director of Mondo Visione and Co-founder of the Index, said: "October saw a brutal structural split across market infrastructure. Western giants led by Cboe, LSEG and Nasdaq weaponised macro volatility, converting options volume and data models into premium equity value. Conversely, emerging market cash venues suffered severe capital flight, with Brazil's B3 SA shedding almost a third of its value alongside steep slides in Kuwait and Singapore."

item.title: DIP Holding Debuts On DFM As The UAE’s First IPO For 2026
item.content:encoded:
• The IPO attracted strong demand from local, regional and international investors.
  • The offering raised AED 1.9 billion (USD 529 million), implying a market capitalisation of AED 9.7 billion (USD 2.6 billion) at listing, with shares priced at AED 1.12 per share.
  • DIP Holding’s listing brings an established infrastructure-like ground rent and services platform to DFM.

Dubai Financial Market (“DFM”) today welcomed the successful debut of DIP Holding PLC (“DIP Holding” or the “Company”), the owner of Dubai Investments Park (“DIP” or the “Park”). The listing marks the UAE’s first initial public offering (IPO) in 2026, underscoring confidence in the UAE and Dubai’s capital markets and position as a leading global investment hub.

The IPO raised approximately AED 1.9 billion (USD 529 million) through the sale of 1,735,243,300 existing ordinary shares, representing 20% of the Company’s issued share capital, by Dubai Investments PJSC, the sole selling shareholder, which retains an 80% stake following the listing.

The IPO was priced at AED 1.12 per share, implying a market capitalisation of approximately AED 9.7 billion (USD 2.6 billion) at listing and an implied dividend yield of approximately 7.5% based on the Company's expected annualised dividend of AED 725 million in respect of FY2027. The Offering attracted strong demand from local, regional and international investors, with strong coverage across the previously announced price range.

To mark the listing, Khalid bin Kalban, Chairman of DIP Holding and Vice Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Dubai Investments PJSC and Omar AlMesmar, Chief Executive Officer of DIP Holding, rang the market-opening bell at DFM in the presence of His Excellency Helal Al Marri, Chairman of the DFM Board of Directors and Hamed Ali, Chief Executive Officer of DFM and Nasdaq Dubai. They were joined by Board members, senior management and employees from Dubai Investments and DIP Holding, alongside Al Mal Capital, financial adviser to Dubai Investments on the IPO and representatives of the banks, bookrunners, legal advisers and other transaction partners who supported the successful completion of the Offering and listing.

Khalid Jassim Bin Kalban, Chairman of DIP Holding and Vice Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Dubai Investments PJSC, said: “Today is an incredibly proud moment for both DIP Holding and Dubai Investments. The successful completion of this IPO and Dubai Investments’ first partial exit through a public offering, represents an important milestone in the Group’s journey and demonstrates its ability to build, scale and bring to market strong, mature and resilient businesses. The strong appetite that has been seen from a broad mix of investors is a clear endorsement of DIP Holding’s differentiated business model, the quality and stability of the business that has been built over more than 25 years, and the strength of Dubai Investments’ approach to long-term value creation. It is also a powerful vote of confidence in Dubai, its growth story and the continued depth and attractiveness of its capital markets. The Group is grateful to all the new shareholders for the confidence they have placed in DIP Holding and particularly pleased to see Dubai Investments shareholders participate in the offering and continue on this next chapter of the company’s journey.”

Omar AlMesmar, Chief Executive Officer of DIP Holding, said: “Today is a moment of immense pride for everyone at DIP Holding and DIP Holding is incredibly excited to begin this next chapter as a publicly listed company. DIP Holding enters the market from a position of strength, with a differentiated capital-light business model that delivers stable, recurring income, supported by long-term leases and a highly committed tenant base that has invested significantly in the Park over the years. The exceptional performance in the first half of 2026 demonstrates the strength and resilience of the business, and this shows significant opportunities to build on this momentum. With clear and visible growth levers through embedded rental repricing, increasing subleasing fees and the repositioning of plots to higher-value uses, DIP Holding is confident in its ability to deliver sustainable earnings growth and strong cash generation, without the need for significant additional capital investment. DIP Holding is delighted to welcome its new shareholders alongside Dubai Investments and looks forward to rewarding their confidence as it builds on the strong foundations, executes its growth strategy and unlocks the full potential of DIP Holding in the years ahead.”

His Excellency Helal Al Marri, Chairman of the DFM Board of Directors, said: “The debut of DIP Holding, as the UAE’s first initial public offering of 2026, signals renewed conviction among issuers and investors alike in the strength and direction of Dubai’s capital markets, where total market capitalisation on DFM has reached over AED 1 trillion. Guided by the vision of His Highness Sheikh Maktoum bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, First Deputy Ruler of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, we continue to widen access to equity markets for established national companies and to bring new income-generating asset classes within reach of investors. Each new listing strengthens Dubai’s standing as a financial centre of choice for companies seeking international capital.”

Hamed Ali, Chief Executive Officer of DFM and Nasdaq Dubai, added: “The listing of DIP Holding reflects the strength of demand in Dubai markets, with the offering attracting strong interest from local, regional and international investors. It also introduces a distinctive, income-generating profile to DFM, underpinned by long-term leases and a committed tenant base. As we continue to strengthen our market infrastructure and widen the opportunities available to investors, our focus remains on supporting companies well beyond listing day.”

In line with its dividend policy, DIP Holding expects to distribute annualised cash dividends of AED 700 million for FY2026, excluding the AED 100 million pre-IPO dividend distributed in September 2026, followed by AED 725 million for FY2027 and AED 750 million for FY2028. The first post-IPO distribution of AED 350 million, relating to the full second half of 2026, is expected to be paid in April 2027.

The Company’s shares commenced trading today under the ticker symbol “DIP” and ISIN “AEE02089D257”. The listing comes amid a period of increased trading activity and continued institutional participation in Dubai’s capital markets. As of September 2026, total market capitalisation on DFM stood at AED 993 billion. Total traded value increased by 22% year-on-year to AED 162 billion during the first nine months of 2026, while average daily traded value rose by 25% to AED 883 million.

item.title: Deutsche Börse Group Offers 24/7 Global Trading For Tokenized DAX 40 Equities On 360X
item.content:encoded:
• xStocks brings the DAX 40 onchain, opening Germany’s largest listed companies to 24/7 global trading on 360X.
  • Tokenized shares of all 40 DAX constituents arrive as part of an xStocks expansion into UK- and EU-listed equities, building on Payward’s strategic partnership with Deutsche Börse Group.
  • Tokenized versions of SAP (SAPx), Siemens (SIEx), Allianz (ALV.DEx), Deutsche Telekom (DTE.DEx) are available from day one.

Tokenized DAX 40 equities are now available on 360X, an affiliated company of Deutsche Börse Group, alongside Xetra-Gold as an xStock. This opens up onchain distribution for Europe's largest gold security with physical backing. In addition to the recently announced 24/7 trading of DAX 40 equities, it extends distribution to digital-native investors.

xStocks, the tokenized equities framework developed by Payward, has deployed tokenized equities representing every constituent of the DAX 40, Germany’s benchmark stock index. The launch brings onchain the 40 largest blue-chip companies listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange and puts them within reach of investors in more than 110 markets. The exchange is operated under Deutsche Börse Group, Payward’s strategic partner. 

Each xStock is backed 1:1 by the underlying share, held by a regulated custodian, and tradable 24/7 across select venues. Tokenized versions of SAP (SAPx), Siemens (SIEx), Allianz (ALV.DEx), Deutsche Telekom (DTE.DEx) and others are available from day one. For many investors around the world, this expansion is the first practical way to gain exposure to German capital markets. It also gives the companies themselves a new distribution channel into a global pool of onchain investors, whose demand feeds back to the underlying shares.

“German companies have a track record of building innovative products which the whole world relies on, yet there are investors on every continent who have been restricted from investing in these companies,” says Mark Greenberg, Payward’s Chief Commercial Officer. “Bringing the DAX 40 fully onchain through our work with Deutsche Börse Group breaks that barriers, allowing someone in Southeast Asia or Latin America to finally hold tokenized Siemens or Allianz from the same wallet they already use, and trade whenever they like, including the hours when Frankfurt is asleep.”

“Our partnership with Payward is exactly the kind of collaboration that accelerates the transformation of capital markets,” says Carlo Kölzer, Head of FX and Digital Asset at Deutsche Börse Group and Co-CEO of 360X. “Our vision is to provide a unified hybrid exchange ecosystem – delivering seamless trading on- and off-chain across traditional and tokenized assets, bridging deep centralized liquidity with interoperable settlement.”

Deutsche Börse Group and Payward have partnered on several initiatives since December 2025 as part of a broader agreement to combine regulated infrastructure with crypto-native expertise and deliver frictionless institutional access. xStocks already trade on 360X, the Deutsche Börse-backed venue regulated under the EU’s DLT Pilot Regime since February 2026.

xStocks launched in June 2025, initially as tokenized representations of U.S. stocks and ETFs, proving that permissionless, onchain and 24/7 markets could unlock global distribution channels for assets to be held, transacted and deployed across DeFi from anywhere in the world. The framework has since grown to span more than 1,300 xStocks, representing tokenized stocks, ETFs and early access to IPOs, the widest range of assets offered by any tokenized equities framework. It has also grown to include more than US$1 billion in assets under management, with more than US$45 billion of total transaction volume and more than 500,000 unique holders worldwide.

item.title: Sharegain’s Keren Halperin Re-Elected To ISLA Board
item.content:encoded:
Sharegain, the global leader in securities lending for retail-facing financial institutions, today announced that Deputy CEO Keren Halperin  has been re-elected to the Board of Directors of the International Securities Lending Association (ISLA) for a second consecutive term.

For over 20 years, Keren’s career has been rooted in capital markets, as a trader at a

pioneering algo-trading firm, later as a regulator in the legal department of a major stock exchange, and for the past decade, Deputy CEO of Sharegain. Keren’s re-appointment is a recognition of this unique blend of experience and the broad perspective it has given her on the securities lending market.

The International Securities Lending Association is the leading trade association for the securities financing industry, with 280+ global members based in 35 jurisdictions, including beneficial owners, investors, asset managers, custodians, lenders, prime brokers and service providers, spanning the breadth of the securities financing ecosystem.

ISLA works with its members, global regulators and policy-makers, to drive clarity and best practice in a rapidly evolving landscape. The fifteen Officers and Directors on the ISLA board, who represent a geographically and functionally diverse group of member firms, work closely with ISLA’s senior management team to ensure that its strategy meets the demands of its growing membership and of society more broadly.

Commenting on her re-election, Keren said:

“Securities lending is experiencing exceptional growth, driven by factors including new sources of supply, developing markets and increased retail participation – with digital assets and tokenization reshaping how securities and collateral move. I will continue to champion this growth, bringing the voice of new participants and the next generation of beneficial owners from the neo-brokers and trading platforms I work with every day.

“I am equally committed to nurturing rising talent, advancing an equitable industry, and extending ISLA’s global footprint, so the brightest minds see our sector as the place to build an innovative, human-centric career.

“I would like to thank ISLA’s members for their continued trust. It’s a privilege to serve alongside such a talented and committed Board.”

item.title: Nasdaq Announces End-Of-Month Open Short Interest Positions In Nasdaq Stocks As Of Settlement Date October 30, 2026
item.content:encoded:
At the end of the settlement date of October 30, 2026, short interest in 3,866 Nasdaq Global MarketSM securities totaled 18,363,213,608 shares compared with 18,609,329,855 shares in 3,885 Global Market issues reported for the prior settlement date of October 15, 2026. The October short interest represents 3.23 days compared with 3.49 days for the prior reporting period.

Short interest in 1,662 securities on The Nasdaq Capital MarketSM totaled 4,537,405,688 shares at the end of the settlement date of October 30, 2026, compared with 4,547,071,138 shares in 1,659 securities for the previous reporting period. This represents a 1.56 day average daily volume; the previous reporting period’s figure was 1.76.

In summary, short interest in all 5,528 Nasdaq® securities totaled 22,900,619,296 shares at the October 30, 2026 settlement date, compared with 5,544 issues and 23,156,400,993 shares at the end of the previous reporting period. This is 2.66 days average daily volume, compared with an average of 2.93 days for the prior reporting period.

The open short interest positions reported for each Nasdaq security reflect the total number of shares sold short by all broker/dealers regardless of their exchange affiliations. A short sale is generally understood to mean the sale of a security that the seller does not own or any sale that is consummated by the delivery of a security borrowed by or for the account of the seller.

For more information on Nasdaq Short interest positions, including publication dates, visit https://www.nasdaq.com/market-activity/quotes/short-interest or http://www.nasdaqtrader.com/asp/short_interest.asp.
