item.title: Machine-Understandable Data In The Age Of Super Intelligence, Joshua White, Chief Economist And Director, SEC Division Of Economic And Risk Analysis, Washington D.C., Nov. 9, 2026
item.content:encoded:
Good morning and thank you for joining us today. I am Josh White, Director of the Division of Economic and Risk Analysis, or DERA.

Before I begin, let me offer our standard disclaimer on behalf of all of today’s SEC participants. Our remarks are provided in our official capacities as Commission staff but do not necessarily reflect the views of the Commission, the Commissioners, or other members of the staff.

We are here today because something fundamental is changing in how financial information is used in our markets.

Investors have long relied on financial disclosures to make informed decisions: reading filings and studying tables. Increasingly, they also use databases, analytical systems, and superintelligence models to help them access and analyze that information.

However, while tools are changing, the purpose of disclosure remains the same: to provide investors with material information to inform their decisions. And this purpose leads me to the focus of today’s event: How disclosed information is organized, accessed, and used; and where structured formats offer benefits that justify their costs. As you will hear shortly, downloads of the SEC’s structured datasets have increased dramatically over the past year. That is a striking change and one that makes understanding how these data are being used especially important.

It also brings us to the topic at the heart of today’s discussion: making information machine-readable may not be the same as making it machine-understandable. The question is not simply whether a system can extract a number from a filing. It is whether that system can identify what the number represents, interpret it in context, and compare it appropriately.

With that in mind, I would like to frame today’s conversation around three questions.

First, what are the benefits? We want to understand whether and how structured data help investors make faster, better-informed decisions, reduce the cost of analysis, and improve the allocation of capital. We are also interested in how these data can help regulators and economists understand market dynamics, and how advances in superintelligence are changing the ways you use structured and unstructured data.

Second, what are the costs and risks? Reliable data require resources to produce, validate, and use. We want to understand where those costs are greatest and where there are opportunities to reduce them. That includes exploring whether superintelligence can help issuers prepare structured disclosures more efficiently while improving their quality. It also means understanding where the same disclosed information can be used effectively without a structured format, and whether the benefits of structuring it justify the associated costs. We want to hear about the risks that arise when automated systems rely on information that is inaccurate, inconsistent, or missing important context, and how those risks can be addressed.

Third, what is working in practice and what is not? We want to hear concrete examples where structured disclosed information is most useful, where it adds less value, and why. That includes your experience with financial statement disclosures and other types of structured information. We also welcome your perspectives on the quality and usability of these data, and on what changes, if any, the SEC should consider.

As analytical tools become more capable, our focus should remain on the investors those tools serve. Reliable information and the context needed to interpret it remain essential.

Our goal today is to better understand when structuring disclosed information makes it more useful, and how to achieve those benefits efficiently.

Thus, the central question before us is how structured formats can best support the use of disclosed financial information, with careful attention to both benefits and costs. Your experience and insights are essential to answering that question. We want to understand not just what the technology promises, but what it delivers: the benefits you are realizing, the costs you are bearing, and the problems that remain. Those insights will help inform how the SEC approaches the format and usability of disclosed information as technology and market practices evolve.

Thank you for being here and sharing your perspectives. I look forward to the conversation ahead.

item.title: Cboe Expands Prediction Markets Suite To Small-Caps With Launch Of Mini-Russell 2000 Index Binary Options
item.content:encoded:
Cboe Global Markets, Inc. (Cboe: CBOE), a leading global markets operator and pioneer in equity and index derivatives, today announced the launch of mini-Russell 2000 Index (MRUT) binary options (ticker: MRTBW). The binary options based on MRUT, which is 1/10th the size of the Russell 2000 Index, began trading on November 9 and are the latest addition to Cboe's prediction market suite.

MRTBW are yes or no directional trades that pay $100 or $0, depending on whether the MRUT settles at, above or below the specified level. For example, an investor who makes a trade that MRUT will close above 280 will receive $100 at settlement if it closes at 280 or above, while the contract will pay $0 if the index closes below 280. Cboe will list P.M.-settled contracts expiring on the same and next trading day, and MRTBW options offerings are centrally cleared through the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC).

"Small-cap stocks are closely watched by retail investors and can play an important role in a portfolio, and Cboe's new MRUT binary options allow investors to make yes-or-no trades on a leading small-cap index," said JJ Kinahan, Head of Retail Expansion and Alternative Investment Products at Cboe. "The Russell 2000 Index is traditionally more volatile than other broad measures, which is part of why demand for zero-days-to-expiry options tied to the index has grown significantly in recent years. As interest in short-dated exposure grows, Cboe continues to expand its SEC-regulated prediction markets offerings and provide investors with the ability to trade and learn more about market outcomes within the safeguards of the securities markets."

"The Russell 2000 Index is the leading benchmark for the U.S. small-cap equity market, providing investors with a trusted and objective measure of this important market," said Shawn Creighton, Director of Index Derivatives Solutions at FTSE Russell. "Our longstanding partnership with Cboe has been instrumental in expanding access to innovative index-based products, and this latest development builds on that relationship by giving investors more ways to access U.S. small caps and manage risk."

The Russell 2000 Index measures the performance of the small-cap segment of the U.S. equity market. The index includes approximately 2,000 of the smallest companies based on a combination of their market capitalization and current index membership. The Russell 2000 Index is a subset of the Russell 3000 Index, which is designed to represent approximately 98% of the investible U.S. equity market. Cboe has seen record demand in its traditional Russell 2000 Index (RUT) options suite, with average daily volume of 85 thousand contracts through the first three quarters.   

With the launch of MRUT binary options, Cboe's prediction markets suite now includes the ability to trade outcomes tied to small-cap and large-cap (S&P 500 Index) equities and will soon include certain SEC-regulated corporate earnings metrics. Cboe's prediction markets offerings are available through select retail brokers and leverage the protections of the U.S. registered securities trading environment.

To learn more about Cboe's offerings, visit Cboe Prediction Markets.

item.title: ICE Mortgage Monitor: 2.4 Million Mortgage Holders Are Equity Millionaires As Q3 Home Equity Hits Record High - Servicer Retention Declined In Q3, With Cash-Out Refinances Accounting For 75% Of Refinance Portfolio Attrition
item.content:encoded:
Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (NYSE: ICE), one of the world’s leading providers of financial market technology and data powering global capital markets, today released the November 2026 ICE Mortgage Monitor Report. The analysis finds that home equity and the number of equity millionaires both reached record third-quarter highs, creating opportunities for lenders and servicers to engage borrowers seeking access to that wealth.

“Homeowners are sitting on substantial housing wealth, with 2.4 million mortgage holders now holding at least $1 million in equity,” said Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at ICE. “In a higher rate environment, cash-outs are making up a greater share of refinances, with those homeowners giving up historically low mortgage rates and taking on higher monthly payments to tap into their equity.”

Key findings from the November ICE Mortgage Monitor include:

  • Home equity reached a record third-quarter high
    Mortgage holders collectively held $17.5 trillion in equity in Q3, up 1.4% year over year. Tappable equity that can be accessed while maintaining a 20% cushion rose 1.2% to an average of $204,000 per borrower, an increase of $16,600 from a year ago.
  • The number of equity millionaires reached a Q3 record
    2.4 million mortgage holders had at least $1 million in equity, up 6% year over year, while nearly 9 million held $500,000 or more, up 4%. California accounted for 49% of the nation’s equity millionaires, followed by New York (189,000), New Jersey (141,000) and Florida (104,000).
  • Rising rates drove increased share of cash-out refinances
    Cash-out transactions accounted for 1 in 7 rate locks in recent weeks, and purchase loans accounted for roughly 80% of rate locks.
  • ARMs remained popular due to higher rates and more attractive spreads
    Adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) accounted for more than 10% of early October rate locks as 30-year fixed rates moved above 7%. The points-adjusted spread between 5/1 ARMs and 30-year fixed loans widened from roughly 75 basis points over the summer to more than 100 basis points in early October, further increasing the attractiveness of ARMs.
  • Refinance retention declined as cash-out activity grew
    Servicers retained 27% of refinancing borrowers, down four percentage points from the prior quarter, while retention among rate-and-term refinancers fell nine percentage points to 30%. Cash-out retention held at 26%, with servicers retaining just 15% of cash-out borrowers who took out loans in 2019 or earlier. Cash-out refinances accounted for 75% of all refinance-portfolio attrition.

“Traditional rate-based retention strategies aren’t effective for borrowers who are motivated by access to equity rather than interest rate savings,” said Bob Hart, President of Mortgage Technology at ICE. “To retain these borrowers, servicers need better visibility into their equity positions and the ability to engage them before they look elsewhere. By combining ICE’s retention analytics with connected technologies like MSP, Servicing Digital and Encompass, we’re helping lenders and servicers identify opportunities, connect borrowers with financing options and keep those relationships intact.”

Further detail on home equity, servicer retention, home price, and mortgage performance trends — including charts — can be found in the full ICE Mortgage Monitor report at https://mortgagetech.ice.com/resources/data-reports.

item.title: Tradeweb Collaborates With BNY To Expand ICD Portal Investment Options - New Integration With BNY’s LiquidityDirect[SM] Platform Will Provide ICD Portal Clients With Greater Choice And Flexibility, Including Support For International Investing Needs
item.content:encoded:
Tradeweb Markets Inc. (Nasdaq: TW), a global leader in electronic trading across asset classes, today announced a strategic collaboration with BNY’s (NYSE: BNY) LiquidityDirect to expand investment options available through Tradeweb ICD Portal (“ICD Portal”), a multi-fund platform through which Tradeweb’s corporate treasury clients can access and trade money market funds and other short-term investments. The new offering is expected to launch in Q1 2027.

The integration with LiquidityDirect will enable ICD Portal clients to select BNY as a custody and short term investment platform at the individual account level, providing greater flexibility based on their operational requirements, geography and cash management preferences. The offering will provide ICD Portal clients with BNY’s LiquidityDirect-enabled capabilities within their existing ICD Portal workflow, supporting U.S. and international investment needs.

The new offering will be supported by a direct integration between ICD Portal and BNY’s LiquidityDirect platform, designed to streamline management of their short-term investments through a single point of access. Once live, new and existing clients will be able to select BNY when establishing new accounts, enabling firms to diversify their investment options without changing their broader ICD Portal workflow.

Tom Britton, Co-Head of Corporates at Tradeweb said: “Providing clients with more choice across their investment and operational workflows is an important part of how we continue to evolve ICD Portal. By adding BNY LiquidityDirect as an option, we will offer clients greater flexibility in how they structure their accounts, while also expanding the infrastructure available to support our international client base.”

Clint Craft, Head of Liquidity & Margin at BNY said: “We’re pleased to be bringing BNY’s LiquidityDirect platform to Tradeweb ICD Portal clients. By combining our capabilities with Tradeweb’s established client network and workflow, we will be able to provide firms with greater connectivity and support their evolving investment needs across markets globally.”

item.title: Companies Optimistic On International Growth Despite Energy-Driven Cost Pressures, HSBC Survey Finds
item.content:encoded:
• 44% of businesses identify energy as the most significant factor affecting their cost base over the past six months, ahead of tariffs and freight
  • 72% expect their costs to rise further over the next two years
  • 85% of respondents have deployed AI in at least one trade-related function, but 76% have implemented no more than five of the ten AI safeguards
  • 86% remain confident in their ability to grow international trade over the next two years

Amid ongoing trade disruption and tariff uncertainty, energy has emerged as the leading cost pressure facing global firms, according to HSBC’s Global Trade Pulse Survey 2026. The survey captures the views of 10,000 senior business leaders across 26 markets on trade, tariffs, supply chains and technology. 

Energy costs were the highest ranked factor affecting the cost base of businesses over the past six months (44% of respondents), followed by tariffs (43%) and freight (41%). According to the survey, these pressures are expected to persist. Sixty-eight per cent of business leaders say they have already experienced higher overall costs, 72% expect costs to rise further over the next two years, and 59% report higher working capital requirements since 2025. In addition to increased expenditure, uncertainty is also weighing on revenues, with 92% of respondents expecting supply chain delays or disruption to impact their revenues over the next two years.

Businesses are taking practical steps to protect margins and stay competitive. Improving efficiency and productivity is the most common response to rising costs, cited by 53% of business leaders, followed by renegotiating supplier arrangements (43%), absorbing costs into profit margins (38%) and passing costs on to customers (36%).

Businesses are confident and are strengthening resilience despite uncertainty

Despite continued uncertainty, 86% of businesses leaders say they remain confident in their ability to grow international trade over the next two years. The vast majority of firms have or are planning to take action to stay agile and strengthen resilience in response to trade uncertainty and disruption. This includes broadening supplier bases across regions (88%), securing energy supplies (86%), optimising trade routes (86%), and building more self-contained supply chains within key regions or increasing inventories (85% each).

These measures are already delivering results, with 78% of respondents reporting that their supply-chain changes have improved working capital and cash flow.

Businesses are also shifting towards more flexible and digitally enabled operating models. Eighty-one per cent of respondents say they have shifted towards services or digital business models, while 86% have expanded or plan to expand their online sales channels to reach new markets. Nearly half of respondents (44%) regard shifts towards services or digital business models as the most effective response to trade and tariff uncertainty.

Vivek Ramachandran, Head of Global Trade Solutions, HSBC, said: “Energy costs have become a defining consideration for businesses managing international supply chains. Companies are responding by securing energy supply, improving efficiency and building greater flexibility into their operating models.

“These actions reflect a broader shift in how businesses think about resilience. Rather than simply reacting to individual cost pressures, they are redesigning supply chains, trade routes and sources of supply to manage uncertainty over the longer term. The businesses best positioned for growth will be those that combine operational flexibility with disciplined management of liquidity, working capital and risk.”

AI is being adopted at scale in trade

Companies expect AI infrastructure investments to contribute to new sources of demand. According to the survey, 70% of respondents anticipate that AI investments in infrastructure and supporting power infrastructure will increase demand for their products and services over the next two years.

AI is already being used across a range of trade-related activities. More than half of business leaders (55%) say they have deployed it in customer service and sales support, while 50% use AI for strategy and scenario planning. Business leaders of larger companies, with an annual turnover of $2bn or more, say they are particularly focused on strategic applications. Respondents of larger companies (59%) say they use AI for supply-chain monitoring and risk assessment, compared with 47% of respondents of smaller businesses with an annual turnover of $50m–$500m.

However, the survey indicates that AI adoption may be advancing faster than the governance frameworks needed to support it. Although businesses are deploying AI across a range of trade-related functions, they report uneven levels of testing, accountability and formal oversight. The survey finds that 85% of respondents say they have deployed AI in at least one trade-related function, but 76% have implemented no more than five of the 10 AI safeguards1 identified as important for effective governance. For example, only 36% routinely test AI outputs, while just 30% have appointed a Chief AI Officer or an equivalent role.

Companies diversify international networks to stay ahead

Businesses are broadening their international market relationships to manage cost and supply-chain pressures. Across the 26 markets surveyed, Europe is the destination businesses are most likely to turn to, with 48% doing so, up from 40% in HSBC’s previous Trade Pulse Survey2. Southeast Asia follows at 44%, up from 36%, while reliance on North Asia has risen from 32% to 38% over the past year.

Reliance on North America is also increasing, with 38% of businesses reporting greater reliance on the region, up from 32% in the previous survey. At the same time, the proportion reducing their exposure to North America has fallen from 22% to 16% over the past 12 months.

The US is driving much of this shift, with 30% of global businesses planning to increase their reliance on the country, up from 25% in last year’s survey. The trend is particularly pronounced in the automotive sector, where 45% of businesses are increasing their reliance on North America. Meanwhile, interest in Europe is especially strong among technology companies, with 53% of respondents planning to increase their reliance on the region.

item.title: ICE To Launch Wind Futures In Expansion Of Global Energy Markets - ICE’s First Climatic Variable Contracts Cover Wind Generation In Seven European Countries
item.content:encoded:
Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (NYSE: ICE), one of the world’s leading providers of financial market technology and data powering global capital markets, and home to the largest and most liquid markets to trade energy derivatives, today announced it plans to launch wind futures on December 14, 2026, subject to completion of relevant regulatory processes, expanding ICE’s energy markets into climatic variable contracts.

The 15 cash-settled wind futures are based on wind power output indices published by ENWEX GmbH (ENWEX) for Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and the U.K. ENWEX is a provider of weather and renewable energy indices for temperature, wind and solar. The new contracts cover onshore wind (turbines on land), offshore wind (turbines at sea) and the two combined, depending on the country.

Wind supplies a large and growing share of European electricity, and its output changes with the weather. The seven countries covered by the new contracts account for over 70% of Europe’s total installed wind generation capacity. Combined with ICE’s European power futures, the contracts allow wind producers, utilities, suppliers and buyers under power purchase agreements to manage the volume risk of wind generation as well as the price risk of electricity.

“Climatic variable futures are a natural addition to the energy markets we already offer,” said Gordon Bennett, Managing Director, Utility Markets at ICE. “Wind volume is now a significant part of the power sector, and customers want a way to manage it alongside what they already trade with us. Our energy and environmental portfolio allow participants to hedge across commodities, hubs and time periods, and to manage the links between natural gas, power and carbon in one place.”

“Because the amount of wind generated affects how much gas-fired power is needed, wind futures give customers a way to manage exposures that run through all three, with the same trading and clearing relationships they already have with ICE,” continued Bennett.

“As renewable generation grows, managing weather-driven volume risk is increasingly essential, particularly in the expanding market for renewable power purchase agreements,” said Robin Girmes, Managing Director at ENWEX. “We believe transparent, standardized and independently calculated indices are fundamental to making renewable energy generation risks measurable, tradable and hedgeable. We are proud that ICE has chosen ENWEX indices as the foundation for these new wind contracts, a step towards establishing weather risk as an integral part of modern energy markets.”

ICE’s energy markets span benchmark natural gas contracts such as TTF, NBP, Henry Hub and JKM, oil contracts including Brent, Gasoil and Dubai (Platts), and global power futures, alongside environmental markets.

item.title: Settrade Launches “New Streaming” To Transform Trading Experience For Thai Investors
item.content:encoded:
KEY POINTS

  • Settrade launches the new Streaming, rebuilt on new technology and an investor-centric design to meet evolving investment needs.
  • The platform offers a more seamless experience, from stock discovery and analysis to trade execution, with enhanced trading tools and TFEX capabilities.
  • Available now on the App Store and Google Play, with hands-on demonstrations at Streaming Day 2026: SHIFT TO NEW! on November 22. 

Settrade.com Company Limited (Settrade) has launched a new version of Streaming, marking a major step in the development of its platform for Thai investors. Redesigned and rebuilt on new front-end and back-end technology, the platform delivers a more intuitive and seamless trading experience, meets investors’ changing needs, while laying the foundation for future enhancements.

Settrade Managing Director Amatee Prapapant stated, "Streaming has long been a trusted platform among Thai investors. The new Streaming goes beyond a visual redesign, putting investors’ evolving needs at the heart of the experience, making every step easier, from accessing information and analysis to trading. The new Streaming delivers better performance and higher data security standards, and we will continue to develop it further."

Key enhancements include easier stock searches by company name or keyword without requiring stock symbols; consolidated access to market and company information with side-by-side securities comparisons; a redesigned trading interface with estimated costs and profit-and-loss calculations; and enhancements to the derivatives market (TFEX) trading functions, including Take Profit and Stop Loss order settings.

The new Streaming is available for download today on the App Store and Google Play and can be used with a trading account at a participating broker. Investors can use the new and previous versions side by side during the transition period, with the previous version expected to be discontinued by March 2027. For more information, visit www.settrade.com/streaming or call +66 (0) 2009 9999.

Settrade invites investors to experience the new platform at Streaming Day 2026: SHIFT TO NEW! on November 22, 2026, from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. at the Stock Exchange of Thailand, featuring demonstrations and guidance from participating brokers and the Streaming team.

item.title: New WFE Research Finds M&A Accounts For Most Delistings, With Higher Market Liquidity Linked To Fewer Exits
item.content:encoded:
The World Federation of Exchanges (WFE), the global industry association for exchanges and central counterparties (CCPs), today published new research showing that mergers and acquisitions (M&A) account for the majority of companies leaving public markets, and that exchanges with more liquid secondary markets tend to have lower delisting rates. The research also finds that changes in net listings are more closely tied to IPO activity than to delistings.

The research, Public Market Trend: A Global Analysis of Delisting Patterns, by Dr Ishak Demir, Dr Erfan Ghofrani and Dr Ying Liu, analyses listing and delisting activity across 60 exchanges in 55 jurisdictions between 2010 and 2024. It distinguishes between three exit routes: M&A, voluntary delistings, and involuntary delistings. On average, companies leaving via M&A tend to be larger and financially stronger, while involuntary delistings are more common among smaller and financially weaker companies.

Delisting activity has varied considerably over time, with M&A-related exits accounting for most of the changes in overall delisting activity. Involuntary delistings are fewer in number but more volatile, while voluntary delistings have remained relatively limited and stable.

The research also examines the relationship between market conditions and delisting activity. Higher secondary-market liquidity is associated with lower overall delisting rates, suggesting that more liquid markets may help companies remain publicly listed, while involuntary delistings are more prevalent when exchange liquidity is weaker. M&A-related delistings are also associated with stronger market returns and lower volatility. These relationships differ between advanced economies (AEs) and emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs). In AEs, M&A-related exits account for a larger share of delistings and exchange-level trading conditions are more closely linked to delisting rates. In EMDEs, voluntary and involuntary exits account for a larger share of delistings.

The paper also finds that changes in net listings are much more closely tied to changes in IPO activity than to changes in delistings. Stronger market returns and GDP growth are positively associated with net listing, while declines in the number of listed companies often reflect weaker listing conditions, particularly weaker IPO activity, rather than delisting waves alone.

Pedro Gurrola-Perez, Head of Research, WFE, said: “The data show that delisting activity is driven by very different forces. M&A accounts for the majority of exits and tends to involve larger, financially stronger companies, while involuntary delistings are more concentrated among smaller and weaker companies. The relationship between liquidity and delisting rates also highlights the importance of well-functioning secondary markets to the resilience of public listings.”

Nandini Sukumar, Chief Executive Officer, WFE, said: “Efforts to strengthen public markets should not focus only on reducing delistings. Our research shows that changes in net listings are more closely tied to IPO activity than to delistings, so the conditions that attract new listings are at least as important as those affecting companies’ decisions to remain listed.”

  • Read in full: Public Market Trend: A Global Analysis of Delisting Patterns

item.title: AlRayan Bank Selects Monument Technology As Strategic Partner For Landmark Technology Transformation - The Bank’s Largest-Ever Technology Investment Will Transform Core Systems, Operations And Digital Services
item.content:encoded:
The UK’s longest-established Islamic bank is investing in technology to deliver capabilities that will rival many of the UK’s leading challenger banks.

AlRayan Bank, also the UK’s largest and most successful Islamic bank, has signed an agreement with Monument Technology to move onto a modern, cloud-based and modular banking platform.

Monument Technology’s award-winning ‘Bank in a Box’ Banking Platform as a Service (BPaaS) will provide the technology foundation for the Bank’s operations, bringing together best-of-breed capabilities across savings, current accounts, property finance products, customer servicing and digital channels within a single platform, with integration to regulatory and financial reporting.

The programme will help AlRayan Bank deliver enhanced digital services and more seamless customer experiences, while creating a simpler and more flexible technology environment and enabling new products to be launched more quickly.

Monument Technology took the original platform which is used by Monument Bank and is significantly developing it to serve the needs of other financial institutions, already including Ecology Building Society and Castle Trust Bank. Its modular design will give AlRayan Bank the flexibility to benefit from new capabilities and the upgrade or replacement of individual components as technology develops, without being forced to move to another technology provider.

It will be Monument’s first move into Islamic banking, as the sector continues to grow worldwide, with TheCityUK estimating that global Islamic finance assets will reach $10 trillion by 2030, and the UK accounting for 85% of Europe’s Islamic finance market.

Giles Cunningham, CEO of AlRayan Bank said: “This is the most significant technology investment AlRayan Bank has ever made. Start-up challengers have great technology and big banks have great brands. What we have is harder to copy: relationships with our customers built over more than twenty years, and values-based banking that they trust. This partnership will give us the technology to match.

“This agreement isn’t just a technology upgrade. It’s about giving customers the seamless digital banking they expect, and we hope it becomes a case study for how mid-sized, specialist banks can modernise without losing what makes them unique.”

Steve Britain, CEO of Monument Technology, said: “AlRayan Bank has a strong reputation, trusted relationships with its customers and ambitious plans for the future. Working with AlRayan Bank is an important step for Monument Technology, particularly as it takes us into Islamic banking and current accounts for the first time.

“Our approach is to give banks and building societies access to modern banking technology without the cost and complexity of developing and maintaining everything themselves. With three institutions now having selected our platform, we’re seeing growing interest in a model that allows banks to modernise while retaining control over how their businesses develop.”

The platform will be tailored to support the Bank’s Sharia-compliant product offering and operating model. The two organisations will now work together on detailed implementation planning, with the new platform introduced in phases to ensure customers can continue banking as normal while new capabilities and features are rolled out.

item.title: From Risk To Trust: Regulation, Judgment And Responsibility In A Changing World, Panel Chair’s Remarks At The Accounting And Financial Reporting, Council Regional Regulatory Forum 2026, Dr Kelvin Wong, Chairman, Hong Kong Securities And Futures Commission, 9 November 2026
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, everyone.

It is a pleasure to be back at the Accounting and Financial Reporting Council (AFRC) Regional Regulatory Forum, and to chair this first panel on regulating emerging risks, strengthening governance and protecting public trust.

When we speak about a successful financial centre, we naturally refer to the capital it attracts, the listings it hosts, and the products it offers. Those numbers matter. But behind every investment decision lies something more fundamental: financial information that investors can trust, supported by independent, high-quality audits.

Without reliable financial reporting, investors cannot properly distinguish performance from promise, or sustainable value from short-term appearance. Capital may still come, but it will not stay with confidence

item.title: New Zealand Financial Markets Authority Consults On Clearer Regulatory Pathway For NZD Referenced And Backed Payment Stablecoins
item.content:encoded:
The Financial Markets Authority (FMA) – Te Mana Tātai Hokohoko is asking for feedback on a proposed regulatory approach for certain New Zealand dollar referenced and backed stablecoins that are designed to be used for payments rather than investment.

Under the proposal, qualifying stablecoins would no longer be treated as financial products under the Financial Markets Conduct Act, provided they meet specific requirements and safeguards.

FMA General Counsel Liam Mason says the FMA wants to test whether the proposal would provide a clearer and more appropriate regulatory pathway for these products, while supporting innovation and maintaining confidence in New Zealand’s financial markets.

“Stablecoins are generally designed to work more like a payment method than an investment,” Mason says. “We want to test whether the way they are regulated should better reflect how they are designed and used, while making sure appropriate safeguards are in place.”

Stablecoins are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value, usually by being linked to a currency such as the New Zealand dollar. They can be used to make payments and transfer value using digital technology.

The proposed approach would only apply to stablecoins that meet specific requirements. These include being referenced and backed by New Zealand dollars held at a registered bank and being redeemable at face value.

“We want to hear from stablecoin issuers, digital asset businesses, financial institutions, consumers and other interested stakeholders about whether the proposed approach is appropriate and, if so, what safeguards and ongoing requirements should apply,” Mason says.

“No decisions have been made. Feedback will help us understand the benefits, risks and practical implications before we decide on next steps.”

The proposal is intended as an interim step while broader work on the future regulation of digital assets continues.

Related

Consultation: Proposed class designation for New Zealand dollar-referenced and -backed stablecoins

item.title: Tehran Securities Exchange - Pakshoo: Celebrating A Legacy Of Market Excellence
item.content:encoded:
The CEO of Pakshoo Industrial Group rang the opening bell of Tehran Securities Exchange (TSE) on Sunday, 8 November 2026, marking the 13th anniversary of the Group’s listing on Iran’s capital market.

Pakshoo Industrial Group, a pioneering leader in Iran’s detergent, personal care, and cosmetic industry founded in 2013, celebrated its 13th anniversary of listing on Tehran Securities Exchange (TSE) with an official trading bell-ringing ceremony. Since its initial public offering (IPO) on TSE in 2013, Pakshoo under the ticker “PASH”, has consistently demonstrated robust growth, market leadership, and a steadfast commitment to corporate transparency and shareholder value.

During the ceremony, Mr. Hasan Bayati, Pakshoo’s CEO, highlighted the Group’s recent achievements, notably a surge in export volume of over 40% in the first half of the Iranian year compared to the previous period. He emphasized that despite economic challenges and regional instability, the Group maintained 24/7 production cycles to prevent product shortages. Furthermore, Mr. Bayati noted that recent semi-annual financial statements demonstrate improved profitability indices, driven by the company’s commitment to transparency and shareholder engagement.

Over the past 13 years, Pakshoo has expanded its footprint across domestic and international markets through its renowned brands—such as Golrang, Ave, Softlan, Merident, and Home Plus. Driven by its core philosophy that defines product quality as consumer satisfaction, Pakshoo continues to reinforce private-sector dynamism in Iran’s financial and industrial sectors while pursuing sustainable growth and innovation.

Currently, the “Chemicals & By-products” industry on TSE comprises 38 listed companies, with Pakshoo Industrial Group maintaining a prominent position, ranking 10th in terms of market capitalization within this sector.

With the industry’s total market capitalization reaching IRR 55,000 trillion, Pakshoo maintains a significant presence with a market capitalization of IRR 1,150 trillion.

The ceremony concluded with a presentation of a commemorative listing icon to the Group’s leadership by Dr. Mahmoud Goudarzi, CEO of TSE, recognizing Pakshoo’s more than a decade-long contribution to the capital market.

The ceremony, which was accompanied by a media Q&A session, provided an opportunity for closer interaction between listed issuers and capital market participants.

item.title: EEX Group Monthly Volumes – October 2026
item.content:encoded:
EEX Group reports its October monthly volumes with the following developments:

In October, traded volumes on the EEX Group Global Power markets increased by 19% year-on-year (YoY) to 1,464.2 TWh.

  • The European Power Spot markets registered 92.8 TWh, an increase of 18% YoY. Day-Ahead volumes increased by 12% to 64.9 TWh, while Intraday markets grew by 32% to 28.0 TWh.
  • Trading volumes on the European Power Derivatives markets increased by 28% compared to October 2025, reaching 1,043.8 TWh. German Power Futures grew by 26% to 684.6 TWh, while French Power Futures increased by 30% to 173.8 TWh. Strong year-on-year growth was also recorded in Spanish (+68%), Dutch (+59%), Greek (+61%) and CSEE Power Futures markets (+122%). The GB Power Futures market continued the monthly trading volumes growth with over +400% increase YoY.
  • The EEX Nordic Power Futures continued trading volume growth, increasing by 12% YoY and 10% month-on-month. On this market, the EEX System Price Open Interest* has seen a further increase of +36.4% YoY and +7.5% month-on-month. 
  • In October, the recently launched EEX Renewable Energy Futures contracts saw close to 2.5 GWh traded volume, primary across the new French and German TB2 contracts. 
  • The EEX Japanese Power Derivatives market continued to see increasing trading volumes, with a 88% YoY-growth to 28.3 TWh.


 The EEX Group Natural Gas markets registered a total trading volume of 725.3 TWh (+2% YoY). European gas spot volumes increased by 2% to 306.7 TWh, while the European gas derivatives traded volumes rose by 3% to 394.9 TWh. 

  • On the European gas spot markets, the EEX Dutch TTF volumes increased by 19% to 138.9 TWh and the Spanish PVB trading volumes rose significantly YoY once again.
  • On the EEX natural gas derivatives markets, Dutch TTF Gas Futures increased by 14% YoY to 258.7 TWh, while Italian PSV Gas Futures recorded growth of 54% to 15.9 TWh. In addition, the UK NBP Gas Futures market saw a +215% increase in trading volumes YoY.

Trading in Guarantees of Origin increased by 21% to 10.6 TWh in total, including a 36% YoY growth for the GO Futures (5.8 TWh) market. 

On the EEX European environmental markets, a total volume of 77.6 million tonnes of CO₂ was traded. Secondary market options volumes increased by 255% year-on-year to 1.8 million tonnes of CO₂.

Please find the full volume report here

*The Open Interest (OI) is the total number of unsettled derivatives contracts (open positions in futures and options) in a given market, indicating the interest level and liquidity of this market. The calculation of the Open Interest at EEX is considering the proprietary accounts in net terms.

Notes

Please note that EPEX SPOT changed its external reporting methodology in Aug 2026 for their direct reporting purposes. EPEX now reports both buy and sell volumes, while the Group-level reporting only considers one side.

EEX Group builds secure, successful and sustainable commodity markets worldwide – together with its customers. The group offers trading in power, natural gas, environmental products, freight and agriculturals as well as subsequent clearing and registry services, connecting a network of more than 1,000 trading participants. EEX Group consists of European Energy Exchange (EEX), EPEX SPOT, Power Exchange Central Europe (PXE) and Nodal Exchange as well as the software companies KB Tech and Lacima. Clearing is provided by EEX Group’s clearing houses European Commodity Clearing (ECC) and Nodal Clear. EEX Group is part of Deutsche Börse Group. More information: www.eex-group.com

item.title: Statement By The Eurogroup President On The Nominations For The Post Of ECB President
item.content:encoded:
On 29 October, the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde, informed the President of the European Council that she would resign from her position by 7 February 2027. I therefore started the procedure for appointing a successor to the ECB President and asked member states to send their nominations by today, 6 November.

By the deadline, I have received two candidacies:

  • Pablo Hernández de Cos (Spain)
  • Klaas Knot (Netherlands)

At its next meeting on 9 November, the Eurogroup will take stock of these candidacies.

Background

The members of the ECB Executive Board, including its President, are appointed by the European Council, on a recommendation from the Council. The Council acts by reinforced qualified majority of the euro area member states. Such majority requires the support of 72% of euro area member states (i.e. at least 16 of the 21 euro area countries), representing at least 65% of the population of the euro area.

In line with the selection process established in the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, the ECB and the European Parliament will be consulted before a final decision is taken by the European Council.

Appointment of the European Central Bank executive board (background information)

item.title: October 2026 Figures At Eurex
item.content:encoded:
• Interest rate derivatives posted a 42 percent increase in October 2026.
  • OTC Clearing continued to deliver strong growth, with notional outstanding volumes increasing by 31 percent year on year.
  • Eurex Repo maintained its positive momentum, growing by 14 percent in October, driven by a 28 percent increase in GC Pooling.

Eurex – one of the leading European derivatives exchanges and – with Eurex Clearing – one of the leading central counterparties globally – reported a 27 percent year-on-year increase in derivatives trading volume in October 2026, reaching a total of 200 million contracts. Equity derivatives trading volume rose by 4 percent, from 24.2 million contracts in October 2025 to 25.1 million contracts in October 2026. Index derivatives recorded stronger growth, increasing by 15 percent from 53.0 million to 60.7 million contracts. Interest rate derivatives were the strongest growth driver, with trading volume surging by 42 percent to 114.2 million contracts, compared with 80.4 million contracts in the same month of the previous year.

OTC Clearing posted strong growth in October 2026: The notional outstanding volumes rose by 31 percent year on year to EUR 64,589 billion. The swaps product group was the main growth driver, led by overnight index swaps, which surged by 75 percent year on year to EUR 11,550 billion, while interest rate swaps contributed with a 24 percent increase to EUR 25,460 billion. Accordingly, cleared volumes maintained a strong upward trajectory, rising by 123 percent year on year to EUR 532 billion in average daily volume (ADV). Again, overnight index swaps made a significant contribution, rising 158 percent to EUR 97 billion ADV in October 2026, while interest rate swaps rose by 86 percent to EUR 75 billion ADV.

Eurex Repo, Eurex’s leading electronic marketplace for secured funding and financing, also continued its strong momentum in October. Average term-adjusted volumes rose by 14 percent to EUR 534.4 billion driven by the GC Pooling segment, which increased by 28 percent to EUR 294.8 billion.

item.title: The EBA Outlines Next Steps On Supervisory Reporting Simplification And Extends Implementation Timelines Following Consultation Feedback On The ITS
item.content:encoded:
The European Banking Authority (EBA) today outlines the way forward for the finalisation of proposals to simplify EU supervisory reporting, following extensive dialogue with the banking industry and feedback received during the public consultation. The package that is currently being finalised will introduce additional simplification measures, greater proportionality and extended implementation timelines, reducing reporting costs while preserving the information necessary for effective supervision. The final report on the draft Implementing Technical Standards (ITS) on supervisory reporting will be published by the EBA in December 2026.

Key measures to reduce reporting burden

Building on consultation feedback, industry workshops and discussions with the Reporting Contact Group (RCG) of the Joint Bank Reporting Committee (JBRC), the EBA has further refined its proposals to address the main concerns raised by stakeholders and deliver a tangible reduction in reporting requirements.

The final package will include:

  • Further simplification of reporting templates, including greater proportionality, clarified instructions, reduced reporting frequencies and closer alignment with disclosure requirements. Key changes include a reduction of collateral reporting, stress testing, and ESG-related reporting, as well as the removal of selected reporting thresholds;
  • Integration of credit risk and IFRS 9 benchmarking reporting into the supervisory reporting framework, accompanied by a substantial streamlining of IFRS 9 reporting requirements and a stronger focus on consolidated-level reporting;
  • A simplified granular operational risk loss reporting, with streamlined data fields, and clearer reporting instructions;
  • A dedicated stress-testing reporting module, introducing separate remittance timelines and frequencies, while further reducing reporting requirements and eliminating selected data points;
  • Longer implementation timelines, to support an enhanced reporting change management framework, the first reference date for new requirements postponed to December 2027, and selected reporting areas, including liquidity, asset encumbrance, supervisory benchmarking and ESG reporting, deferred until December 2028.
Beyond the simplification of EU reporting requirements

The EBA and national competent authorities are also taking steps to reduce reporting burden beyond the EBA framework.

The EBA Board of Supervisors’ members have committed to reducing overlapping national and supervisory data requests where equivalent information is collected through the EBA reporting framework, acknowledging that supervisors may need access to other data for the performance of their tasks. This will promote greater consistency, reduce duplication and encourage the use of common definitions and concepts across the EU.

The EBA is also advancing with wider initiatives to improve data collection practices across the supervisory system, including:

  • Guidelines on making and designing supervisory and resolution data requests, aimed at improving coordination, reducing duplication and enhancing data sharing between authorities expected to be published by the end of 2026.
  • An EU-wide public repository of supervisory and resolution data requests, expected to become operational in Q1 2027, providing greater transparency and visibility over reporting demands placed on institutions.
  • Further proposals to strengthen reporting change management, which the EBA will present in the first half of 2027.

Next steps

The EBA will publish the final report on the draft ITS package in December 2026 and will submit it to the EU Commission for adoptions. Institutions will benefit from at least a one-year implementation period before the application of the new requirements, with longer implementation periods for selected reporting areas.

To support implementation, in early 2027 the EBA will publish the accompanying technical package, including the data point model, taxonomies and validation rules.

During the transition period, institutions and competent authorities should (1) continue to follow the EBA Opinion on IFRS-18 reporting; (2) to take into account the EBA consideration on the application of the FRTB from 1 January 2027; (3) to report the existing reporting templates for operational risk losses where the data to be reported should include only the data not affected by the new granular operational risk taxonomy; and (4) for supervisory benchmarking reporting for credit risk and IFRS 9 benchmarking the institutions covered by the benchmarking exercise should continue using 2026 ITS on supervisory benchmarking reporting.

Background

On 10 April 2026 the EBA published proposals for the revisions of the European Commission’s Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/3117 (ITS on Supervisory reporting) for the public consultation that ended on 10 July. In parallel, the EBA also consulted on the proposals for the revision of ITS on supervisory benchmarking reporting with a view of integrating the reporting requirements into the ITS on supervisory reporting. Both consultation papers and the consultation feedback is available here CP on the changes to the ITS on supervisory reporting and CP on the changes to ITS on supervisory benchmarking reporting.

item.title: ACER: Is Energy Grids Development Keeping Pace With Europe’s Evolving Needs?
item.content:encoded:
ACER’s 2026 Monitoring Report on energy infrastructure development in Europe examines whether electricity, gas and hydrogen networks are adapting to changing energy needs, and what this means for investment costs, delays and consumer costs.

As renewable generation expands and electricity demand grows (driven by heat pumps, electric vehicles and data centres), electricity grids need to accommodate new connections and shifting generation and consumption patterns. Meanwhile, gas networks must adapt to lower demand, and hydrogen is still at an early stage. Developing the right infrastructure, efficiently and on time, will determine whether Europe can meet its decarbonisation goals and keep energy affordable for households and industry.

What trends did ACER monitoring find?

  • Electricity grid investment is rising fast. Annual investment in electricity transmission nearly tripled, from €10.4 billion in 2019 to €30.5 billion in 2025.

  • Cross-border projects are often delayed. On average, 22% of electricity transmission projects of common interest (PCIs) and mutual interest (PMIs) is delayed each year, mainly due to lengthy permitting procedures. A one-year delay can cost around €4 billion in lost economic welfare. 

  • Electricity grid congestion is costly. Remedial actions taken by transmission system operators (TSOs) to relieve congestion cost European consumers €5.4 billion in 2025, over 25% more than in 2024.

  • Income collected to manage electricity grid congestion is largely set aside for later use. Annual congestion income from day-ahead markets exceeded €9 billion in 2025, seven times the 2019 level. Yet, 60% (about €12.5 billion) of the total available is set aside rather than reinvested in cross-border grids or used to reduce tariffs.

  • Rising electricity network costs weigh on household bills. Electricity network costs for EU households rose by 40% between 2019 and 2025, reaching 84 EUR/MWh. They now account for around 28% of the average electricity bill.

  • Gas networks are adapting to lower demand. Gas investments are broadly stable, while demand remains 16% below its 2017-2021 baseline. Average transmission tariffs increased by 40% between gas years 2020/2021 and 2024/2025.

  • Hydrogen networks are at an early stage. EU electrolyser capacity (used to produce hydrogen with electricity) reached 0.49 GW, well below the 30-58 GW target envisaged for 2030 in national strategies and EU scenarios.

What are ACER’s recommendations?

  • Make better use of existing networks through demand response, market-based congestion management, full implementation of the 70% cross-border capacity requirement, cost-reflective network tariffs and grid-enhancing technologies.

  • Improve infrastructure planning and delivery with transparent, more integrated planning across electricity, gas and hydrogen networks, and simpler, more predictable permitting procedures.

  • Address shortcomings in cost-sharing mechanisms by distributing network costs fairly among users over time and reviewing how costs and benefits of cross-border projects are shared.

Read more

item.title: Broadridge’s Distributed Ledger Repo Processes $7.6 Trillion In October - October 2026 ADV Reaches $345 Billion As Broadridge Continues To Advance Institutional Tokenization Infrastructure
item.content:encoded:
Broadridge (NYSE: BR), global Fintech leader, today announced that its Distributed Ledger Repo (DLR) processed an average of $345 billion in daily repo transactions during October, with volumes totaling $7.6 trillion. The total settled volume reflects the continued scale of tokenized securities financing activity as Broadridge expands its digital asset infrastructure through its recently launched DLX platform.

“DLR has laid the groundwork for the next phase of tokenization, as institutions increasingly shift their focus from exploring initial digital assets use cases to scaling these capabilities across their businesses,” said Horacio Barakat, Global Head of Digital Innovation at Broadridge. “In 2027, we anticipate further integration of tokenized assets into everyday financial market operations, helping institutions unlock efficiencies across the asset lifecycle. Through DLR and our broader DLX platform, we’re focused on making these capabilities more accessible and practical for financial institutions.”

Building on DLR's proven infrastructure and institutional experience, DLX extends Broadridge’s tokenization capabilities beyond securities financing into a broader range of assets and workflows, spanning issuance, trading, settlement, servicing and distribution. Together, DLR and DLX equip financial institutions with the trusted, resilient technology and operational controls needed to integrate tokenized assets into existing market operations, helping bridge traditional and digital markets while reducing complexity.

To learn more about DLR, the world’s largest institutional platform for settling tokenized real assets, visit Broadridge’s DLR.

item.title: Samsung Securities Introduces Six Commodity-Linked ETNs Tracking Solactive Copper, Gold, And Silver Indices
item.content:encoded:
Solactive is pleased to announce its collaboration with Samsung Securities on the launch of six exchange-traded notes (ETNs) tracking Solactive indices covering copper, gold, and silver. Listed on the Korea Exchange (KRX), the ETNs provide exposure to the daily performance of commodity futures-based indices through long and inverse strategies, reflecting different directions of commodity price movements.

Commodity markets play an important role in global financial markets, reflecting developments in industrial demand, monetary policy, and geopolitical conditions. Copper is widely used in infrastructure development, electrification, and renewable energy technologies, while gold has traditionally served as a store of value during periods of economic uncertainty. Silver combines precious metal characteristics with industrial applications, particularly electronics and solar energy. These distinct market drivers highlight the different economic characteristics of the three commodities.

The Solactive Gold, Silver and Copper Leveraged Index families are designed to reflect the performance of their respective underlying commodity futures-based excess return indices, incorporating the US 3-Month T-Bill Investment rate and specified leverage factors. The index families include long and inverse variants, providing rules-based benchmarks for different directions and levels of daily commodity futures exposure.

The indices are calculated intraday based on their respective underlying indices and incorporate daily exposure adjustments to maintain their specified leverage factors. Their total return calculation also accounts for the applicable interest rate component. Due to daily compounding, index performance over periods longer than one day may differ from the stated leverage factor multiplied by the cumulative return of the underlying index.

The six ETNs are scheduled to be listed on 06 November 2026 on the Korea Exchange (KRX), with the following launch details:

ETN NameTickerSolactive Index
Samsung Securities Samsung Gold Futures ETN 151 530151.KS Solactive Gold Total Return 1x Long Leverage
Samsung Securities Samsung Inverse Gold Futures ETN 152 530152.KS Solactive Gold Total Return 1x Short Leverage
Samsung Securities Samsung Silver Futures ETN 153 530153.KS Solactive Silver Total Return 1x Long Leverage
Samsung Securities Samsung Inverse Silver Futures ETN 154 530154.KS Solactive Silver Total Return 1x Short Leverage
Samsung Securities Samsung Copper Futures ETN 155 530155.KS Solactive Copper Total Return 1x Long Leverage
Samsung Securities Samsung Inverse Copper Futures ETN 156 530156.KS Solactive Copper Total Return 1x Short Leverage

 

Timo Pfeiffer, Chief Markets Officer at Solactive, commented: “We are pleased to collaborate with Samsung Securities in expanding the range of commodity-linked financial products in Korea. Copper, gold, and silver reflect distinct economic and market dynamics. Through our rules-based indices, we support Samsung Securities in offering products linked to different directions and levels of commodity futures exposure.”

Samsung Securities, commented: “With these six new ETNs, we aim to broaden the investment choices available to Korean investors by providing access to gold, silver and copper across both upward and downward market movements.”

item.title: SIX Exchange Regulation Concludes Investigation Into ASMALLWORLD AG
item.content:encoded:
SIX Exchange Regulation AG (SER) has imposed a total fine of CHF 40,000 for violations of the rules on financial reporting and on ad hoc publicity.

SER has sanctioned ASMALLWORLD AG with a total fine of CHF 40,000 by way of a sanction notice for violations of the rules on financial reporting and on ad hoc publicity.

ASMALLWORLD AG materially overstated cash flow from operating activities and understated cash flow from investing activities by the same amount in its 2025 annual financial statements due to an error in the cash flow statement. The error had no impact on the Company's cash position at the balance sheet date.

In connection with the dissemination of an ad hoc announcement, ASMALLWORLD AG repeatedly failed to use the e-mail distribution list for interested parties (push system). The announcement in question concerned a change in the Board of Directors.

In both cases, the fault was judged to be negligent. The infringement regarding financial reporting was assessed as moderately severe and that regarding ad hoc publicity as severe. In determining the amount of the fine, SER also considered the impact of the sanction on the listed company concerned.

The sanction notice is not yet legally binding.

item.title: Putting A Premium On Trust: Getting The Basics Right In Insurance - Speech By ASIC Commissioner Alan Kirkland At The Insurance Council Of Australia Annual Conference In Sydney On 6 November 2026
item.content:encoded:
Key points

  • When life is complex and consumers’ household budgets are under pressure, financial products that they depend on for peace of mind need to work efficiently, honestly and fairly.
  • That theme has underpinned ASIC’s recent work in general insurance, which has examined insurers’ pricing promises, claims handling, dispute resolution practices, approaches to cash settlements for home insurance claims and communication of motor vehicle insurance premiums.
  • ASIC has commenced a review into the practices of licensed for-profit third-party claims managers in the home insurance space – and will shortly commence seeking the views of stakeholders on the draft revised General Insurance Code of Practice.

I’d like to begin by acknowledging the Gadigal people of the Eora nation - by paying respects to Elders past and present, and I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the room today.

It’s a pleasure to be here – and to follow on from the Assistant Treasurer [the Hon Dr Daniel Mulino MP, Assistant Treasurer and Minister for Financial Services], who of course takes a close interest in our work on general insurance.

Getting the basics right

When I first spoke at this event in 2024, the effects of the major floods of 2022 were still front of mind. The House of Representatives Standing Committee on Economics inquiry into insurers’ handling of claims arising from those events was coming to a close, and insurers were still working their way through a number of those claims.

Two years on, the industry faces a range of other forces – cost-of-living concerns for consumers, inflationary pressures on supply chains and increased cybersecurity threats, to name a few.

In this increasingly complex context, it is now more important than ever to focus on getting the basics right.

When life is complex, and consumers’ household budgets are under pressure, the financial products that they depend on for peace of mind need to work efficiently, honestly and fairly.

This is a theme that has underpinned ASIC’s work on general insurance across the past three years, as we have examined insurers’ pricing promises, claims handling and dispute resolution practices.

It’s a theme that has continued over this past year, as we have examined insurers’ approaches to cash settlements for home insurance claims and communication of motor vehicle insurance premiums (REP 838).

And it’s a theme that has been reinforced through recent enforcement action. Notably our commencement of proceedings against Auto & General for alleged policy discount misrepresentations[1] and our action against Hollard, resulting in a civil penalty of $2 million, the first ordered against an insurer for breaching its duty of utmost good faith[2].

Cash settlements

When a consumer is offered a cash settlement for a home insurance claim, getting the basics right means being able to understand what is being offered, how it was calculated, and their rights if they are not happy.

This is particularly important given the widespread use of cash settlements.

Around two-thirds [63%] of all claims we reviewed involved a cash component. For Cyclone Jasper, two of five insurers used them in more than 80% of claims.

But the evidence we gathered raised a number of concerns about the way in which they are being used. A key concern is that cash settlements may not always reflect the real cost of repairs.

When we looked specifically at claims relating to Cyclone Jasper, just over half [52%] of the cash settlement offers were based on a single quote, often from an insurer’s preferred supplier.

In one case, when a consumer went to the preferred builder who quoted on the work to see whether they would do the repairs for the quoted amount, they were told that the builder had undercut their costs by 40% for the insurer.

That consumer complained and the insurer increased the offer. But that, in itself, raises concerns about the fairness of some initial offers made by insurers.

We’re also concerned that some consumers aren’t being given enough information to make informed decisions – including about their ability to change their mind after accepting a cash settlement, where policies allow for this.

Motor vehicle insurance premiums

Turning now to motor vehicle insurance premiums.

When an insurer provides a premium quotation or renewal document, getting the basics right means providing clear information that can help a consumer to decide whether it seems fair or whether to shop around. That includes providing some information on the factors behind the quoted premium.

We were keen to review motor vehicle insurers’ practices in this area, given the steep price increases customers have experienced in recent years. In the 12 months to July 2025, premiums rose by 8% – outpacing inflation. This followed growth of more than 42% between 2019 and 2024.

Perhaps not surprisingly, this has been accompanied by a rise in complaints, with motor vehicle insurance the most complained-about product in the internal dispute resolution data, and premiums being the most common reason for complaint.

Despite the clear importance of price to consumers, none of the insurers in ASIC’s review explained the key factors that affected how premiums were calculated in their quote and renewal documents. Nor why they had changed from year to year.

Insurers who charged more for paying by instalments, rather than annually, did not highlight the additional cost in renewal notices.

And five of the insurers in our review did not provide a clear year-on-year comparison of changes to insured value or excess – factors that it is clearly important to understand when assessing a change in price.

This is an area where there is a clear opportunity to do more to get the basics right.

Claims management firms

As we look ahead, everybody in this room will be conscious that we are approaching the season when Australia is particularly exposed to disasters that can lead to more insurance claims.

Unfortunately, this is also a time when so-called ‘disaster chasers’ – a subset of third-party claims managers that target consumers affected by severe weather events – gear up their operations.

With this in mind – and following representations from the ICA and consumer groups – ASIC has commenced a review into the practices of licensed for-profit third-party claims managers in the home insurance space.

We will consider these firms’ sales and client acquisition practices, fee and cancellation arrangements, their role in claims and complaints handling, and commercial relationships with repairers and other suppliers.

We will also examine what distinguishes legitimate claims management services from practices that create or increase risks of consumer harm.

We have already engaged with a range of insurers to inform this review and we look forward to engaging further as this work progresses.

General Insurance Code of Practice

The other key area of work for ASIC in the coming months will of course be our review of the draft revised General Insurance Code of Practice, which was submitted on 22 October.

We acknowledge the significant amount of work that has gone into the development of the revised Code, including through the final stage of consultation led by the ICA over recent months.

I’m pleased to announce that next week ASIC will commence seeking the views of stakeholders on the revised draft. This will involve direct engagement with key stakeholders, as well as inviting written comments.

This will inform further discussions with the ICA about any changes that may be required before a final Code is submitted for formal consideration, which can hopefully occur early in 2027.

This work is a priority for ASIC because we see the Code as an important foundation to my core message today – that in general insurance, getting the basics right is now more important than ever.

Conclusion

Thank you for the opportunity to share these opening remarks. I’m now very pleased to hand over to my peer regulator, Suzanne Smith from APRA.

 

[1] 26-036MR ASIC sues Auto & General alleging policy discount misrepresentations made to millions of consumers in Budget Direct insurance ads | ASIC

[2] 26-236MR Hollard fined $2 million for serious insurance claim delay | ASIC

item.title: Financial Services Agency Of Japan And Climate Data Steering Committee Launch Jurisdictional Data Partnership For The Climate Data Utility
item.content:encoded:
The Financial Services Agency (FSA) and the Climate Data Steering Committee (CDSC) have announced a partnership to promote the use and accessibility of climate-related data disclosed by Japanese companies through the Climate Data Utility (the “Utility”).

As part of its efforts to improve access to climate-related data, the FSA will support the CDSC’s initiative to integrate climate-related data disclosed by Japanese companies through the Electronic Disclosure for Investors’ NETwork (EDINET) into the Utility.

Under this partnership, climate-related data disclosed by Japanese companies through EDINET will become available through the Utility.

For further details, please see the following:

  • Press Release (Original) (Japanese Translation)
(Reference)
  • Overview of the CDSC

    The CDSC was established in June 2022 under the leadership of Emmanuel Macron, President of the French Republic, and Michael Bloomberg, UN Special Envoy on Climate Ambition and Solutions, with the objective of improving access to climate-related data. The FSA participates in the CDSC as a member.

  • Overview of the Utility

    The Utility (formerly the Net-Zero Data Public Utility (NZDPU)) is a global open-data platform that aggregates climate-related data disclosed by companies and facilitates access to and use of such data by market participants.

Related Websites:
  • CDSC Website (https://www.climatedatasc.org/)
